meta.name: The Law Tome
meta.description: Index metadata for every named law, principle, and effect in The Law Tome. Metadata only — the full explanations live on each law's page (see each record's url).
meta.fields: no, slug, name, aliases, category, reliability, statement, coinedYear, namedAfter, sameAs, sources, related (graph edges), url

laws.name: Campbell's Law
laws.statement: The more any quantitative social indicator is used for social decision-making, the more subject it will be to corruption pressures and the more apt it will be to distort and corrupt the social processes it is intended to monitor.

sources.text: Campbell, D.T. (1975). "Assessing the Impact of Planned Social Change." In G.M. Lyons (ed.), Social Research and Public Policies. Hanover, NH: The Public Affairs Center, Dartmouth College. — first publication.

Campbell, D.T. (December 1976). "Assessing the Impact of Planned Social Change." Occasional Paper Series #8, The Evaluation Center, Western Michigan University; reprinted with permission of the Public Affairs Center, Dartmouth College. — carries the law verbatim. (ERIC ED303512)
Campbell, D.T. (1979). "Assessing the impact of planned social change." Evaluation and Program Planning, 2(1), 67–90.
Campbell's law, Wikipedia. — the Atlanta and rankings cases, and the relationship to Goodhart's Law.

laws.name: The Cobra Effect
laws.statement: A reward offered to solve a problem can end up paying people to manufacture it.

sources.text: Siebert, H. (2001). Der Kobra-Effekt. Wie man Irrwege der Wirtschaftspolitik vermeidet. Munich: Deutsche Verlags-Anstalt. ISBN 3-421-05562-9.
Vann, M.G. (2003). "Of Rats, Rice, and Race: The Great Hanoi Rat Massacre, an Episode in French Colonial History." French Colonial History, 4, 191–203.

Davis, L.W. (2008). "The Effect of Driving Restrictions on Air Quality in Mexico City." Journal of Political Economy, 116(1), 38–81. — finds the restriction raised vehicle numbers rather than improving air quality.

"The Cobra Effect: Colonial Misinformation Masquerading as Economic Theory." Friends of Snakes Society (2025). — traces the Delhi cobra story to an 1873 newspaper allegation and finds no supporting documentation.
Perverse incentive, Wikipedia. — the Hanoi rats, Wells Fargo, Fort Benning pig bounty, and Hacktoberfest cases.

laws.name: Conway's Law
laws.statement: Any organization that designs a system (defined broadly) will produce a design whose structure is a copy of the organization's communication structure.

sources.text: Conway, M.E. (1968). "How Do Committees Invent?" Datamation, 14(5), 28–31. Full text hosted by the author.
Conway, M.E. "Conway's Law" — the author's own page, giving his preferred statement and the account of the Harvard Business Review rejection.
MacCormack, A., Baldwin, C. & Rusnak, J. (2012). "Exploring the Duality Between Product and Organizational Architectures: A Test of the 'Mirroring' Hypothesis." Research Policy, 41(8), 1309–1324.
Fowler, M. "Conway's Law." — the Brooks naming, the inverse Conway manoeuvre, and the scope caveats.
Conway's law, Wikipedia.

laws.name: The Dunning–Kruger Effect
laws.statement: The skills you need to do a task well are the same skills you need to know you are doing it badly.

sources.text: Kruger, J. & Dunning, D. (1999). "Unskilled and Unaware of It: How Difficulties in Recognizing One's Own Incompetence Lead to Inflated Self-Assessments." Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 77(6), 1121–1134.
Gignac, G. E. & Zajenkowski, M. (2020) argue much of the effect is a statistical artefact (autocorrelation / regression to the mean).

Dawson, C. & de Meza, D. (2026). "Talking the Talk, Not Walking the Walk: The Coevolution of Overconfidence and Loss Aversion." Psychological Review — on corrected analysis the Dunning–Kruger pattern inverts, with the highest performers the most overconfident.
Dunning–Kruger effect, Wikipedia.

laws.name: Goodhart's Law
laws.statement: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.

sources.text: Goodhart, C.A.E. (1975). "Problems of Monetary Management: the U.K. Experience."
Strathern, M. (1997). "'Improving ratings': audit in the British University system." European Review, 5(3), 305–321.
Manheim, D. & Garrabrant, S. (2018). "Categorizing Variants of Goodhart's Law." Machine Intelligence Research Institute.
Goodhart's law, Wikipedia.

laws.name: Hanlon's Razor
laws.statement: Never attribute to malice that which is adequately explained by stupidity.

sources.text: Bloch, A. (1980). Murphy's Law Book Two: More Reasons Why Things Go Wrong! Price/Stern/Sloan. p. 52. ISBN 0-8431-0674-3. — first known appearance in print.
Heinlein, R.A. (1941). "Logic of Empire." Astounding Science Fiction, March 1941. — contains the antecedent phrasing.
"Never Attribute to Malice That Which Is Adequately Explained by Stupidity." Quote Investigator (2016). — dated timeline from Hume to Hanlon; debunks the Napoleon attribution.
Hanlon's razor, Wikipedia. — attribution uncertainty, the Heinlein antecedent, and Grey's law.

laws.name: Hofstadter's Law
laws.statement: It always takes longer than you expect, even when you take into account Hofstadter's Law.

sources.text: Hofstadter, D.R. (1979). Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid. New York: Basic Books. p. 152.
Hofstadter's law, Wikipedia. — the statement, its chess-estimation origin, and the link to the planning fallacy.
Planning fallacy, Wikipedia. — Kahneman & Tversky (1979); the megaproject overruns; reference-class forecasting as the mitigation.

laws.name: Occam's Razor
laws.statement: Entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity.

sources.text: Ockham, William of. Summa Logicae, part I, ch. 12. — one of Ockham's own statements of the principle.
Baker, A. "Simplicity." Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (rev. 2022). — the syntactic-vs-ontological simplicity distinction and the problem of justifying the razor.
Occam's razor, Wikipedia. — traces the 1639 Punch phrasing and Froidmont's 1649 coinage, the antecedents, Hickam's dictum, and the historical counter-examples.

laws.name: Parkinson's Law
laws.statement: Work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion.

sources.text: Parkinson, C. N. (19 November 1955). "Parkinson's Law." The Economist.
Parkinson, C. N. (1957). Parkinson's Law, or The Pursuit of Progress. John Murray.
Parkinson's law, Wikipedia.

laws.name: The Streisand Effect
laws.statement: Trying to suppress information is often what makes it spread.

sources.text: Masnick, M. (5 January 2005). "Since When Is It Illegal To Just Mention A Trademark Online?" Techdirt. — the post that coined the term.
California Coastal Records Project — Streisand v. Adelman lawsuit page. — primary record of the 2003 suit, its dismissal, and the fee award.
Streisand effect, Wikipedia. — the 2003 suit, the download/visitor figures, and later examples including the AACS key and Trafigura.

laws.name: The Peter Principle
laws.statement: In a hierarchy, every employee tends to rise to his level of incompetence.

sources.text: Peter, L. J. & Hull, R. (1969). The Peter Principle: Why Things Always Go Wrong. William Morrow.
Peter principle, Wikipedia.

laws.name: Brooks's Law
laws.statement: Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later.

sources.text: Brooks, F. P. (1975; anniversary ed. 1995). The Mythical Man-Month: Essays on Software Engineering. Addison-Wesley.
Brooks's law, Wikipedia. — the two mechanisms, the n(n−1)/2 channel count, and the documented exceptions.
The Mythical Man-Month, Wikipedia. — the book, the 50-people-to-1,225-channels example, and the partitionability analogy.

laws.name: Gall's Law
laws.statement: A complex system that works is invariably found to have evolved from a simple system that worked.

sources.text: Gall, J. (1975). General Systemantics: An Essay on How Systems Work, and Especially How They Fail. (both halves of the law at pp. 65 and 71)
Spolsky, J. (6 April 2000). "Things You Should Never Do, Part I." Joel on Software. — the Netscape from-scratch-rewrite cautionary tale.
John Gall (author), Wikipedia. — editions, the exact wording, and the note that 'Gall's Law' is a later label.

laws.name: The Pareto Principle
aliases: The law of the vital few
laws.statement: Roughly 80% of effects come from 20% of causes.

sources.text: Pareto, V. (1896). Cours d'économie politique.
Juran, J. M. (1951). Quality Control Handbook. McGraw-Hill.
Rooney, P. (3 October 2002). "Microsoft's CEO: 80-20 Rule Applies To Bugs, Not Just Features." CRN. — the source of Ballmer's 80/20 and 1%/50% bug figures.
Pareto principle, Wikipedia. — the power-law basis, the numbers-need-not-sum-to-100 point, and the software-bugs and healthcare-cost examples.

laws.name: Sturgeon's Law
laws.statement: Ninety percent of everything is crap.

sources.text: Sturgeon, T. (March 1958). Book column, Venture Science Fiction. — the 'Sturgeon's Revelation' passage with its two corollaries.
Sturgeon's law, Wikipedia. — the Revelation-versus-Law distinction, the 1951/1953/1958 timeline, and the 'crud'/'crap' wording.

laws.name: Murphy's Law
laws.statement: Anything that can go wrong will go wrong.

sources.text: Spark, N. T. (2006). A History of Murphy's Law. Periscope Film.
"The Real-Life Murphy and How 'Murphy's Law' Came to Be." Military.com. — corroborates the MX981 'Gee Whiz' sled, the Murphy team, and Stapp's press-conference popularisation.
Murphy's law, Wikipedia. — origin, contested wording, the 1952 Anne Roe citation, and the Hand/Dawkins selection-bias critiques.

laws.name: Betteridge's Law of Headlines
laws.statement: Any headline that ends in a question mark can be answered by the word no.

sources.text: Betteridge, I. (23 February 2009). 'TechCrunch: Irresponsible journalism.' Technovia. — the post that named the maxim, on Betteridge's own blog.
Marr, A. (2004). My Trade: A Short History of British Journalism. Macmillan. — the earlier 'answer no' formulation.
Betteridge's law of headlines, Wikipedia. — the Last.fm origin headline, the Marr and 'Davis's law' antecedents, and the scholarly studies that qualify it.

laws.name: Dunbar's Number
laws.statement: There is a cognitive limit, about 150, on the number of stable relationships one person can maintain.

sources.text: Dunbar, R.I.M. (1992). "Neocortex size as a constraint on group size in primates." Journal of Human Evolution, 22(6), 469–493.
Lindenfors, P., Wartel, A. & Lind, J. (2021). "'Dunbar's number' deconstructed." Biology Letters, 17(5), 20210158.
Dunbar's number, Wikipedia. — the ~150 figure, the layered structure, the real-world examples, and the replication debate.

laws.name: Godwin's Law
laws.statement: As an online discussion grows longer, the probability of a comparison to Hitler or the Nazis approaches one.

sources.text: Godwin, M. "I created Godwin's Law in 1990, but it wasn't a prediction — it was a warning." R Street Institute. — Godwin's own account of its purpose.
"Godwin of Godwin's Law: 'By All Means, Compare These Shitheads to the Nazis.'" Gizmodo (2017). — the Charlottesville statement.
Godwin's law, Wikipedia. — the 1990 Usenet origin, the Jargon File corollary, and the reductio ad Hitlerum connection.

laws.name: Cunningham's Law
laws.statement: The best way to get the right answer on the internet is not to ask a question; it's to post the wrong answer.

sources.text: "Cunningham's Law." Wikimedia Meta-Wiki. — the canonical wording, the McGeady attribution, and the 2010 origin.
Ward Cunningham, Wikipedia. — documents Cunningham's own disavowal of the law named after him.
Munroe, R. "Duty Calls." xkcd #386. — the 'someone is wrong on the internet' comic.

laws.name: Hyrum's Law
laws.statement: With enough users of an API, every observable behaviour of your system will be depended on by somebody: whatever the contract says.

sources.text: Wright, H. & Winters, T. "Hyrum's Law." hyrumslaw.com. — the canonical statement and attribution.
Winters, T., Manshreck, T. & Wright, H. (eds.) (2020). Software Engineering at Google. O'Reilly. — the source that popularised the law.
Munroe, R. "Workflow." xkcd #1172. — the 'spacebar heating' archetype of a depended-upon side effect.

laws.name: Metcalfe's Law
laws.statement: The value of a network grows with the square of the number of its users.

sources.text: Metcalfe's law, Wikipedia. — the statement, the n(n−1)/2 mechanism, the 1980 device framing, and Gilder's 1993 naming.
Briscoe, B., Odlyzko, A. & Tilly, B. (2006). "Metcalfe's Law Is Wrong." IEEE Spectrum. — the n·log(n) critique and the dot-com-hype argument.
Zhang, X.-Z., Liu, J.-J. & Xu, Z.-W. (2015). "Tencent and Facebook Data Validate Metcalfe's Law." Journal of Computer Science and Technology, 30(2), 246–251.

laws.name: Moore's Law
laws.statement: The number of transistors on a chip roughly doubles every two years.

sources.text: Moore, G.E. (19 April 1965). "Cramming more components onto integrated circuits." Electronics, 38(8), 114 ff.
Moore's law, Wikipedia. — the 1965 original and 1975 revision, the House '18 months' misattribution, Dennard-scaling breakdown, and the recent slowdown.
Computer History Museum. "1965: 'Moore's Law' Predicts the Future of Integrated Circuits."

laws.name: Amara's Law
laws.statement: We overestimate the effect of a technology in the short run and underestimate it in the long run.

sources.text: Roy Amara, Wikipedia. — his role at the Institute for the Future and the 'coined in 1978' attribution (loosely sourced).

"We Tend To Overestimate the Effect of a Technology in the Short Run and Underestimate the Effect in the Long Run." Quote Investigator (2019). — traces the maxim to Licklider (1965) and notes the shaky attribution.
Gartner hype cycle, Wikipedia. — the related curve model and evidence that many technologies never leave the trough.

laws.name: The Lindy Effect
laws.statement: For non-perishable things, the longer something has already lasted, the longer it is likely to last.

sources.text: Lindy effect, Wikipedia. — Goldman's 1964 origin, Mandelbrot's 1982 inversion, Taleb's popularisation, and the non-perishable scope.
Taleb, N.N. (2012). Antifragile: Things That Gain from Disorder. Random House. — the modern statement and the books-in-print example.
Ord, T. (2023). "The Lindy Effect." arXiv:2308.09045. — an academic treatment of its assumptions and the decreasing-hazard mechanism.

laws.name: Chesterton's Fence
laws.statement: Do not tear down a fence until you know why it was put up.

sources.text: Chesterton, G.K. (1929). The Thing, ch. 'The Drift from Domesticity'. — the original fence passage.
The American Chesterton Society. "Taking a Fence Down." — reproduces the passage and cites The Thing (1929).
Wikipedia: Chesterton's fence. — the origin, the JFK-attributed paraphrase, and the principle's modern use.

laws.name: Poe's Law
laws.statement: Without a clear signal of intent, a sincere expression of extremism is indistinguishable from a parody of it.

sources.text: Poe's law, Wikipedia. — the origin, the Schwarz 1983 precedent, the generalisation, and the criticism.
"Poe's Law." Know Your Meme. — the 11 August 2005 thread, the original wording, and the corollary and paradox.
"Poe's Law." Dictionary.com. — the modern definition and the paralinguistic-cue mechanism.

laws.name: Brandolini's Law
laws.statement: The amount of energy needed to refute bullshit is an order of magnitude bigger than that needed to produce it.

sources.text: Brandolini's law, Wikipedia. — the canonical wording, the January 2013 origin, the Berlusconi/Travaglio trigger, and the Swift antecedent.
Gish gallop, Wikipedia. — the debate tactic that operationalises the asymmetry (coined 1994 by Eugenie Scott).
Paul, C. & Matthews, M. (2016). "The Russian 'Firehose of Falsehood' Propaganda Model." RAND Corporation.

laws.name: Postel's Law
laws.statement: Be conservative in what you do; be liberal in what you accept from others.

sources.text: Postel, J. (ed.) (1981). RFC 793: Transmission Control Protocol, §2.10. — the Robustness Principle, verbatim.
Thomson, M. & Schinazi, D. (2023). RFC 9413: Maintaining Robust Protocols. — the IETF reversal (drafted as 'The Harmful Consequences of the Robustness Principle').
Robustness principle, Wikipedia. — the origin, the browser/HTML example, and the modern critique.

laws.name: Sayre's Law
laws.statement: In any dispute, the intensity of feeling is inversely proportional to the value of the issues at stake.

sources.text: Sayre's law, Wikipedia. — the wording, Sayre's biography, the 1973 attribution, and the rival claimants.
"Academic Politics Are So Vicious Because the Stakes Are So Small." Quote Investigator (2013). — the dated attribution history from Samuel Johnson (1765) to Issawi (1973).

laws.name: Kranzberg's First Law
laws.statement: Technology is neither good nor bad; nor is it neutral.

sources.text: Kranzberg, M. (1986). "Technology and History: 'Kranzberg's Laws.'" Technology and Culture, 27(3), 544–560. — the six laws and the DDT example, verbatim.
Melvin Kranzberg, Wikipedia. — biography, the six laws, and his role in founding the history of technology as a field.

laws.name: Wirth's Law
laws.statement: Software gets slower faster than hardware gets faster.

sources.text: Wirth, N. (February 1995). "A Plea for Lean Software." Computer, 28(2), 64–68. IEEE Computer Society.
Wirth's law, Wikipedia. — the statement, the Reiser attribution, and the Gates's/May's/Page's law variants.
Andy and Bill's law, Wikipedia. — 'what Andy giveth, Bill taketh away'.

laws.name: The Gell-Mann Amnesia Effect
laws.statement: You spot a newspaper's errors on subjects you know, then trust it on subjects you don't.

sources.text: Crichton, M. (2002). "Why Speculate?" Talk to the International Leadership Forum, La Jolla; reproduced at Ritholtz, The Big Picture. — the passage coining the effect.
Gell-Mann amnesia effect, Wikipedia (redirects to Michael Crichton). — the effect and its naming.

laws.name: Parkinson's Law of Triviality
laws.statement: The time a committee spends on an item is inversely proportional to the money involved.

sources.text: Parkinson, C.N. (1957). Parkinson's Law, or The Pursuit of Progress, essay 'High Finance, or the Point of Vanishing Interest'. — the reactor / bike-shed / refreshments committee.
Kamp, P.-H. (2 October 1999). "A bike shed (any colour will do)…" FreeBSD mailing list. — the origin of 'bikeshedding'.
Law of triviality, Wikipedia. — Parkinson's 1957 origin, the agenda figures, and Kamp's 1999 popularisation.

laws.name: Segal's Law
laws.statement: A man with a watch knows what time it is. A man with two watches is never sure.

sources.text: Segal's law, Wikipedia. — the wording, the 1930 anonymous origin, the Lee Segall attribution, and the redundancy cross-references.
"A Person With One Watch Knows What Time It Is. A Person With Two Watches Is Never Sure." Quote Investigator (2022). — the 1930 first citation and the debunked Twain/Einstein attributions.

laws.name: Stigler's Law of Eponymy
laws.statement: No scientific discovery is named after its original discoverer.

sources.text: Stigler, S.M. (1980). "Stigler's Law of Eponymy." Transactions of the New York Academy of Sciences, 39, 147–157.
Stigler's law of eponymy, Wikipedia. — the statement, the Merton self-reference, Boyer's law, and the examples.
"IAU members vote to recommend renaming the Hubble law as the Hubble–Lemaître law." IAU (2018). — the Lemaître priority case.

laws.name: Clarke's Three Laws
laws.statement: Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.

sources.text: Clarke, A.C. (1962; rev. 1973). "Hazards of Prophecy: The Failure of Imagination," in Profiles of the Future. — the three laws and the Newcomb/Rutherford examples.
Clarke's three laws, Wikipedia. — the wording, the 1968 Science letter, and the 1973 addition of the Third Law.

laws.name: The Sagan Standard
laws.statement: Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence.

sources.text: Sagan, C. (1980). Cosmos: A Personal Voyage, episode 12. — the phrase's popular source.
"Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence," Wikipedia. — the Sagan/Truzzi/Laplace/Hume lineage and the critique of the undefined 'extraordinary'.
"Extraordinary Claims Require Extraordinary Evidence." Quote Investigator (2021). — the dated history back through Truzzi and Laplace.

laws.name: Russell's Teapot
laws.statement: The burden of proof for an unfalsifiable claim lies with whoever asserts it.

sources.text: Russell, B. (1952). "Is There a God?" — commissioned by Illustrated; first published posthumously in his Collected Papers, vol. 11.
Russell's teapot, Wikipedia. — the verbatim passage, its use, and the disanalogy objections (Garvey, Plantinga).

laws.name: Newton's Flaming Laser Sword
laws.statement: What cannot be settled by experiment is not worth debating.

sources.text: Alder, M. (2004). "Newton's Flaming Laser Sword." Philosophy Now, issue 46. — the essay coining the razor.
Newton's flaming laser sword, Wikipedia. — the statement, the Occam contrast, and the empiricist framing.

laws.name: The Matthew Effect
laws.statement: To those who have, more is given: advantage accumulates and the eminent gain more than their share.

sources.text: Merton, R.K. (1968). "The Matthew Effect in Science." Science, 159(3810), 56–63.
Matthew effect, Wikipedia. — the origin, Zuckerman's contribution, the relative-age and preferential-attachment cases, and the boundary conditions.
Barabási, A.-L. & Albert, R. (1999). "Emergence of Scaling in Random Networks." Science, 286, 509–512. — preferential attachment.

laws.name: The Overton Window
laws.statement: At any moment, only a limited range of policies is politically acceptable to the mainstream.

sources.text: "The Overton Window." Mackinac Center for Public Policy. — the model, its spectrum, and Lehman's 'detect the window' framing.
Overton window, Wikipedia. — the origin, Overton's death, Lehman's naming, and the criticism of the 'shift' strategy.

laws.name: The Dilbert Principle
laws.statement: Companies tend to promote their least-competent employees to management, to limit the damage they can do.

sources.text: Adams, S. (1996). The Dilbert Principle. HarperBusiness. — the book expanding the 1995 Wall Street Journal article.
Dilbert principle, Wikipedia. — the definition, the 1995 origin, and the contrast with the Peter principle.

laws.name: Putt's Law
laws.statement: Technology is dominated by two types of people: those who understand what they do not manage, and those who manage what they do not understand.

sources.text: Putt, A. (1981; rev. 2006). Putt's Law and the Successful Technocrat. Wiley-IEEE Press. — the law and its corollary.
Putt's Law and the Successful Technocrat, Wikipedia. — the pseudonymous author, the negative-selection framing, and the unconfirmed identity.
"Archibald Putt: The Unknown Technocrat Returns." IEEE Spectrum. — on the pseudonym and the 2006 edition.

laws.name: The Iron Law of Oligarchy
laws.statement: Who says organization, says oligarchy.

sources.text: Michels, R. (1911). Political Parties: A Sociological Study of the Oligarchical Tendencies of Modern Democracy.
Iron law of oligarchy, Wikipedia. — the thesis, the SPD case, and the Lipset ITU counterexample.
"Iron law of oligarchy." Encyclopaedia Britannica. — Michels' debt to Mosca, Pareto, and Weber.

laws.name: Benford's Law
laws.statement: In real-world data spanning many orders of magnitude, the leading digit is a 1 about 30% of the time.

sources.text: Newcomb, S. (1881). "Note on the Frequency of Use of the Different Digits in Natural Numbers." American Journal of Mathematics, 4, 39–40.
Benford's law, Wikipedia. — the formula, the scale-invariance mechanism, the Newcomb priority, and the election-forensics caveat.
Deckert, Myagkov & Ordeshook. "Benford's Law and the Detection of Election Fraud." Political Analysis (with Mebane's rebuttal). — why it is unreliable for elections.

laws.name: Littlewood's Law
laws.statement: You can expect a one-in-a-million 'miracle' about once a month.

sources.text: Littlewood, J.E. (1953). A Mathematician's Miscellany. — the one-in-a-million coincidence threshold.
Littlewood's law, Wikipedia. — the statement and the arithmetic.
gwern.net, "The Origin of Littlewood's Law." — the evidence that Dyson (2004), not Littlewood, formulated the monthly-miracle law.

laws.name: Zipf's Law
laws.statement: A word's frequency is inversely proportional to its rank: the second-commonest word appears about half as often as the first.

sources.text: Zipf, G.K. (1949). Human Behavior and the Principle of Least Effort. Addison-Wesley.
Zipf's law, Wikipedia. — the statement, the Brown Corpus figures, the antecedents, and Wentian Li's random-text critique.
Rank–size distribution, Wikipedia. — the city-size (Auerbach) case and where it fails.

laws.name: Regression to the Mean
laws.statement: Extreme measurements tend to be followed by ones closer to the average.

sources.text: Galton, F. (1886). "Regression towards Mediocrity in Hereditary Stature." Journal of the Anthropological Institute, 15, 246–263.
Regression toward the mean, Wikipedia. — the mechanism, the clinical-trial and jinx examples, and the regression fallacy.
Kahneman, D. (2011). Thinking, Fast and Slow, ch. 17. — the flight-instructor anecdote and the intuition it fools.

laws.name: Simpson's Paradox
laws.statement: A trend that appears in every group of data can reverse when the groups are combined.

sources.text: Simpson, E.H. (1951). "The Interpretation of Interaction in Contingency Tables." Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 13(2), 238–241.
Bickel, P., Hammel, E. & O'Connell, J.W. (1975). "Sex Bias in Graduate Admissions: Data from Berkeley." Science, 187(4175), 398–404.
Simpson's paradox, Wikipedia. — the mechanism, the Berkeley/kidney-stone/batting cases, and Pearl's causal resolution.

laws.name: Twyman's Law
laws.statement: Any figure that looks interesting or different is usually wrong.

sources.text: Twyman's law, Wikipedia. — the canonical wording, the base-rate reasoning, and the attribution to Tony Twyman.
Kohavi, R., Tang, D. & Xu, Y. (2020). Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments. Cambridge University Press. — Twyman's law in A/B-testing practice.

laws.name: Berkson's Paradox
laws.statement: Two unrelated traits can look negatively correlated within a group selected on having at least one of them.

sources.text: Berkson, J. (1946). "Limitations of the Application of Fourfold Table Analysis to Hospital Data." Biometrics Bulletin, 2(3), 47–53.
Berkson's paradox, Wikipedia. — the mechanism, the hospital and dating-pool examples, and the link to collider bias.
Downey, A. (2021). "Berkson Goes to College." — the selective-admissions worked example.

laws.name: Cromwell's Rule
laws.statement: Never assign a probability of exactly 0 or 1 to anything that is not logically certain.

sources.text: Lindley, D.V. Making Decisions / Understanding Uncertainty. — where Lindley names and states the rule.
Cromwell's rule, Wikipedia. — the statement, the Bayes-theorem mechanism, the green-cheese illustration, and the Cromwell quote.

laws.name: Gresham's Law
laws.statement: Bad money drives out good.

sources.text: Macleod, H. D. (1858). “The Elements of Political Economy.” London: Longman, Brown, Green, Longmans and Roberts. — the book that NAMED the law after Gresham. Gresham never stated it, and Macleod’s attribution is the source of the name rather than of the idea — which is why this entry is also in the misattributed set.
Gresham's law, Wikipedia. — the statement, Mundell's qualifier, the Macleod naming, and the earlier statements by Copernicus, Oresme, and Aristophanes.
Thiers' law, Wikipedia. — the reverse case under collapsed legal tender.
Coinage Act of 1965, Wikipedia. — the removal of silver and the disappearance of silver coins from US circulation.

laws.name: Say's Law
laws.statement: Producing a good creates the income and means to buy other goods.

sources.text: Say, J.-B. (1803). A Treatise on Political Economy (Traité d'économie politique). — the law of markets.
Say's law, Wikipedia. — the doctrine, the mechanism, and Keynes's critique.
"Supply creates its own demand," Wikipedia. — that the slogan is a paraphrase popularised by Keynes, not Say's own words.

laws.name: The Jevons Paradox
laws.statement: Making a resource more efficient to use can increase, not decrease, how much of it is used.

sources.text: Jevons, W.S. (1865). The Coal Question. — the original observation about coal and steam engines.
Jevons paradox, Wikipedia. — the rebound mechanism, the lighting example, and the debate over backfire.
Khazzoom–Brookes postulate, Wikipedia. — the macro-level version and Saunders's naming.

laws.name: Hotelling's Law
laws.statement: Competitors tend to make their products as similar as possible, clustering in the middle of the market.

sources.text: Hotelling, H. (1929). "Stability in Competition." The Economic Journal, 39(153), 41–57.

laws.statement: Every non-trivial question about what a program does is undecidable.

sources.text: Rice, H. (1953). “Classes of recursively enumerable sets and their decision problems.” Transactions of the American Mathematical Society, vol. 74. — the paper proving the theorem.
Rice's theorem, Wikipedia. — the non-trivial-semantic-property statement, the halting-problem reduction, and the semantic-versus-syntactic distinction.
Rice's theorem, Wolfram MathWorld. — the index-set formulation and the 1953 citation.

laws.name: Shannon's Source Coding Theorem
laws.statement: You cannot losslessly compress data below its entropy.

sources.text: Shannon, C. (1948). “A Mathematical Theory of Communication.” Bell System Technical Journal, vol. 27. — the paper that founded information theory.
Shannon's source coding theorem, Wikipedia. — the entropy limit on lossless compression and the per-symbol bound.
A Mathematical Theory of Communication, Wikipedia. — the 1948 Shannon paper, entropy, and the distinction between source and channel coding.

laws.name: The Four Color Theorem
laws.statement: Any map can be coloured with just four colours so no two neighbours match.

sources.text: Appel, K. & Haken, W. (1977). “Every planar map is four colorable. Part I: Discharging.” Illinois Journal of Mathematics, vol. 21. — Part I of the computer-assisted proof.
Four color theorem, Wikipedia. — the statement, the adjacency definition, the Guthrie/Kempe/Appel-Haken history, and the computer-proof debate.

laws.name: Cantor's Theorem
laws.statement: Some infinities are bigger than others, and there is no biggest.

sources.text: Cantor's theorem, Wikipedia. — the power-set result, its consequences, and the general proof.
Cantor's diagonal argument, Wikipedia. — the 1891 diagonal proof of uncountability and its later reuse.

laws.name: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
laws.statement: Every whole number above one factors into primes in exactly one way.

"Fundamental theorem of arithmetic," Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the unique-factorization statement and Gauss's 1801 proof.

laws.statement: Primes thin out predictably: near a number, about one in its natural-log-many is prime.

sources.text: Prime number theorem, Wikipedia. — the asymptotic statement, the logarithmic integral, the zeta-function connection, and the conjecture-to-proof history.
Prime number theorem, Wolfram MathWorld. — the statement, the Riemann-hypothesis error bound, and the proof history.

laws.name: The Anchoring Effect
laws.statement: The first number you hear drags your estimate toward it, even when it's irrelevant.

sources.text: Anchoring effect, Wikipedia. — the statement, the competing mechanisms, the wheel and multiplication examples, and the replication record.
Tversky & Kahneman, "Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases," Science 185:1124-1131 (1974).

laws.name: The Availability Heuristic
laws.statement: We judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind.

sources.text: Availability heuristic, Wikipedia. — the ease-of-retrieval statement, the letter-K and lethal-events examples, and the ease-versus-content debate.
Tversky & Kahneman, "Availability: A heuristic for judging frequency and probability," Cognitive Psychology 5(2):207-232 (1973).

laws.name: Confirmation Bias
laws.statement: We seek, read, and remember evidence that confirms what we already believe.

sources.text: Confirmation bias, Wikipedia. — the biased search, interpretation, and memory processes, the Wason tasks, and the contested backfire effect.
Mercier & Sperber, "Why do humans reason? Arguments for an argumentative theory," Behavioral and Brain Sciences 34(2):57-74 (2011). — the argumentative reinterpretation.

laws.name: Loss Aversion
laws.statement: Losses hurt more than equivalent gains please.

sources.text: Kahneman, D. & Tversky, A. (1979). “Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk.” Econometrica, vol. 47, p. 263. — the paper introducing prospect theory and the loss-aversion asymmetry.
Loss aversion, Wikipedia. — the losses-loom-larger statement, the roughly twofold ratio, and the Gal-Rucker critique.
Prospect theory, Wikipedia. — the value function, the 1979 and 1992 papers, and the framework's status.

laws.name: The Endowment Effect
laws.statement: We value a thing more once we own it.

sources.text: Endowment effect, Wikipedia. — the ownership-valuation statement, the mug experiments, and the List and Plott-Zeiler critiques.
Kahneman, Knetsch & Thaler, "Experimental Tests of the Endowment Effect and the Coase Theorem," Journal of Political Economy 98(6):1325-1348 (1990).

laws.name: The Mere-Exposure Effect
laws.statement: The more often we encounter something, the more we tend to like it.

Mere-exposure effect, Wikipedia. — the familiarity-liking statement, the fluency mechanism, the subliminal studies, and the inverted-U satiation caveat.
"Mere Exposure Effect," Simply Psychology. — the Zajonc 1968 origin and the word-frequency and mirror-image examples.

laws.name: Cognitive Dissonance
laws.statement: Holding clashing beliefs feels uncomfortable, so we change one to ease the tension.

Festinger & Carlsmith, "Cognitive Consequences of Forced Compliance," Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology 58:203-210 (1959).

laws.name: The Bystander Effect
laws.statement: The more people who witness an emergency, the less likely any one of them helps.

Manning, Levine & Collins, "The Kitty Genovese murder and the social psychology of helping," American Psychologist 62(6):555-562 (2007), PubMed.

laws.name: The Flynn Effect
laws.statement: Measured IQ scores rose steadily across the twentieth century, about three points a decade.

laws.name: The Serial Position Effect
laws.statement: We remember the first and last items on a list best, the middle worst.

sources.text: Ebbinghaus, H. (1913). “Memory: A contribution to experimental psychology.” — the English translation of Ebbinghaus's 1885 Über das Gedächtnis.
Serial-position effect, Wikipedia. — the primacy and recency effects, the two-store mechanism, and the distractor findings.
"Serial Position Effect," Simply Psychology. — the Murdock 1962 curve and the Glanzer and Cunitz 1966 delay dissociation.

laws.name: The Forer Effect
laws.statement: Vague descriptions that fit almost anyone feel uncannily personal.

Barnum effect, Wikipedia. — the vague-description statement, the factors that strengthen it, and the Meehl naming.
"Forer effect," The Skeptic's Dictionary. — Forer's 1949 demonstration, the original sketch, and the accuracy rating.

laws.name: The Law of Truly Large Numbers
laws.statement: With enough chances, even the wildly unlikely is bound to happen.

sources.text: Diaconis, P. & Mosteller, F. (1989). “Methods for Studying Coincidences.” Journal of the American Statistical Association, vol. 84. — the paper naming the law.

Law of Truly Large Numbers, Wolfram MathWorld. — the Diaconis-Mosteller statement and the Littlewood connection.

laws.name: The Inspection Paradox
laws.statement: When you sample by encounter, big things show up more than their share.

sources.text: Friendship paradox, Wikipedia. — the length-biased sampling mechanism, Feld's 1991 result, and the variance-dependent formula.
Downey, "The Inspection Paradox Is Everywhere." — the class-size example and the general phenomenon.

laws.name: The Law of Laplace
laws.statement: In a pressurised sphere or tube, wall tension rises with the radius.

sources.text: Young-Laplace equation, Wikipedia. — the pressure-curvature-tension relation, the Young and Laplace origins, and the sphere and cylinder forms.

Prange, "Laplace's law and the alveolus: a misconception of anatomy and a misapplication of physics," Advances in Physiology Education (2003), PubMed. — the critique of the alveolar-stability account.

laws.name: The All-or-None Law
laws.statement: A nerve or muscle fibre fires at full strength or not at all.

"All-or-none law," Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the principle, Bowditch's cardiac origin, and the dependence on tissue condition.

laws.name: The Hagen-Poiseuille Equation

laws.statement: Flow through a tube depends on the fourth power of its radius.

sources.text: Hagen-Poiseuille equation, Wikipedia. — the fourth-power flow law, the parabolic profile, and the Hagen, Poiseuille, and Stokes history.

Determinants of Resistance to Flow (Poiseuille's Equation), CV Physiology. — the resistance form and the sixteen-fold radius effect.

laws.name: Grimm's Law
laws.statement: The Germanic languages shifted their consonants in a regular chain away from their Indo-European roots.

"Grimm's law," Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the shift, the examples, and the history of its discovery.

laws.name: The Gricean Maxims
laws.statement: Conversation works because we assume each other to be cooperating.

Cooperative principle, Wikipedia. — the principle, the four maxims and their sub-maxims, flouting versus violating, and the relevance-theory critique.
"Implicature," Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — conversational implicature, the reference-letter example, and scalar implicature.

laws.name: The Sapir-Whorf Hypothesis
laws.statement: The language you speak shapes the way you think.

Pullum, "The Great Eskimo Vocabulary Hoax." — the debunking of the many-words-for-snow myth.

laws.name: The McGurk Effect
laws.statement: What you see a mouth doing changes what you hear it say.

MacDonald, "Hearing Lips and Seeing Voices: the Origins and Development of the McGurk Effect," Multisensory Research (2018), PubMed. — the accidental discovery and the effect's history.

laws.name: The Prisoner's Dilemma
laws.statement: Two rational players, each better off betraying, both betray and end up worse than if they had cooperated.

sources.text: "Prisoner's Dilemma," Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the payoff structure, dominance, the Nash equilibrium, and the iterated game.
Prisoner's dilemma, Wikipedia. — the Flood-Dresher origin, Tucker's story, the examples, and Axelrod's tournaments.

laws.name: The Nash Equilibrium
laws.statement: A stable outcome where no player can do better by changing strategy alone.

sources.text: Nash equilibrium, Wikipedia. — the best-response definition, the existence theorem, the examples, and the non-uniqueness and inefficiency caveats.
Nash, "Non-Cooperative Games," Annals of Mathematics 54(2):286-295 (1951). — the existence theorem.

laws.name: The Tragedy of the Commons
laws.statement: Each user, gaining fully but sharing the cost, overuses a shared resource until it is ruined.

sources.text: Hardin, G. (1968). "The Tragedy of the Commons." Science 162(3859), 1243-1248 — the paper that named it, given as a presidential address to the AAAS Pacific Division.
Tragedy of the commons, Wikipedia. — the depletion mechanism, the Hardin 1968 and Lloyd 1833 origins, and Ostrom's refutation of inevitability.
Elinor Ostrom, Wikipedia. — Governing the Commons, the design principles for self-governance, and the 2009 Nobel Prize.

laws.name: The Free-Rider Problem
laws.statement: When you benefit whether or not you pay, you are tempted to let others foot the bill.

sources.text: Olson, M. (1965). “The Logic of Collective Action.” — the book that framed the problem.
"The Free Rider Problem," Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the structure, the non-excludability mechanism, and the solutions.
Free-rider problem, Wikipedia. — the definition, public-goods properties, and the Samuelson and Olson origins.

laws.name: Moral Hazard
laws.statement: Shielded from the consequences, people take more risks than they otherwise would.

sources.text: Moral hazard, Wikipedia. — the definition, the hidden-action mechanism, the insurance origin and Arrow formalisation, and the distinction from adverse selection.
Arrow, "Uncertainty and the Welfare Economics of Medical Care," American Economic Review 53:941-973 (1963), PubMed reprint.

laws.statement: When buyers can't tell good from bad, the bad drives out the good.

laws.name: The Ultimatum Game

Henrich, "Does Culture Matter in Economic Behavior? Ultimatum Game Bargaining among the Machiguenga," American Economic Review 90(4):973-979 (2000).

laws.statement: Start by cooperating, then do whatever the other did last.

Axelrod & Hamilton, "The Evolution of Cooperation," Science 211:1390-1396 (1981), reference record.

laws.name: The Stag Hunt
laws.statement: Both can win big by cooperating, or play safe alone, but only if each trusts the other.

sources.text: Stag hunt, Wikipedia. — the coordination-game structure, the two equilibria, the Rousseau origin, and the contrast with the prisoner's dilemma.
Rousseau, Discourse on the Origin of Inequality (1755), Part 2, marxists.org translation. — the original stag-and-hare parable.

laws.name: The Shapley Value
laws.statement: Give each member of a coalition their average contribution across every order of joining.

sources.text: Shapley value, Wikipedia. — the marginal-contribution definition, the four axioms, the glove game, and the SHAP application.
Lundberg & Lee, "A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions," NeurIPS (2017), arXiv. — the SHAP feature-attribution method.

laws.statement: In a game repeated forever, almost any outcome can be held in place if players are patient enough.

sources.text: Folk theorem (game theory), Wikipedia. — the feasible-and-individually-rational statement, trigger strategies, the folk-name origin, and the Friedman and Fudenberg-Maskin results.

laws.statement: One player's gain is exactly the other's loss, so the pie is fixed.

sources.text: von Neumann, J. (1928). “Zur Theorie der Gesellschaftsspiele.” Mathematische Annalen, vol. 100. — the paper that formalised two-person zero-sum play.
Zero-sum game, Wikipedia. — the fixed-total definition, the contrast with non-zero-sum games, and the zero-sum-thinking fallacy.
Minimax theorem, Wikipedia. — von Neumann's 1928 result for two-person zero-sum games.

laws.statement: Every strictly competitive game has a value both players can guarantee.

sources.text: von Neumann, J. (1928). “Zur Theorie der Gesellschaftsspiele.” Mathematische Annalen, vol. 100. — the paper proving the theorem.
Minimax theorem, Wikipedia. — the max-min equals min-max statement, the saddle point, and the 1928 von Neumann origin.

laws.name: The Gibbs Phase Rule
laws.statement: Degrees of freedom equal components minus phases, plus two.

sources.text: Gibbs, J. (1878). “On the equilibrium of heterogeneous substances.” American Journal of Science, vol. s3-16. — the memoir in which the phase rule appears.
Phase rule, Wikipedia. — the F = C minus P plus 2 relation, the water examples, the condensed variant, and the Gibbs attribution.

The Gibbs Phase Rule, Chemistry LibreTexts. — the derivation as variables minus chemical-potential constraints and the interpretation of the degrees of freedom.

laws.name: The Third Law of Thermodynamics
laws.statement: As temperature approaches absolute zero, a perfect crystal's entropy approaches zero.

sources.text: Third law of thermodynamics, Wikipedia. — the perfect-crystal entropy statement, the Nernst and Planck formulations, the unattainability principle, and the statistical basis.
Pauling, "The Structure and Entropy of Ice and of Other Crystals with Some Randomness of Atomic Arrangement," J. Am. Chem. Soc. 57:2680-2684 (1935). — the residual entropy of ice.

Masanes & Oppenheim, "A general derivation and quantification of the third law of thermodynamics," Nature Communications 8:14538 (2017). — the quantum derivation of unattainability and its logical independence from the heat theorem.

laws.name: The Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics
laws.statement: Two things each in equilibrium with a third are in equilibrium with each other.

Palffy-Muhoray et al., "Origin of the Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics and its Role in Statistical Mechanics," arXiv:2502.05281. — the subtleties of deriving the existence of temperature from transitivity and the Fowler-Guggenheim framing.

sources.text: Mass-energy equivalence, Wikipedia. — the rest-energy statement, the full energy-momentum relation, the 1905 origin, and the rest-mass interpretation.
Einstein, "Does the Inertia of a Body Depend Upon Its Energy Content?" (1905), English translation. — the original derivation, stated in words as loss of mass on radiating energy.
Mass in special relativity, Wikipedia. — the invariant-mass interpretation and the deprecation of relativistic mass.

Fein, Arndt et al., "Quantum superposition of molecules beyond 25 kDa," Nature Physics (2019). — matter-wave interference of molecules of thousands of atoms.

laws.name: The Equivalence Principle

laws.name: The Conservation of Momentum
laws.statement: In a closed system, total momentum never changes.

sources.text: Conservation of Linear Momentum, OpenStax University Physics (LibreTexts). — the closed-system statement, the Newton's-third-law basis, and elastic versus inelastic collisions.
Baez, "Noether's Theorem in a Nutshell." — momentum conservation as the consequence of the translational symmetry of space.

Dawkins & Carlisle, "Parental investment, mate desertion and a fallacy," Nature 262:131-133 (1976). — the coining of the Concorde fallacy as a normative critique.
Sweis et al., "Sensitivity to 'sunk costs' in mice, rats, and humans," Science 361(6398):178-181 (2018). — sunk-cost-like sensitivity across species after commitment.

laws.statement: We underestimate how long things will take, even knowing how long they took last time.

Flyvbjerg, Holm & Buhl, "Underestimating Costs in Public Works Projects: Error or Lie?" Journal of the American Planning Association (2002). — systematic cost overruns and the strategic-misrepresentation argument.
Planning fallacy, Wikipedia. — the definition, the inside/outside view, reference class forecasting, and the standard examples.

Laibson, "Golden Eggs and Hyperbolic Discounting," Quarterly Journal of Economics 112(2):443-477 (1997). — the quasi-hyperbolic beta-delta model and its application to saving.

Frederick, Lee & Baskin, "The Limits of Attraction," Journal of Marketing Research 51(4):487-507 (2014). — the effect's fragility with perceptual and real stimuli.

laws.name: The Von Restorff Effect

laws.name: The Spacing Effect
laws.statement: Study spread over time sticks; study crammed into one session fades.

sources.text: Cepeda, Pashler, Vul, Wixted & Rohrer, "Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis," Psychological Bulletin 132:354-380 (2006). — the meta-analysis and the joint role of study and retention intervals.

Cepeda, Vul, Rohrer, Wixted & Pashler, "Spacing effects in learning: A temporal ridgeline of optimal retention," Psychological Science 19:1095-1102 (2008). — the optimal gap growing in absolute terms but shrinking as a fraction of test delay.
Spacing effect, Wikipedia. — the distributed-versus-massed statement, the Ebbinghaus origin, and the competing mechanism theories.

laws.name: The Testing Effect
laws.statement: Retrieving a fact from memory fixes it better than reading it again.

sources.text: Roediger & Karpicke, "Test-Enhanced Learning: Taking Memory Tests Improves Long-Term Retention," Psychological Science 17(3):249-255 (2006). — the prose-passage experiments and the delayed-test crossover.

Adesope, Trevisan & Sundararajan, "Rethinking the Use of Tests: A Meta-Analysis of Practice Testing," Review of Educational Research 87(3):659-701 (2017). — practice testing outperforming restudy across 118 articles.
Karpicke & Blunt, "Retrieval Practice Produces More Learning than Elaborative Studying with Concept Mapping," Science 331(6018):772-775 (2011). — retrieval practice and transfer.

laws.name: The Law of Mass Action
laws.statement: At equilibrium, the ratio of products to reactants, each raised to its coefficient, is fixed.

sources.text: Law of mass action, Wikipedia. — the equilibrium and kinetic readings, the Guldberg-Waage history, and the elementary-reaction limit.
Law of mass action, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the statement, the 1864-79 formulation, and the historical status of the rate reading.
Ferner & Aronson, "Cato Guldberg and Peter Waage, the history of the Law of Mass Action..." Br J Clin Pharmacol (2016), PMC4693570. — the two-part origin and its development.

laws.name: The Law of Reflection
laws.statement: The angle a ray strikes a surface equals the angle it leaves.

sources.text: Law of reflection, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the equal-angle and coplanarity conditions and the Hero and Fermat history.
The Law of Reflection, OpenStax College Physics (LibreTexts). — the statement measured from the normal and the ray-optics treatment.
Specular vs. Diffuse Reflection, The Physics Classroom. — how the law holds locally on the microfacets of a rough surface.

laws.name: Huygens' Principle
laws.statement: Every point on a wavefront is itself the source of a new wavelet.

sources.text: Huygens-Fresnel principle, Wikipedia. — the secondary-wavelet construction, the Fresnel interference enrichment, the back-wave problem, and Kirchhoff's obliquity factor.
Christiaan Huygens, Wikipedia. — the 1690 Traite de la Lumiere in which the principle was published.

laws.name: Charles's Law
laws.statement: At constant pressure, a gas expands in step with its absolute temperature.

sources.text: Charles's law, Wikipedia. — the volume-proportional-to-absolute-temperature statement, the attribution to Charles and Gay-Lussac, and the absolute-zero extrapolation.
Charles's law, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the statement, the ~1787 dating, and the ideal-gas validity.

laws.name: The Clausius-Clapeyron Relation
laws.statement: The slope of a phase-boundary line is set by the latent heat and the volume change.

sources.text: Clausius, R. (1850). “Ueber die bewegende Kraft der Wärme und die Gesetze, welche sich daraus für die Wärmelehre selbst ableiten lassen.” Annalen der Physik, vol. 155. — Clausius's paper, which puts Clapeyron's 1834 relation on a thermodynamic footing.
Clausius-Clapeyron relation, Wikipedia. — the exact and approximate forms, the derivation from equal Gibbs energies, the ice-line and moisture-scaling examples, and the near-critical caveats.
The Clapeyron and Clausius-Clapeyron equations, CarnotCycle. — Clapeyron's 1834 memoir, the derivation, and the exactness of the general form.

laws.name: The Law of Definite Proportions
laws.statement: A pure compound always holds its elements in the same fixed proportion by mass.

sources.text: Law of definite proportions, Wikipedia. — the fixed-mass-ratio statement, the Proust-Berthollet controversy, and the tie to atomic theory.
Joseph-Louis Proust, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — Proust's formulation and the dispute with Berthollet.
Non-stoichiometric compound, Wikipedia. — the berthollide exceptions such as wustite that genuinely violate the law.

laws.name: The Law of Multiple Proportions
laws.statement: When two elements form several compounds, the mass ratios are small whole numbers.

sources.text: Law of multiple proportions, Wikipedia. — the small-whole-number statement, Dalton's formulation, and the large-molecule and non-stoichiometric limits.
Law of multiple proportions, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the statement, the 1803 announcement, and its role as evidence for atomic theory.

laws.name: The Rydberg Formula
laws.statement: A hydrogen line's wavelength comes from the difference of two inverse squares.

sources.text: Rydberg formula, Wikipedia. — the difference-of-inverse-squares statement, the spectral series, the Balmer and Rydberg history, and the single-electron limit.
Rydberg constant, NIST CODATA. — the precisely measured value of the Rydberg constant.
Hydrogen spectral series, Wikipedia. — the Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, Brackett, and Pfund series and their wavelengths.

laws.name: Stevens' Power Law
laws.statement: Perceived intensity rises as a power of the stimulus, the exponent set by the sense.

sources.text: Stevens, "On the psychophysical law," Psychological Review 64(3):153-181 (1957). — the power-function statement and the magnitude-estimation method.
Stevens's power law, Wikipedia. — the formula, the modality exponents, and the contrast with the Weber-Fechner law.
"Is Stevens's power law valid?" Behavioral and Brain Sciences (Cambridge). — the critiques of exponent stability and the ratio-judgement assumption.

laws.name: The Square-Cube Law
laws.statement: As a thing grows, its volume outruns its surface: bulk beats strength.

sources.text: Square-cube law, Wikipedia. — the area-as-square, volume-as-cube statement, Galileo's 1638 origin, and the biomechanical and engineering consequences.
Haldane, "On Being the Right Size" (1926), marxists.org. — the falling mouse and the mechanics of scale in organisms.
Kleiber's law, Wikipedia. — metabolic rate scaling as the three-quarter power of mass and the unresolved two-thirds debate.

laws.name: The Phillips Curve
laws.statement: When unemployment is low, inflation tends to run high, and the reverse.

sources.text: Phillips, "The Relation between Unemployment and the Rate of Change of Money Wage Rates in the United Kingdom, 1861-1957," Economica 25(100):283-299 (1958). — the original empirical relationship.
Hoover, "Phillips Curve," Concise Encyclopedia of Economics (Econlib). — the history, the stagflation breakdown, and the natural-rate revision.
Engemann, "What's the Phillips Curve and Why Has It Flattened?" Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (2020). — the flattening and the role of anchored expectations.

laws.name: The Efficient-Market Hypothesis
laws.statement: Asset prices already reflect all available information, so you can't reliably beat the market.

sources.text: Fama, "Efficient Capital Markets: A Review of Theory and Empirical Work," Journal of Finance 25(2):383-417 (1970). — the definitive statement and the three-form taxonomy.

Grossman & Stiglitz, "On the Impossibility of Informationally Efficient Markets," American Economic Review 70(3):393-408 (1980). — the paradox that perfect efficiency removes the incentive to gather information.
Shiller, "From Efficient Markets Theory to Behavioral Finance," Journal of Economic Perspectives (2003). — the excess-volatility and behavioural critique.

laws.name: The Random Walk Hypothesis
laws.statement: Stock prices wander unpredictably; the past path does not forecast the next step.

sources.text: Random walk hypothesis, Wikipedia. — the unpredictability statement, the Bachelier-Kendall-Samuelson-Malkiel history, and the martingale distinction.
Kendall, "The Analysis of Economic Time-Series - Part I: Prices," Journal of the Royal Statistical Society 116:11-34 (1953). — the finding that price changes looked random.
Lo & MacKinlay, A Non-Random Walk Down Wall Street (Princeton University Press, 1999). — variance-ratio evidence rejecting the pure random walk.

laws.name: The Quantity Theory of Money
laws.statement: Print more money and, other things equal, prices rise in proportion.

sources.text: Quantity theory of money, Wikipedia. — the proportionality statement, the equation of exchange, the history, and the velocity and endogenous-money critiques.
Friedman, "The Counter-Revolution in Monetary Theory" (1970), Hoover Institution. — the monetarist restatement and the inflation-is-a-monetary-phenomenon dictum.
Jung, "The Quantity Theory of Money, 1870-2020," ECB Working Paper 2940 (2024). — long-run proportionality and its weakening during the low-inflation decades.

laws.name: The Winner's Curse
laws.statement: The auction winner is the one who most overestimated the prize, and so overpaid.

sources.text: Capen, Clapp & Campbell, "Competitive Bidding in High-Risk Situations," Journal of Petroleum Technology 23:641-653 (1971). — the original account from oil-lease bidding.
Thaler, "Anomalies: The Winner's Curse," Journal of Economic Perspectives 2(1):191-202 (1988). — the survey that popularised the effect.

Dyer, Kagel & Levin, "A Comparison of Naive and Experienced Bidders in Common Value Offer Auctions," Economic Journal 99(394):108-115 (1989). — experienced bidders falling prey to the curse in the laboratory.

laws.name: The Broken Windows Theory
laws.statement: Visible disorder invites more disorder, and eventually serious crime.
laws.namedAfter: James Q. Wilson and George Kelling

sources.text: Wilson & Kelling, "Broken Windows," The Atlantic Monthly (1982). — the founding article and the metaphor.
Keizer, Lindenberg & Steg, "The Spreading of Disorder," Science 322(5908):1681-1685 (2008). — field experiments supporting the disorder-spreads-disorder mechanism.

Harcourt & Ludwig, "Broken Windows: New Evidence from New York City and a Five-City Social Experiment," University of Chicago Law Review 73(1):271-320 (2006). — little causal support for the crime-reduction claim.

laws.name: The Just-World Hypothesis
laws.statement: People need to believe the world is fair, so they decide victims must deserve their fate.

sources.text: Lerner & Simmons, "Observer's reaction to the 'innocent victim': compassion or rejection?" Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 4(2):203-210 (1966). — the foundational experiment and the compensation condition.
Hafer & Begue, "Experimental research on just-world theory: Problems, developments, and future challenges," Psychological Bulletin (2005). — the review of the evidence and its caveats.
Just-world hypothesis, Wikipedia. — the statement, Lerner's history, the personal-versus-general distinction, and cultural variation.

laws.name: The Competitive Exclusion Principle
laws.statement: Two species living the exact same way cannot coexist; one wins out.

sources.text: Competitive exclusion principle, Wikipedia. — the statement, the Gause and Hardin history, niche differentiation, and the widespread-coexistence caveat.
Hardin, "The Competitive Exclusion Principle," Science 131(3409):1292-1297 (1960). — the coining of the term and 'complete competitors cannot coexist.'
Hutchinson, "The Paradox of the Plankton," The American Naturalist 95(882):137-145 (1961). — the apparent violation and its proposed resolutions.
Hardin, G. (1960). "The Competitive Exclusion Principle." Science, 131(3409), 1292–1297.

laws.name: The Allee Effect
laws.statement: Below a certain sparseness, individuals fare worse and the population can spiral to extinction.

sources.text: Allee effect, Wikipedia. — the positive density-fitness relationship, the strong and weak and component and demographic distinctions, and the mechanisms.
Stephens, Sutherland & Freckleton, "What is the Allee effect?" Oikos 87(1):185-190 (1999). — the modern definition as a positive relationship between mean fitness and density.

Courchamp, Clutton-Brock & Grenfell, "Inverse density dependence and the Allee effect," Trends in Ecology & Evolution 14(10):405-410 (1999). — the review reframing the effect and its conservation importance.

laws.name: Hamilton's Rule
laws.statement: Help a relative when the benefit to them, weighted by kinship, outweighs the cost to you.

sources.text: The Genetical Evolution of Social Behaviour, Wikipedia. — Hamilton's 1964 papers, inclusive fitness, and the rB greater than C rule.

Nowak, Tarnita & Wilson, "The evolution of eusociality," Nature 466:1057-1062 (2010), and Abbot et al., "Inclusive fitness theory and eusociality," Nature 471:E1-E4 (2011). — the critique of inclusive fitness and the multi-author rebuttal.
Bourke, "Hamilton's rule and the causes of social evolution," Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B (2014). — the exact-versus-general status of the rule.

laws.name: The Price Equation
laws.statement: Any change in a trait splits into a part from selection and a part from transmission.

sources.text: Price equation, Wikipedia. — the identity, its selection and transmission terms, the Robertson-Price special case, and the multilevel application.
Frank, "Natural selection. IV. The Price equation," Journal of Evolutionary Biology 25:1002-1019 (2012), arXiv. — the equation's structure and its role as a general framework.
van Veelen, "The problem with the Price equation," Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 375:20190355 (2020). — the critique of its generality and dynamic insufficiency.

laws.name: The Baldwin Effect
laws.statement: What a species first learns to do, it may over generations be born able to do.

sources.text: Baldwin effect, Wikipedia. — the statement, the 1896 origins, Simpson's naming, and the relation to genetic assimilation.
Hinton & Nowlan, "How Learning Can Guide Evolution," Complex Systems 1(3):495-502 (1987). — the model showing learning accelerates evolution without inheriting the learned trait.
Genetic assimilation, Wikipedia. — Waddington's crossveinless and bithorax experiments as a related demonstrated mechanism.

laws.name: The Founder Effect
laws.statement: A population started by a few carries only a chance sliver of the original's genes.

sources.text: Founder effect, Wikipedia. — the small-sample definition, the disease examples, the tie to genetic drift, and the bottleneck distinction.
Barton & Charlesworth, "Genetic Revolutions, Founder Effects, and Speciation," Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics 15:133-164 (1984). — the critique of founder-effect speciation.
The Finnish genetic heritage in 2022, Disease Models & Mechanisms 15(10). — the founder bottleneck behind the Finnish disease heritage.

laws.name: Genetic Drift
laws.statement: Allele frequencies wander by pure chance, and in small populations they wander far.

sources.text: Wright, S. (1931). “Evolution in Mendelian Populations.” Genetics, vol. 16. — the paper establishing drift in the Mendelian framework.
Genetic drift, Wikipedia. — the chance-change definition, the Wright-Fisher model, fixation probability and time, and the drift-versus-selection balance.
Genetic drift, UC Berkeley Understanding Evolution. — drift as a directionless mechanism acting in all populations, and its consequences.
Population bottleneck, Wikipedia. — the northern elephant seal bottleneck and the loss of diversity through drift.

laws.name: The Neutral Theory of Molecular Evolution
laws.statement: Most molecular evolution is the random drift of changes that neither help nor harm.

sources.text: Neutral theory of molecular evolution, Wikipedia. — the drift-of-neutral-mutations statement, the molecular clock, and the neutralist-selectionist debate.
Kern & Hahn, "The Neutral Theory in Light of Natural Selection," Molecular Biology and Evolution 35(6):1366-1371 (2018). — the argument that genome-scale data reject the theory's universality.
Jensen et al., "The importance of the Neutral Theory in 1968 and 50 years on: a response to Kern and Hahn 2018," Evolution 73(1):111-114 (2019). — the defence of the theory's foundational ideas.

laws.name: The Biogenetic Law
laws.statement: An embryo was said to replay the adult forms of its evolutionary ancestors.

sources.text: Recapitulation theory, Wikipedia. — the ontogeny-recapitulates-phylogeny statement, Haeckel's 1866 formulation, and its rejection.

Richardson et al., "There is no highly conserved embryonic stage in the vertebrates," Anatomy and Embryology 196:91-106 (1997). — the re-examination showing Haeckel's drawings overstated embryo similarity.
Ernst Haeckel's Biogenetic Law (1866), Embryo Project Encyclopedia (Arizona State University). — the law, terminal addition, and its history.

laws.name: Rapoport's Rule
laws.statement: Species near the poles tend to have wider ranges than those near the equator.

sources.text: Rapoport's rule, Wikipedia. — the range-size-increases-with-latitude statement, the climatic variability hypothesis, and the limits and reversals.

Stevens, "The Latitudinal Gradient in Geographical Range: How So Many Species Coexist in the Tropics," The American Naturalist 133(2):240-256 (1989). — the naming of the rule and its link to the diversity gradient.
Gaston, Blackburn & Spicer, "Rapoport's rule: time for an epitaph?" Trends in Ecology & Evolution 13(2):70-74 (1998). — the argument that the rule is of limited generality.

laws.name: The Species-Area Relationship
laws.statement: The larger the area you look at, the more species you find.

sources.text: He & Hubbell, "Species-area relationships always overestimate extinction rates from habitat loss," Nature 473:368-371 (2011). — the argument against reversing the curve to predict extinction.
Matthews et al., "Island species-area relationships and species accumulation curves are not equivalent," Global Ecology and Biogeography 25 (2016). — the distinction between the curve types.
Tjorve, "The species-area relationship, self-similarity, and the true meaning of the z-value," Ecology (2008). — the exponent's variation and interpretation.

laws.name: Williston's Law
laws.statement: Repeated body parts tend, over evolution, to grow fewer and more specialized.

sources.text: Samuel Wendell Williston, Wikipedia. — the statement of the law and its attribution and history.

Esteve-Altava et al., "Structural Constraints in the Evolution of the Tetrapod Skull Complexity: Williston's Law Revisited Using Network Models," Evolutionary Biology (2013). — the skull-bone support and the loss-and-fusion mechanism.

Wilson et al., "On trends and patterns in macroevolution: Williston's law and the branchiostegal series of extant and extinct osteichthyans," BMC Ecology and Evolution (2019). — the fish survey finding no support for the reduction trend.

laws.name: The Secretary Problem
laws.statement: Look at the first 37 percent, then take the next one better than all of them.

sources.text: Secretary problem, Wikipedia. — the setup, the optimal cutoff and its one-over-e success probability, the derivation, the history, and the variants.
Robbins' problem, Wikipedia. — the expected-rank variant and its still-open status.

laws.name: Survivorship Bias
laws.statement: Studying only the winners misleads you, because the losers vanished from view.

sources.text: Survivorship bias, Wikipedia. — the definition as a subtype of selection bias, the Wald example, and the fund-performance and old-buildings cases.
Wald, A Method of Estimating Plane Vulnerability Based on Damage of Survivors, Center for Naval Analyses reprint (1980). — the original 1943 reasoning that accounts for the downed planes.
Moll, "Abraham Wald and the Red Bullet Holes," cameronmoll.com. — the origin of the dotted-airplane diagram as a later recreation, not Wald's.

laws.name: The End-to-End Principle
laws.statement: Put the smarts at the edges of a network, and keep the core simple.

sources.text: Saltzer, Reed & Clark, "End-to-End Arguments in System Design," ACM Transactions on Computer Systems 2(4):277-288 (1984), author PDF. — the statement, the file-transfer reasoning, and the performance caveat.
End-to-end principle, Wikipedia. — the TCP/IP example, the erosions by NATs and middleboxes, and the net-neutrality lineage.

Blumenthal & Clark, "Rethinking the design of the Internet: the end-to-end arguments vs. the brave new world," ACM Transactions on Internet Technology 1(1) (2001). — the tensions pulling function into the network.

laws.name: Kerckhoffs's Principle
laws.statement: A cipher should stay secure even if everything but the key is public.

sources.text: Kerckhoffs's principle, Wikipedia. — the key-secrecy statement, the six rules, the contrast with obscurity, and Shannon's maxim.
Petitcolas, scans and translation of Kerckhoffs's "La Cryptographie Militaire" (1883). — the original statement of the principle.
The Cornerstone of Cybersecurity, NIST NCCoE. — the open-competition model for AES and SHA-3 that embodies the principle.

laws.name: The Fallacies of Distributed Computing
laws.statement: The network is reliable, instant, infinite, secure, and uniform: all false.

sources.text: Fallacies of distributed computing, Wikipedia. — the eight fallacies, their wording, and the Joy, Lyon, Deutsch, and Gosling attribution.
Rotem-Gal-Oz, "Fallacies of Distributed Computing Explained." — the canonical explanation of each fallacy and its engineering consequence.

laws.name: Dennard Scaling
laws.statement: As transistors shrink, their power density holds constant, so smaller means faster for free.

sources.text: Dennard scaling, Wikipedia. — the constant-power-density statement, the scaling relationships, the 1974 origin, and the breakdown and its consequences.
Dennard et al., "Design of Ion-Implanted MOSFET's with Very Small Physical Dimensions," IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits SC-9(5):256-268 (1974), IBM Research. — the original scaling paper.

laws.name: The McNamara Fallacy
laws.statement: Measure what you can, then decide the rest doesn't matter, and finally that it doesn't exist.

sources.text: McNamara fallacy, Wikipedia. — the four-step statement, the Vietnam body-count example, and the Yankelovich and Handy attributions.
Vietnam War body count controversy, Wikipedia. — the body count as the primary measure of progress and its distortions.

laws.name: Hitchens's Razor
laws.statement: What can be asserted without evidence can be dismissed without evidence.

sources.text: Hitchens's razor, Wikipedia. — the statement, its appearance in God Is Not Great, the naming after Hitchens, and the Latin antecedent.
Reinhardt, "The long history of Hitchens' Razor," Skeptic Ink (2015). — the older provenance and the 1704 Pritius use.

laws.name: The Ship of Theseus
laws.statement: Replace every plank of a ship one at a time, and it is unclear whether the result is the same ship.

sources.text: Ship of Theseus, Wikipedia. — the Plutarch source, the plank-replacement statement, and the Hobbes reassembly variant.
Identity Over Time, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — numerical versus qualitative identity, endurantism and perdurantism, and the problem of persistence.

laws.name: The Sorites Paradox
laws.statement: One grain isn't a heap, and adding one never makes a heap, yet heaps exist.

sources.text: Hyde & Raffman, "Sorites Paradox," Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the statement, the vague-predicate framing, and the competing resolutions.
Eubulides, Wikipedia. — the Megarian school and the family of paradoxes including the heap and the bald man.

laws.name: The Liar Paradox
laws.statement: "This sentence is false" is false if true and true if false.

sources.text: Liar Paradox, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the self-referential statement, the strengthened liar, and the Tarski and Kripke responses.
Liar paradox, Wikipedia. — the Eubulides and Epimenides attributions and the family of self-referential paradoxes.

laws.name: Russell's Paradox
laws.statement: The set of all sets that do not contain themselves both must and cannot contain itself.

sources.text: Russell's Paradox, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the contradiction, the letter to Frege, and the type-theoretic and axiomatic responses.
Russell's paradox, Wikipedia. — the statement, the barber illustration, and Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory as the standard resolution.

laws.name: The Münchhausen Trilemma
laws.statement: Every attempt to justify a claim ends in infinite regress, circularity, or an unjustified stopping point.

sources.text: Münchhausen trilemma, Wikipedia. — the three horns, the Hans Albert coinage, and the Agrippan ancestry.
Foundationalist Theories of Epistemic Justification, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the regress problem the trilemma formalises, and the foundationalist response to it.

laws.name: Newcomb's Paradox
laws.statement: Two rules of rational choice, dominance and expected value, give opposite answers to the same decision.

sources.text: Nozick, R. (1969). “Newcomb’s Problem and Two Principles of Choice.” Essays in Honor of Carl G. Hempel. — Nozick's paper, which introduced Newcomb's problem to philosophy.
Causal Decision Theory, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Newcomb's problem and the causal-versus-evidential divide it created.
Newcomb's paradox, Wikipedia. — the two-box setup, the Newcomb and Nozick attribution, and the one-boxer and two-boxer arguments.

laws.name: The Trolley Problem
laws.statement: Most would divert a runaway trolley to kill one instead of five, but few would push a man to do the same.

sources.text: Doctrine of Double Effect, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Foot's 1967 case, the intended-versus-foreseen distinction, and the trolley cases.
Greene et al., "An fMRI Investigation of Emotional Engagement in Moral Judgment," Science 293 (2001): 2105-2108. — the personal-versus-impersonal dilemma finding.
Trolley problem, Wikipedia. — the switch and footbridge cases and the Foot and Thomson attributions.

laws.name: The Chinese Room
laws.statement: Following rules to manipulate symbols can pass for understanding without any understanding at all.

sources.text: The Chinese Room Argument, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the thought experiment, the syntax-semantics premise, and the major replies.
Searle, "Minds, Brains, and Programs," Behavioral and Brain Sciences 3(3) (1980): 417-424. — the original argument and the strong-versus-weak-AI distinction.

laws.name: The Problem of Induction
laws.statement: That the future will resemble the past cannot be justified without assuming the very thing in question.

sources.text: The Problem of Induction, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Hume's dilemma, the circularity of justifying induction, and the range of responses.
Problem of induction, Wikipedia. — the uniformity-of-nature assumption, Hume's works, and the absence of consensus on a solution.

laws.name: Moravec's Paradox
aliases: Moravec's paradox in AI and robotics
laws.statement: For machines, high-level reasoning is easy and a toddler's perception and movement are hard.

sources.text: Moravec's paradox, Wikipedia. — Moravec's one-year-old quote, the evolutionary explanation, and the Minsky, Brooks, and Pinker statements.
Moravec, Mind Children: The Future of Robot and Human Intelligence (Harvard University Press, 1988). — the original formulation and the 'thinnest veneer' passage.

laws.name: The Veil of Ignorance
laws.statement: Choose the rules of society without knowing which person in it you will be.

sources.text: Rawls, J. (1971). “A Theory of Justice.” — the book setting out the original position.
Original Position, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the veil of ignorance, maximin reasoning, and the Harsanyi contrast and critiques.
John Rawls, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — A Theory of Justice, the two principles, and the difference principle.

laws.name: Torricelli's Law
laws.statement: Fluid escapes a hole at the speed it would reach falling from the surface above it.

sources.text: Torricelli's law, Wikipedia. — the v equals square-root of 2gh statement, the Bernoulli derivation, and the vena-contracta discharge coefficient.
Torricelli's law, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the efflux speed and its equality with free-fall from the surface height.

laws.name: Stokes' Law
laws.statement: Drag on a tiny sphere creeping through a viscous fluid grows in proportion to its speed.

sources.text: Stokes, G. (2009). “Mathematical and Physical Papers.” — the collected papers, containing the 1851 memoir on internal friction in which the drag law appears.
Stokes's law, Wikipedia. — the F equals 6 pi mu r v drag force, the creeping-flow derivation, and the low-Reynolds-number condition.
Stokes's law, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the drag on a sphere and the resulting terminal-velocity relation.

laws.name: Brewster's Angle
laws.statement: At one special angle, light reflecting off glass or water comes back fully polarized.

sources.text: Brewster, D. (1815). “On the laws which regulate the polarisation of light by reflexion from transparent bodies. By David Brewster, LL. D. F. R. S. Edin. and F. S. A. Edin. In a letter addressed to Right Hon. Sir Joseph Banks, Bart. K. B. P. R. S.” Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London. — the paper giving the polarising angle.
Brewster's angle, Wikipedia. — the polarizing angle, the tan(theta) equals n2/n1 rule, and the perpendicular-reflected-ray geometry.
Brewster's law, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the tangent relation to refractive index and the air-to-glass worked angle.

laws.name: Rayleigh Scattering
laws.statement: Small particles scatter short blue light far more than long red light, so the sky is blue.

sources.text: Strutt, J. (1871). “On the light from the sky, its polarization and colour.” The London, Edinburgh, and Dublin Philosophical Magazine and Journal of Science, vol. 41. — published under his name before he succeeded to the title.
Rayleigh scattering, Wikipedia. — the inverse-fourth-power wavelength law, the induced-dipole mechanism, and the contrast with Mie scattering.
Rayleigh scattering, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the effect, its naming after Rayleigh's 1871 paper, and the small-particle condition.

laws.name: The Titius-Bode Law
laws.statement: The planets' distances from the Sun seem to follow a simple doubling pattern, until Neptune.
laws.namedAfter: Johann Daniel Titius and Johann Elert Bode

sources.text: Titius-Bode law, Wikipedia. — the distance formula, the Titius and Bode attribution, the Uranus and Ceres fits, and the Neptune failure.
Bode's law, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the empirical distance rule and its status as a numerological curiosity with no known justification.

laws.name: Braess's Paradox
laws.statement: Adding a road to a congested network can make everyone's journey slower.

sources.text: Braess, D. (1968). “Über ein Paradoxon aus der Verkehrsplanung.” Unternehmensforschung Operations Research - Recherche Opérationnelle, vol. 12. — the paper describing the paradox.
Braess's paradox, Wikipedia. — the added-road-slows-traffic result, the Nash-equilibrium mechanism, and the cited real-world cases.
Braess, Nagurney & Wakolbinger, "On a Paradox of Traffic Planning," Transportation Science 39 (2005): 446-450. — the English translation of the 1968 original.

laws.name: Parrondo's Paradox
laws.statement: Two games that each lose on their own can, played in the right sequence, win.

sources.text: Parrondo's paradox, Wikipedia. — the losing-games construction, the capital-dependence mechanism, and the flashing-ratchet analogy.
Harmer & Abbott, "Losing strategies can win by Parrondo's paradox," Nature 402 (1999): 864. — the naming and formal demonstration.

laws.name: The Will Rogers Phenomenon
laws.statement: Move one item between two groups and the average of both groups can rise, though nothing changed.

sources.text: Will Rogers phenomenon, Wikipedia. — the both-means-rise mechanism, the apocryphal Rogers quote, and the Feinstein stage-migration coinage.
