Feinstein, Sosin & Wells, "The Will Rogers Phenomenon," New England Journal of Medicine 312 (1985): 1604-1608. — stage migration inflating apparent cancer survival.

laws.name: Verner's Law
laws.statement: Grimm's law's exceptions dissolve once you know where the ancient word-accent fell.

sources.text: Verner's law, Wikipedia. — the accent conditioning, the voicing of Grimm's-law fricatives and inherited s, and grammatischer Wechsel.
Verner's law, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the voicing of non-initial fricatives after an unaccented syllable.

laws.name: The Shirky Principle
laws.statement: Institutions will try to preserve the problem to which they are the solution.

sources.text: Kevin Kelly, "The Shirky Principle," The Technium (2010). — the statement and Kelly's naming of the principle after Shirky.
Clay Shirky, "The Collapse of Complex Business Models" (2010). — the thematically related argument about institutions and simplification.

laws.name: Kernighan's Law
laws.statement: Debugging is twice as hard as writing the code, so write it less cleverly than you can.

sources.text: Brian Kernighan, Wikiquote. — the verified original wording from The Elements of Programming Style, 2nd edition.
The Elements of Programming Style, Wikipedia. — the Kernighan and Plauger authorship and the book's editions.

laws.name: The Law of Leaky Abstractions
laws.statement: All non-trivial abstractions, to some degree, are leaky.

sources.text: Joel Spolsky, "The Law of Leaky Abstractions," Joel on Software (2002). — the statement, the saves-working-not-learning corollary, and the worked examples.
Leaky abstraction, Wikipedia. — the principle, its popularisation by Spolsky, and related prior work on imperfect abstractions.

laws.name: Tesler's Law
aliases: The Law of Conservation of Complexity
laws.statement: Every system has irreducible complexity; you can move it around but never remove it.

sources.text: Larry Tesler, "The Law of Conservation of Complexity," nomodes.com. — the canonical statement and the three parties who may bear the complexity.
Law of conservation of complexity, Wikipedia. — the shifted-not-removed mechanism and its status as a design heuristic.

laws.name: Olbers' Paradox
laws.statement: If the universe were infinite and eternal, the night sky would blaze as bright as the Sun.

sources.text: Olbers's paradox, Wikipedia. — the equal-shells argument, the finite-age resolution, and the secondary role of redshift.
Olbers' paradox, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the dark-sky contradiction and its cosmological significance.

laws.name: The Fermi Paradox
laws.statement: The galaxy should be full of civilizations, yet we see no sign of any. Where is everybody?

sources.text: Fermi paradox, Wikipedia. — the contradiction, the 1950 lunch and its differing recollections, and the Hart and Tipler formalisations.
Fermi paradox, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the tension between likelihood and absence of evidence.

laws.name: The Drake Equation
laws.statement: Multiply seven uncertain factors to estimate how many civilizations we might hear from.

sources.text: Drake equation, Wikipedia. — the seven factors, the Green Bank origin, and its purpose as a framework rather than a calculator.
Drake equation, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the factor definitions and the compounding uncertainty down the chain.

laws.name: Zeno's Paradoxes
laws.statement: To cross a room you must first cross half, then half again, so motion seems impossible.

sources.text: Zeno's Paradoxes, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the Dichotomy, Achilles, and Arrow, the convergent-series reply, and the supertask debate.
Zeno's paradoxes, Wikipedia. — the arguments, their transmission through Aristotle, and their relation to Parmenides.

laws.name: The Banach-Tarski Paradox
laws.statement: A solid ball can be cut into a few pieces and rearranged into two balls of the same size.

sources.text: Banach, S. & Tarski, A. (1924). “Sur la décomposition des ensembles de points en parties respectivement congruentes.” Fundamenta Mathematicae, vol. 6. — the paper proving the decomposition.
Banach-Tarski paradox, Wikipedia. — the doubling theorem, non-measurable pieces, the Axiom of Choice, and failure in low dimensions.
Banach-Tarski Paradox, Wolfram MathWorld. — the five-piece minimum and the equidecomposability statement.

laws.name: The Infinite Monkey Theorem
laws.statement: A monkey typing at random for infinite time will almost surely type all of Shakespeare.

sources.text: Borel, É. (1913). “La mécanique statique et l'irréversibilité.” Journal de Physique Théorique et Appliquée, vol. 3. — the paper in which the typing monkeys appear.
Infinite monkey theorem, Wikipedia. — the almost-surely statement, the Borel and Eddington history, and the Hamlet and real-monkey figures.

Woodcock & Falletta, "A numerical evaluation of the Finite Monkeys Theorem," reported by Phys.org (2024). — the finding that finite monkeys could not produce Shakespeare within the universe's lifespan.

laws.name: The Coriolis Effect
laws.statement: On a spinning Earth, moving air and water veer right in the north and left in the south.

sources.text: Coriolis force, Wikipedia. — the rotating-frame deflection, its latitude dependence, and the debunking of the drain myth.
Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the 1835 paper and the inertial force acting at right angles to motion.

laws.name: The Magnus Effect
laws.statement: A spinning ball curves, because its spin pushes the air and the air pushes back sideways.

sources.text: Magnus, G. (1853). “Ueber die Abweichung der Geschosse, und: Ueber eine auffallende Erscheinung bei rotirenden Körpern.” Annalen der Physik, vol. 164. — the paper reporting the deflection of spinning bodies.
Magnus effect, Wikipedia. — the perpendicular force, the entrainment mechanism, and the reverse Magnus effect.
Ideal Lift of a Spinning Ball, NASA Glenn Research Center. — the flow-turning explanation and the complexity of the real boundary layer.

laws.name: The Mpemba Effect
laws.statement: Hot water is sometimes claimed to freeze faster than cold, but the effect may not be real.

sources.text: Mpemba & Osborne, "Cool?," Physics Education 4 (1969): 172-175. — the original published observation.
Burridge & Linden, "Questioning the Mpemba effect," Scientific Reports 6 (2016): 37665. — the controlled study finding no evidence for a meaningful effect.
Mpemba effect, Wikipedia. — the claim, the ancient antecedents, the proposed mechanisms, and the contested status.

laws.name: Brownian Motion
laws.statement: Tiny suspended particles jiggle at random, kicked about by the unseen molecules of the fluid.

sources.text: Brown, R. (1828). “A brief account of microscopical observations made in the months of June, July and August 1827, on the particles contained in the pollen of plants; and on the general existence of active molecules in organic and inorganic bodies.” The Philosophical Magazine, vol. 4. — Brown's account of the motion of pollen particles in water.
Brownian motion, Wikipedia. — the molecular-bombardment mechanism, the Brown, Einstein, Smoluchowski, and Perrin history, and the Wiener process.
Brownian motion, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the random movement of suspended particles and its explanation.

laws.name: Michaelis-Menten Kinetics
laws.statement: An enzyme's rate rises with substrate, then levels off as the enzyme saturates.

sources.text: Johnson, K. & Goody, R. (2011). “The Original Michaelis Constant: Translation of the 1913 Michaelis–Menten Paper.” Biochemistry, vol. 50. — a full English translation of the 1913 paper, with the original alongside.
Michaelis-Menten kinetics, Wikipedia. — the rate equation, the two parameters, the Henri and Briggs-Haldane history, and the assumptions.
Johnson & Goody, "The Original Michaelis Constant," Biochemistry (2011). — the 1913 paper, its translation, and the meaning of the Michaelis constant.

laws.name: The Easterlin Paradox
laws.statement: Within a country the rich are happier, yet growing richer over decades leaves a nation no happier.

sources.text: Easterlin paradox, Wikipedia. — the point-in-time versus over-time findings, the explanations, and the Stevenson-Wolfers challenge.
Stevenson & Wolfers, "Economic Growth and Subjective Well-Being: Reassessing the Easterlin Paradox," NBER Working Paper 14282 (2008). — the reassessment finding a robust income-wellbeing link.

laws.name: The Spotlight Effect
laws.statement: We think everyone noticed our stumble or stain, but far fewer did than we imagine.

sources.text: Gilovich, Medvec & Savitsky, "The Spotlight Effect in Social Judgment," Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 78 (2000): 211-222. — the effect, the T-shirt study, and the egocentric-anchoring account.
Spotlight effect, Wikipedia. — the overestimation of others' attention and its relation to the illusion of transparency.

laws.name: The Curse of Knowledge
laws.statement: Once you know something, you cannot imagine what it is like not to know it.

sources.text: Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, "The Curse of Knowledge in Economic Settings," Journal of Political Economy 97 (1989): 1232-1254. — the coining of the term and the market experiments.
Curse of knowledge, Wikipedia. — the perspective-taking failure, the tappers-and-listeners study, and the link to hindsight bias.

laws.name: The Illusory Truth Effect
laws.statement: Repeat a claim often enough and it starts to feel true, whether or not it is.

sources.text: Hasher, Goldstein & Toppino, "Frequency and the conference of referential validity," Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior 16 (1977): 107-112. — the original demonstration.
Illusory truth effect, Wikipedia. — the effect, the processing-fluency mechanism, and the knowledge and plausibility nuances.

laws.name: The Hindsight Bias
laws.statement: Once you know how it turned out, it feels as if you knew it all along.

sources.text: Fischhoff & Beyth, "I knew it would happen," Organizational Behavior and Human Performance 13 (1975): 1-16. — the remembered-probabilities demonstration.
Hindsight bias, Wikipedia. — the I-knew-it-all-along effect, the three levels, and applications in law and medicine.

laws.name: The Fundamental Attribution Error
laws.statement: We blame others' behaviour on their character and our own on the circumstances.

sources.text: Jones & Harris, "The attribution of attitudes," Journal of Experimental Social Psychology 3 (1967): 1-24. — the paradigm demonstration.
Fundamental attribution error, Wikipedia. — the dispositional-over-situational tendency, the Ross coinage, and the cultural and actor-observer caveats.

laws.name: The Self-Serving Bias
laws.statement: We take credit for our successes and blame our failures on everything else.

sources.text: Miller & Ross, "Self-Serving Biases in the Attribution of Causality: Fact or Fiction?," Psychological Bulletin 82 (1975): 213-225. — the critical review and the enhancement-versus-protection distinction.
Self-serving bias, Wikipedia. — the success-internal failure-external pattern, the motivational-cognitive debate, and cultural moderation.

laws.name: The Optimism Bias
laws.statement: We expect good things to happen to us and bad things to happen to other people.

sources.text: Sharot, Korn & Dolan, "How unrealistic optimism is maintained in the face of reality," Nature Neuroscience 14 (2011): 1475-1479. — the asymmetric belief-updating account, building on Weinstein's 1980 work.
Optimism bias, Wikipedia. — the comparative-optimism pattern, the motivational and updating accounts, and the measurement caveats.

laws.name: The Peak-End Rule
laws.statement: We judge an experience by its most intense moment and its ending, not its whole.

sources.text: Redelmeier & Kahneman, "Patients' memories of painful medical treatments," Pain 66 (1996): 3-8. — the colonoscopy study of peak and end.
Peak-end rule, Wikipedia. — the rule, duration neglect, the two selves, and the meta-analytic scope.

laws.name: The IKEA Effect
laws.statement: We value the things we build ourselves more than they are objectively worth.

sources.text: Norton, Mochon & Ariely, "The IKEA effect: When labor leads to love," Journal of Consumer Psychology 22 (2012): 453-460. — the definition, experiments, and completion condition.
IKEA effect, Wikipedia. — the self-made valuation boost, its mechanisms, and its boundary conditions.

laws.name: The Backfire Effect
laws.statement: The claim that correcting a falsehood makes people believe it more, which mostly does not hold.

sources.text: Nyhan & Reifler, "When Corrections Fail," Political Behavior 32 (2010): 303-330. — the original proposal of the effect.
Wood & Porter, "The Elusive Backfire Effect," Political Behavior 41 (2019). — the large-scale non-replication finding corrections generally work.
Backfire effect, Wikipedia. — the claim, its contested status, and the consensus that corrections usually reduce misperceptions.

laws.name: The Negativity Bias
laws.statement: Bad events, emotions, and news hit us harder than equally strong good ones.

sources.text: Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer & Vohs, "Bad Is Stronger Than Good," Review of General Psychology 5 (2001): 323-370. — the cross-domain review of the asymmetry.
Negativity bias, Wikipedia. — the greater weight of the negative, the four facets, and the lifespan and loss-aversion caveats.

laws.name: The Diderot Effect
laws.statement: One fine new thing can make everything you own look shabby, so you buy more.

sources.text: Denis Diderot, "Regrets on Parting with My Old Dressing Gown" (1769). — the original description of the spiral.
Diderot effect, Wikipedia. — the Diderot unity, the consumption spiral, and McCracken's coinage.

laws.name: The Bandwagon Effect
laws.statement: The more people adopt something, the more others adopt it, just because others have.

sources.text: Leibenstein, "Bandwagon, Snob, and Veblen Effects in the Theory of Consumers' Demand," Quarterly Journal of Economics 64 (1950): 183-207. — the economic formalisation and the contrast with snob and Veblen effects.
Bandwagon effect, Wikipedia. — the herd-behaviour definition, the etymology, and the mechanisms and examples.

laws.name: The Central Dogma of Molecular Biology
laws.statement: Sequence information can flow from nucleic acids into protein, but never back out of protein.

sources.text: Crick, "Central Dogma of Molecular Biology," Nature 227 (1970): 561-563. — the precise statement, the three classes of transfer, and the reverse-transcription clarification.
Central dogma of molecular biology, Wikipedia. — the general, special, and forbidden transfers and the common misconceptions.

laws.name: Mendelian Inheritance
laws.statement: Traits pass to offspring as discrete factors that separate and recombine by simple rules.

sources.text: Mendel, G. "Experiments in Plant Hybridisation" (1866; Bateson translation, 1925) — the pea-plant experiments, scanned by the Biodiversity Heritage Library.
Mendelian inheritance, Wikipedia. — the laws of segregation, independent assortment, and dominance, and their extensions and exceptions.
Miko, "Gregor Mendel and the Principles of Inheritance," Nature Education. — the pea experiments, the ratios, and the rediscovery.

laws.name: Chargaff's Rules
laws.statement: In DNA, adenine equals thymine and guanine equals cytosine.

sources.text: Chargaff, E. (1950). “Chemical specificity of nucleic acids and mechanism of their enzymatic degradation.” Experientia, vol. 6. — the paper reporting the base ratios.
Chargaff's rules, Wikipedia. — the two parity rules, the tetranucleotide disproof, and the role in the double-helix model.
Erwin Chargaff, Wikipedia. — the chromatography method and the base-ratio findings.

laws.name: Cell Theory
laws.statement: All living things are made of cells, the basic unit of life, and every cell comes from a cell.

sources.text: Cell theory, Wikipedia. — the three tenets, the Hooke, Schleiden, Schwann, and Virchow history, and the modern additions.
Foundations of Modern Cell Theory, Lumen Learning (SUNY Microbiology). — the classical tenets and their historical development.

laws.name: The Germ Theory of Disease
laws.statement: Many diseases are caused by microorganisms that invade the body, not by bad air.

sources.text: Germ theory of disease, Wikipedia. — the microbial cause of infectious disease, the miasma predecessor, and the cumulative history.
Germ theory, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the microorganism cause and its transformation of medicine.

laws.name: Koch's Postulates
laws.statement: Four tests to prove a specific microbe causes a specific disease.

sources.text: Koch, R. (1890). “The Aetiology of Tuberculosis.” New York: William R. Jenkins. — the English translation of Die Aetiologie der Tuberkulose, where the postulates are set out.
Koch's postulates, Wikipedia. — the four criteria, the Loeffler and Henle history, and the known exceptions.
Exceptions to Koch's Postulates, Biology LibreTexts. — asymptomatic carriers, unculturable pathogens, and the sufficient-not-necessary status.

laws.name: The Endosymbiotic Theory
laws.statement: Mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free-living bacteria that came to live inside other cells.

sources.text: Sagan, L. (1967). “On the origin of mitosing cells.” Journal of Theoretical Biology, vol. 14. — published under Lynn Margulis’s then-married name, Lynn Sagan.
Symbiogenesis, Wikipedia. — the bacterial origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts, the evidence, and Margulis's revival and rejected extensions.
Endosymbiont hypothesis, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the engulfment origin of organelles and the supporting evidence.

laws.name: The One Gene-One Enzyme Hypothesis
laws.statement: Each gene works by directing the making of one specific enzyme.

sources.text: Beadle & Tatum, "Genetic Control of Biochemical Reactions in Neurospora," PNAS 27 (1941): 499-506. — the founding experiments.
One gene-one enzyme hypothesis, Wikipedia. — the hypothesis, its Garrod precursor, and its progressive refinement.

laws.name: The Hill Equation
laws.statement: Cooperative binding gives an S-shaped curve of how saturated a molecule is with its ligand.

sources.text: Hill equation (biochemistry), Wikipedia. — the saturation equation, the Hill coefficient's meaning, and the caveat that it is not a site count.
Colquhoun, "A hundred years ago: the Hill equation" (2010). — the 1910 origin and Hill's own disclaimer of physical meaning.

laws.name: The Monro-Kellie Doctrine
laws.statement: The skull holds a fixed volume, so more of one thing inside means less of another or the pressure rises.

sources.text: Mokri, "The Monro-Kellie hypothesis: applications in CSF volume depletion," Neurology 56 (2001): 1746-1748. — the doctrine, its history, and the role of cerebrospinal fluid.
Intracranial Pressure Monitoring, StatPearls. — the fixed-volume principle, staged compensation, and the pressure-volume curve.

laws.name: The Lyon Hypothesis
laws.statement: In female mammals, one X chromosome in each cell is switched off, making females genetic mosaics.

sources.text: Lyon, "Gene Action in the X-chromosome of the Mouse," Nature 190 (1961): 372-373. — the random-inactivation hypothesis.
X-inactivation, Wikipedia. — dosage compensation, the XIST mechanism, calico cats, and escape genes.

laws.name: The Weismann Barrier
aliases: The continuity of the germ line
laws.statement: Heredity flows from germ cells to the body, never from the body back to the germ cells.

sources.text: Weismann, A. (1893). “The germ-plasm: a theory of heredity.” — the book setting out the germ-plasm theory.
Weismann barrier, Wikipedia. — the one-way germ-to-soma information flow, the argument against Lamarckism, and the plant and epigenetic caveats.
Germ plasm, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — Weismann's germ plasm theory and the continuity of the germ line.

laws.name: The Lock-and-Key Model
laws.statement: An enzyme fits its substrate like a lock fits one specific key.

sources.text: Fischer, "Einfluss der Configuration auf die Wirkung der Enzyme," Berichte der deutschen chemischen Gesellschaft 27 (1894): 2985-2993. — the original lock-and-key analogy.
Enzyme catalysis, Wikipedia. — enzyme specificity, the lock-and-key model, and its supersession by induced fit.

laws.name: The Law of Comparative Advantage
laws.statement: Trade benefits both sides when each specializes in what it gives up the least to produce.

sources.text: Ricardo, On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation (1817), Ch. 7. — the England-Portugal example and the doctrine of comparative advantage.
Comparative advantage, Wikipedia. — opportunity cost, the contrast with absolute advantage, and the model's limits.

laws.name: Creative Destruction
aliases: The perennial gale of creative destruction
laws.statement: Innovation renews an economy by continually destroying the old to make room for the new.

sources.text: Schumpeter, J. A. "The Process of Creative Destruction", chapter VII of Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy (1942) — where the phrase is introduced.
Schumpeter, Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy (1942), Ch. 7, 'The Process of Creative Destruction.' — the perennial gale and the essential fact about capitalism.
Alm and Cox, 'Creative Destruction,' Concise Encyclopedia of Economics (Econlib). — the process, its examples, and Schumpeter's account.

laws.name: The Fisher Equation
laws.statement: The nominal interest rate is roughly the real interest rate plus expected inflation.

sources.text: Fisher equation, Wikipedia. — the exact and approximate forms and the role of expected inflation.

Dimand and Gomez Betancourt, 'Retrospectives: Irving Fisher's Appreciation and Interest (1896) and the Fisher Relation,' Journal of Economic Perspectives 26(4) (2012): 185-196. — the origin of the relation and Fisher's own synthesis.

laws.name: Purchasing Power Parity
aliases: The purchasing-power-parity theory of exchange rates
laws.statement: Exchange rates should adjust until the same basket of goods costs the same across countries.

sources.text: Cassel, G. (1918). "Abnormal Deviations in International Exchanges." The Economic Journal 28(112), p. 413 — the paper that set out purchasing power parity.
Purchasing power parity, Wikipedia. — absolute and relative parity, the law of one price, the Big Mac index, and the limits.
Gustav Cassel, Concise Encyclopedia of Economics (Econlib). — Cassel's development of the theory and his League of Nations work.

laws.name: The Broken Window Fallacy
aliases: The parable of the broken window
That which is seen and that which is not seen
laws.statement: Destruction is not wealth: the spending it forces only diverts what would have been spent elsewhere.

sources.text: Bastiat, 'That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen' (1850), Section 1, 'The Broken Window' (Econlib translation). — the parable, the glazier, and the seen and the unseen.
Parable of the broken window, Wikipedia. — the fallacy, opportunity cost, Hazlitt's popularisation, and the distinction from broken windows theory.

laws.name: The Lump of Labour Fallacy
laws.statement: There is no fixed amount of work to share out, so one group working more need not leave less for others.

sources.text: Lump of labour fallacy, Wikipedia. — the fixed-work misconception, its applications, and Schloss's coinage.

Schloss, 'Why Working-Men Dislike Piece-Work,' The Economic Review, Vol. I, No. 3 (1891), pp. 311-326 (transcription). — the original naming of 'the theory of the Lump of Labour' among output-restricting pieceworkers.

laws.name: The Impossible Trinity
laws.statement: A country can have any two of a fixed exchange rate, free capital flows, and its own monetary policy, but never all three.

sources.text: Impossible trinity, Wikipedia. — the three-way constraint, the arbitrage mechanism, the Mundell-Fleming origin, and Rey's dilemma critique.

Mundell, 'Capital Mobility and Stabilization Policy under Fixed and Flexible Exchange Rates,' Canadian Journal of Economics and Political Science 29(4) (1963): 475-485. — the underlying open-economy model.

laws.name: Ricardian Equivalence
laws.statement: How a government funds its spending, by taxes now or borrowing to be repaid later, makes no difference to the economy.

sources.text: Barro, 'Are Government Bonds Net Wealth?,' Journal of Political Economy 82(6) (1974): 1095-1117 (Harvard DASH full text). — the modern formalisation and the bequest-motive argument.
Ricardian equivalence, Wikipedia. — the proposition, Ricardo's own doubt, the assumptions, and the mixed empirical record.

laws.name: The Median Voter Theorem
laws.statement: Under majority rule on a single issue, the median voter's preferred option beats every other.

sources.text: Black, 'On the Rationale of Group Decision-making,' Journal of Political Economy 56(1) (1948): 23-34. — the theorem that the median voter's motion beats every other under single-peaked preferences.
Median voter theorem, Wikipedia. — single-peakedness, the Condorcet-winner result, the Hotelling-Downs corollary, and the multidimensional breakdown.

laws.name: The Game of Chicken
laws.statement: Two players race toward a collision; each wants the other to swerve, and mutual nerve is the worst outcome for both.

sources.text: Chicken (game), Wikipedia. — the anti-coordination structure, the two equilibria, brinkmanship, and the hawk-dove equivalence.
Maynard Smith and Price, 'The Logic of Animal Conflict,' Nature 246 (1973): 15-18. — the hawk-dove game and the evolutionarily stable strategy.

laws.name: The Centipede Game
laws.statement: Two players can keep passing a growing pot, but backward reasoning says grab it all on the very first move.

sources.text: Rosenthal, 'Games of Perfect Information, Predatory Pricing and the Chain-Store Paradox,' Journal of Economic Theory 25(1) (1981): 92-100. — the original centipede game and the backward-induction prediction.
McKelvey and Palfrey, 'An Experimental Study of the Centipede Game,' Econometrica 60(4) (1992): 803-836. — the experimental refutation and the altruist explanation.

laws.name: The Dictator Game
laws.statement: Given money to split with a powerless stranger, people give away more than pure self-interest predicts.

sources.text: Forsythe, Horowitz, Savin, and Sefton, 'Fairness in Simple Bargaining Experiments,' Games and Economic Behavior 6(3) (1994): 347-369. — the standard two-player dictator design and the comparison with the ultimatum game.
Engel, 'Dictator games: a meta study,' Experimental Economics 14(4) (2011): 583-610. — the average gift, the tri-modal distribution, and the design sensitivities.

laws.name: The Law of the Instrument
laws.statement: If the only tool you have is a hammer, everything starts to look like a nail.

sources.text: Law of the instrument, Wikipedia. — Kaplan's naming, Maslow's phrasing, Tomkins, and the golden-hammer anti-pattern.
'If Your Only Tool Is a Hammer Then Every Problem Looks Like a Nail,' Quote Investigator. — the sourced origin chronology and the debunking of the Twain attribution.

laws.name: The Network Effect
laws.statement: A network grows more valuable to each user as more people join it.

sources.text: Network effect, Wikipedia. — the definition, direct and indirect effects, tipping and lock-in, and the contrast with economies of scale.
Katz and Shapiro, 'Network Externalities, Competition, and Compatibility,' American Economic Review 75(3) (1985): 424-440. — the canonical economic formalisation.

laws.name: The Bullwhip Effect
laws.statement: Small wobbles in consumer demand swell into ever-larger swings in orders as they travel up a supply chain.

sources.text: Lee, Padmanabhan, and Whang, 'The Bullwhip Effect in Supply Chains,' Sloan Management Review 38(3) (1997): 93-102. — the four causes, the P&G and HP cases, and the remedies.
Lee, Padmanabhan, and Whang, 'Information Distortion in a Supply Chain: The Bullwhip Effect,' Management Science 43(4) (1997): 546-558. — the analytical model of demand amplification.

laws.name: Heaps' Law
laws.statement: The number of distinct words in a text grows as a fractional power of its length.
laws.namedAfter: Harold Stanley Heaps and Gustav Herdan

sources.text: Heaps' law, Wikipedia. — the V=K n^beta form, the K and beta ranges, the Herdan 1960 and Heaps 1978 attributions, and the Zipf link.
Cook, 'Heaps' law: estimating vocabulary size from total words' (2019). — the formula, parameter ranges, and empirical fits to the King James Bible and Jane Austen.

laws.name: Menzerath's Law
aliases: The greater the whole, the smaller its parts
laws.statement: The larger a language construct, the shorter, on average, its parts.

sources.text: Menzerath's law, Wikipedia. — the whole-and-parts statement, Altmann's formula, and the cross-domain applications.
Torre, Debowski, and Hernandez-Fernandez, 'Can Menzerath's law be a criterion of complexity in communication?' (2021). — the triviality critique and the memoryless-source caveat.

laws.name: The Rank-Size Rule
laws.statement: A country's nth-largest city tends to be about one-nth the size of its largest.
laws.namedAfter: Felix Auerbach, Alfred Lotka, and George Kingsley Zipf

sources.text: Rank-size distribution, Wikipedia. — the one-over-n statement, the NYC-LA and Kinshasa examples, the King effect, and the log-normal caveat.
Gabaix, 'Zipf's Law for Cities: An Explanation,' Quarterly Journal of Economics 114(3) (1999): 739-767. — the proportionate-growth (Gibrat) mechanism for the exponent-one tail.

laws.name: The Experience Curve
laws.statement: Each time cumulative production doubles, unit costs fall by a roughly constant percentage.
laws.namedAfter: Bruce Henderson and the Boston Consulting Group

sources.text: Experience curve effects, Wikipedia. — the constant-percentage-per-doubling form, the mechanisms, the Henderson-Wright relationship, and the criticisms.
Boston Consulting Group, 'BCG Classics Revisited: The Experience Curve' (2013). — the 1966 semiconductor origin and the 20-30 percent per doubling figure.

laws.name: Swanson's Law
laws.statement: Solar module prices fall about 20% for every doubling of cumulative shipped volume.

sources.text: Swanson's law, Wikipedia. — the ~20 percent per doubling statement, the price history, and the naming by The Economist.
Our World in Data, 'Solar photovoltaic panel prices.' — the long-run module price series and learning-curve dataset.

laws.name: Pournelle's Iron Law of Bureaucracy
laws.statement: In any bureaucracy, those devoted to the organization itself end up controlling it, not those devoted to its goals.

sources.text: Pournelle, 'Pournelle's Iron Law of Bureaucracy,' Chaos Manor special report. — the two kinds of people, the control claim, and the school, NASA, and Soviet examples.
Jerry Pournelle, Wikipedia. — biography and the sourced statement of the iron law.

laws.name: Lehman's Laws of Software Evolution
laws.statement: Software that is actually used must keep changing, and grows more complex unless work is spent to fight it.

sources.text: Lehman, 'Programs, Life Cycles, and Laws of Software Evolution,' Proceedings of the IEEE 68(9) (1980): 1060-1076. — the laws and the S/P/E program classification.
Lehman's laws of software evolution, Wikipedia. — the eight laws, the E-type scope, and the open-source critiques.

laws.name: Beckstrom's Law
aliases: The transaction theory of network value
laws.statement: A network is worth the net value it adds to all the transactions its users conduct through it.

sources.text: Beckstrom's law, Wikipedia. — the transaction-summation statement, the general formula, the contrast with Metcalfe's and Reed's laws, and the negative-value example.
Lemos, 'Taking on Security with Beckstrom's Law,' MIT Technology Review, 3 August 2009. — the security decomposition and the degradation and bad-actor rationale.

laws.name: The Great Filter
laws.statement: Somewhere between dead matter and a galaxy-spanning civilization lies at least one barrier almost nothing gets past.

sources.text: Hanson, 'The Great Filter - Are We Almost Past It?' (1998). — the filter, the chain of steps, and the past-versus-future logic.
Bostrom, 'Where Are They? Why I Hope the Search for Extraterrestrial Life Finds Nothing,' MIT Technology Review (2008). — the formalisation and the 'bad news' implication.

laws.name: The Kardashev Scale
laws.statement: A civilization's advancement can be ranked by how much energy it can harness: a planet, a star, or a galaxy.

sources.text: Kardashev scale, Wikipedia. — the three types, Kardashev's original figures, Sagan's interpolation, and the later extensions.
Kardashev scale, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the definition, the round power figures, and Earth's rating near 0.7.

laws.name: The Copernican Principle
laws.statement: We occupy no special or privileged place in the universe; assume our vantage point is typical.

sources.text: Copernican principle, Wikipedia. — the typicality claim, the link to the cosmological principle, and Gott's temporal argument.
Cosmological principle, Wikipedia. — homogeneity and isotropy as the empirical cosmological form of the Copernican assumption.

laws.name: The Anthropic Principle
laws.statement: The universe we observe must be one that permits observers, so we should not be surprised it allows life.

sources.text: Carter, B. (1974). "Large Number Coincidences and the Anthropic Principle in Cosmology." IAU Symposium 63, 291-298 — the paper that named it.
Anthropic principle, Wikipedia. — the weak and strong forms, Carter's coinage, and the multiverse and fine-tuning connections.
Anthropic principle: Forms of the anthropic principle, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the WAP/SAP distinction and Dicke's earlier reasoning.

laws.name: The Fine-Tuned Universe
laws.statement: The constants of nature seem to lie in a narrow range that permits complex structure and life.

sources.text: Fine-Tuning, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the statement, the examples, the four explanations, and the critiques of the probability reasoning.
Cosmological constant problem, Wikipedia. — the vacuum-energy mismatch and Weinberg's anthropic bound.

laws.name: The Doomsday Argument
laws.statement: If you are a random human in the sequence of all who will ever live, humanity is unlikely to last vastly longer.

sources.text: Doomsday argument, Wikipedia. — the self-sampling reasoning, the birth-rank bound, and the Carter, Leslie, and Gott versions.
Dieks, 'Doomsday - or: The Dangers of Statistics,' The Philosophical Quarterly 42(166) (1992): 78-86. — the objection that the argument mis-samples one's temporal position.

laws.name: The Simulation Argument
laws.statement: At least one holds: civilizations die before maturity, mature ones shun ancestor-simulations, or we are almost certainly simulated.

sources.text: Bostrom, 'Are You Living in a Computer Simulation?,' The Philosophical Quarterly 53(211) (2003): 243-255. — the trilemma, the substrate-independence and indifference steps, and the even-credence conclusion.
Simulation hypothesis, Wikipedia. — the argument, its reception, and the distinction from the hypothesis.

laws.name: The Boltzmann Brain
laws.statement: In some cosmologies, brains fluctuating at random from chaos should vastly outnumber brains evolved by orderly history.

sources.text: Boltzmann brain, Wikipedia. — the fluctuation statistics, the cosmological problem, and the proposed resolutions.
Carroll, 'Why Boltzmann Brains Are Bad' (2017), arXiv:1702.00850. — the cognitive-instability argument for rejecting Boltzmann-brain-dominated theories.

laws.name: The Rare Earth Hypothesis
laws.statement: Microbial life may be common, but the chain of accidents needed for complex life makes it exceedingly rare.

sources.text: Ward, P. & Brownlee, D. (2000). “Rare Earth.” — the book making the argument.
Rare Earth hypothesis, Wikipedia. — the rarity-of-complex-life claim, the enumerated factors, and the Fermi and Copernican framing.
Rare Earth: Why Complex Life Is Uncommon in the Universe, Wikipedia. — the Ward and Brownlee book that originated the hypothesis.

laws.name: The Gaia Hypothesis
laws.statement: Life and its environment form one self-regulating system that keeps the Earth fit for life.

sources.text: Gaia hypothesis, Wikipedia. — the self-regulating-system claim, the weak-to-strong spectrum, and the Doolittle and Dawkins critiques.
Watson and Lovelock, 'Biological homeostasis of the global environment: the parable of Daisyworld,' Tellus B 35 (1983): 284-289. — the model showing regulation without teleology.

laws.name: The Medea Hypothesis
laws.statement: Life is ultimately self-destructive, repeatedly poisoning its own world rather than nurturing it.

sources.text: Medea hypothesis, Wikipedia. — the self-destructive-life claim, the biogenic extinction evidence, and the anti-Gaia framing.
Ward, The Medea Hypothesis: Is Life on Earth Ultimately Self-Destructive? (Princeton University Press, 2009). — the hypothesis and its evidence.

laws.name: Panspermia
laws.statement: Life may be spread between worlds, so life on Earth could have arrived from space rather than started here.

sources.text: Panspermia, Wikipedia. — the transport hypothesis, its variants, and the meteorite and orbital-survival evidence.
Crick and Orgel, 'Directed Panspermia,' Icarus 19 (1973): 341-346. — the directed-seeding proposal.

laws.name: The Faint Young Sun Paradox
laws.statement: The early Sun was far dimmer, yet the young Earth had liquid water instead of being frozen solid.

sources.text: Sagan and Mullen, 'Earth and Mars: Evolution of Atmospheres and Surface Temperatures,' Science 177(4043) (1972): 52-56. — the original statement of the paradox.
Feulner, 'The faint young Sun problem,' Reviews of Geophysics (2012). — the luminosity history, the proposed resolutions, and the proxy tension.

laws.name: Plate Tectonics
laws.statement: Earth's rigid outer shell is broken into moving plates, and the geology happens where they meet.

sources.text: Plate tectonics, Wikipedia. — the plate model, the three boundary types, the driving forces, and the historical synthesis.
This Dynamic Earth: Understanding plate motions, USGS. — the boundary types and how plates move.

laws.name: Continental Drift
laws.statement: The continents were once joined and have since drifted apart across the face of the Earth.

sources.text: Wegener, A. (1912). "Die Entstehung der Kontinente." Geologische Rundschau 3, 276-292 — the lecture in which continental drift was first put to geologists.
Alfred Wegener, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the 1912 lectures, the 1915 book, Pangaea, and the rejection over implausible driving forces.
Wegener's Puzzling Continental Drift Evidence, USGS. — the fossil, rock, and continental-fit evidence.

laws.name: Isostasy
laws.statement: Earth's crust floats in balance on the denser mantle, riding higher where it is thicker or lighter.

sources.text: Isostasy, Wikipedia. — the floating-crust principle, the Airy, Pratt, and flexural models, and the depth of compensation.
Airy, 'On the computation of the effect of the attraction of mountain-masses,' Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society 145 (1855). — the roots model of compensation.

laws.name: The Uniformitarian Principle
aliases: The present is the key to the past
laws.statement: The same natural processes at work today have always shaped the Earth: the present is the key to the past.

sources.text: Uniformitarianism, Wikipedia. — the principle, Hutton and Lyell, Whewell's coinage, and Gould's distinction.
Gould, 'Is uniformitarianism necessary?,' American Journal of Science 263 (1965): 223-228. — the methodological versus substantive distinction.

laws.name: The Principle of Superposition
laws.statement: In undisturbed layered rock, each bed is younger than the one below and older than the one above.

sources.text: Law of superposition, Wikipedia. — the principle, its qualifier for undeformed sequences, and Steno's authorship.
Geologic Principles: Superposition and Original Horizontality, U.S. National Park Service. — the statement and its role in relative dating.

laws.name: The Principle of Faunal Succession
laws.statement: Fossils follow one another through the rock record in a fixed, recognizable order, so strata can be dated by what they contain.

sources.text: Principle of faunal succession, Wikipedia. — the ordered succession of fossils and its use in correlation and relative dating.
Law of faunal succession, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the principle as the fundamental tool of stratigraphy and basis of the time scale.

laws.name: Milankovitch Cycles
aliases: The astronomical theory of ice ages
laws.statement: Slow changes in Earth's orbit and tilt pace the ice ages by redistributing sunlight.

sources.text: Milankovitch cycles, Wikipedia. — the three orbital cycles, their periods, and the open problems.
Hays, Imbrie, and Shackleton, 'Variations in the Earth's Orbit: Pacemaker of the Ice Ages,' Science 194 (1976): 1121-1132. — the deep-sea-core confirmation of orbital pacing.

laws.name: Snowball Earth
laws.statement: At times in the deep past, ice may have spread from the poles all the way to the equator, freezing the whole planet.

sources.text: Hoffman, Kaufman, Halverson, and Schrag, 'A Neoproterozoic Snowball Earth,' Science 281 (1998): 1342-1346. — the modern hypothesis, cap carbonates, and the carbon-isotope evidence.
Snowball Earth, Wikipedia. — the hypothesis, the Cryogenian glaciations, the mechanism, and the slushball debate.

laws.name: The Great Oxidation Event
laws.statement: Around 2.4 billion years ago, oxygen from photosynthesis first built up in the air, transforming the planet.

sources.text: Great Oxidation Event, Wikipedia. — the ~2.4 Ga rise, the oxygen-sink mechanism, the sulfur marker, and the consequences.
Farquhar, Bao, and Thiemens, 'Atmospheric Influence of Earth's Earliest Sulfur Cycle,' Science 289 (2000): 756-758. — the mass-independent sulfur-isotope evidence for the oxygenation threshold.

laws.name: The Thermohaline Circulation
laws.statement: Density differences from heat and salt drive a slow, globe-spanning overturning of the oceans.

sources.text: Broecker, 'The Great Ocean Conveyor,' Oceanography 4(2) (1991): 79-89. — the conveyor-belt concept and the density-driven overturning.
Thermohaline circulation, Wikipedia. — the density-driven circulation, deep-water formation, and its climate role.

laws.name: The Hadley Cell
laws.statement: Warm air rises at the equator, sinks in the subtropics, and returns as the trade winds.

sources.text: Hadley cell, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the tropical overturning cell, the trade winds, and the subtropical descent.
Hadley cell, Wikipedia. — the mechanism, the three-cell circulation, and the observed poleward widening.

laws.name: The El Nino-Southern Oscillation
laws.statement: The tropical Pacific swings every few years between a warm El Nino and a cool La Nina, reshaping weather worldwide.

sources.text: Bjerknes, J. (1969). “Atmospheric teleconnections from the equatorial Pacific.” Monthly Weather Review, vol. 97. — the paper linking the ocean and atmosphere halves, building on Walker’s 1920s Southern Oscillation.
El Nino, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the coupled ocean-atmosphere phenomenon, the phases, and the global impacts.
What is the El Nino-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) in a nutshell?, NOAA Climate.gov. — the normal, El Nino, and La Nina states and the wind-and-temperature mechanism.

laws.name: The Keeling Curve
laws.statement: A rising, saw-toothed record of atmospheric carbon dioxide, measured continuously since 1958.

sources.text: Trends in Atmospheric Carbon Dioxide (Mauna Loa), NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory. — the continuous record, current values, and the 1959 annual mean.
The History of the Keeling Curve, Scripps Institution of Oceanography. — Keeling's 1958 start, the seasonal cycle, and the record's significance.

laws.name: The Hodgkin-Huxley Model
aliases: The conductance-based model of the action potential
laws.statement: The nerve impulse arises from voltage-gated sodium and potassium currents, captured in a set of equations.

sources.text: Hodgkin and Huxley, 'A quantitative description of membrane current and its application to conduction and excitation in nerve,' Journal of Physiology 117 (1952): 500-544. — the model and its equations.
Hodgkin-Huxley model, Wikipedia. — the circuit picture, the gating variables, and the model's legacy.

laws.name: Hebb's Rule
aliases: Neurons that fire together wire together
laws.statement: When one neuron repeatedly helps fire another, the connection between them strengthens.

sources.text: Hebb, D. (2005). “The Organization of Behavior.” — the book stating the learning rule; this is the modern reissue of the 1949 edition.
Donald Olding Hebb, Canadian Association for Neuroscience. — the Hebb postulate, biography, and the Hebb synapse.
Hebbian theory overview, ScienceDirect Topics. — the postulate, the cell assembly, and the link to long-term potentiation.

laws.name: Long-Term Potentiation
laws.statement: Brief intense activity can lastingly strengthen a synapse, the leading cellular model of memory.

sources.text: Bliss and Lomo, 'Long-lasting potentiation of synaptic transmission in the dentate area of the anaesthetized rabbit following stimulation of the perforant path,' Journal of Physiology 232 (1973): 331-356. — the first demonstration.
Long-term potentiation overview, ScienceDirect Topics. — the NMDA-receptor mechanism, the Hebbian properties, and long-term depression.

laws.name: The Sodium-Potassium Pump
laws.statement: An ATP-powered pump drives sodium out of the cell and potassium in, three for two, building the gradients life runs on.

sources.text: Skou, 'The influence of some cations on an adenosine triphosphatase from peripheral nerves,' Biochimica et Biophysica Acta 23 (1957): 394-401. — the discovery of the pump.
Purves et al., Neuroscience, 'Active Transporters Create and Maintain Ion Gradients' (NCBI Bookshelf). — the pump's stoichiometry, function, and role in the membrane potential.

laws.name: The Frank-Starling Law of the Heart
laws.statement: The more the heart fills, the harder it contracts, so it ejects what it receives.

sources.text: Physiology, Frank Starling Law, StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf). — the preload-stroke volume relationship, its mechanism, and clinical relevance.
Han et al., 'Cardiac efficiency and Starling's Law of the Heart,' Journal of Physiology (2022). — the history and the length-dependent basis of the law.

laws.name: Starling's Principle
laws.statement: Fluid crosses a capillary wall according to the balance of hydrostatic and oncotic pressures.

sources.text: Levick, 'Revision of the Starling principle: new views of tissue fluid balance,' Journal of Physiology 557 (2004). — the glycocalyx model and the no-absorption rule.
Levick and Michel, 'Microvascular fluid exchange and the revised Starling principle,' Cardiovascular Research 87 (2010): 198-210. — the four forces and the revised steady state.

laws.name: The Fick Principle
aliases: The Fick method for cardiac output
laws.statement: An organ's uptake of a substance equals blood flow times the difference in its arterial and venous concentrations.

sources.text: Fick principle, Wikipedia. — the conservation-of-mass relation and its application to cardiac output.
Calculating Fick Cardiac Output, StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf). — the oxygen formula, the direct and indirect methods, and the limits.

laws.name: The Bohr Effect
laws.statement: Acid and carbon dioxide make hemoglobin release oxygen, unloading it where tissues need it most.

sources.text: Physiology, Bohr Effect, StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf). — the affinity shift, its allosteric mechanism, and P50.
Bohr, Hasselbalch, and Krogh (1904), English translation. — the original description of the carbon-dioxide influence on oxygen binding.

laws.name: The Haldane Effect
laws.statement: Deoxygenated blood carries more carbon dioxide, so unloading oxygen helps the blood pick up carbon dioxide.

sources.text: Christiansen, Douglas, and Haldane, 'The absorption and dissociation of carbon dioxide by human blood,' Journal of Physiology 48 (1914): 244-271. — the original description.
Physiology, Carbon Dioxide Retention, StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf). — the Haldane effect, carbon-dioxide transport, and the clinical context.

laws.name: The Henderson-Hasselbalch Equation
laws.statement: A buffer's pH equals the acid's pKa plus the log of the base-to-acid ratio.

sources.text: Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, Wikipedia. — the buffer and bicarbonate forms and the history.
de Levie, 'The Henderson-Hasselbalch Equation: Its History and Limitations,' Journal of Chemical Education 80(2) (2003): 146. — the derivation, the history, and the approximation's limits.

laws.name: The Oxygen-Hemoglobin Dissociation Curve
laws.statement: Hemoglobin's oxygen saturation rises with oxygen pressure along an S-shaped curve, thanks to cooperative binding.

sources.text: Physiology, Oxyhemoglobin Dissociation Curve, StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf). — the sigmoidal shape, cooperativity, P50, and the shift factors.
Oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, Wikipedia. — the curve, its shifts, and the contrast with myoglobin.

laws.name: The Baroreceptor Reflex
laws.statement: Stretch sensors in the arteries detect blood-pressure changes and trigger reflex corrections within seconds.
laws.namedAfter: Heinrich Ewald Hering and Corneille Heymans

sources.text: Physiology, Baroreceptors, StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf). — the anatomy, the reflex arc, and the short-term and resetting caveats.
Arterial Baroreceptors, CV Physiology. — the mechanism, direction, and clinical relevance.

laws.name: The Fog of War
laws.statement: In war, information is pervasively uncertain, so commanders must act on conjecture, not knowledge.

sources.text: Fog of war, Wikipedia. — the definition, the coinage flag, and the concept's spread.
Clausewitz, On War, Book 1, Chapter 3 (Graham translation, ClausewitzStudies.org). — the uncertainty, twilight, and guesses-at-truth passages.

laws.name: Lanchester's Laws
laws.statement: Under aimed fire, a force's combat power grows with the square of its numbers, rewarding concentration.

sources.text: Lanchester's laws, Wikipedia. — the linear and square laws, the mathematics, and the Osipov derivation.
Lanchester, Aircraft in Warfare: The Dawn of the Fourth Arm (1916), Internet Archive. — the original formulation and the principle of concentration.

laws.name: The OODA Loop
laws.statement: Whoever cycles through observe, orient, decide, and act faster and truer gets inside the other's decisions.

sources.text: OODA loop, Wikipedia. — the four phases, getting inside the opponent's cycle, and the primacy of orientation.
Richards, 'Boyd's OODA Loop' (peer-reviewed article by a Boyd associate). — the dominance of orientation and the non-linear structure.

laws.name: The Culminating Point of Victory
laws.statement: An offensive can be pushed past the point where its strength is spent, turning victory into defeat.

sources.text: Clausewitz, On War, Book 7, Chapter 22, 'On the Culminating Point of Victory' (Graham translation, ClausewitzStudies.org). — the strategic threshold and its reaction.
Culminating point, Wikipedia. — the concept, its two forms, and its place in doctrine.

laws.name: The Strategy of the Indirect Approach
laws.statement: Defeat the enemy not by attacking their strength head-on, but by dislocating their balance from an unexpected direction.

sources.text: Strategy (Liddell Hart book), Wikipedia. — the indirect approach, the title history, and the dislocation concept.
'B. H. Liddell Hart, Strategy (1954),' Classics of Strategy and Diplomacy. — dislocation, the two lines, the eight maxims, and the Mearsheimer critique.

laws.name: Mutual Assured Destruction
laws.statement: If both sides can annihilate each other even after being struck first, neither dares strike at all.

sources.text: Mutual assured destruction, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the doctrine, McNamara's assured destruction, and Brennan as critic.
McNamara, 'Mutual Deterrence' speech, San Francisco, 18 September 1967 (AtomicArchive). — the definition of assured second-strike capability.

laws.name: The Security Dilemma
laws.statement: One state arming for its own safety makes others feel less safe, spiralling toward conflict no one intended.

sources.text: Security dilemma, Wikipedia. — the definition, the anarchy and uncertainty conditions, and Jervis's four worlds.
Jervis, 'Cooperation Under the Security Dilemma,' World Politics 30(2) (1978): 167-214. — the offence-defence balance and the severity of the dilemma.

laws.name: The Thucydides Trap
laws.statement: When a rising power threatens to displace a ruling one, the resulting fear makes war dangerously likely.

sources.text: Allison, 'The Thucydides Trap: Are the U.S. and China Headed for War?,' The Atlantic (2015). — the concept and the US-China application.
Thucydides's Trap Case File, Harvard Belfer Center. — the sixteen cases and twelve wars.

laws.name: The Balance of Power
laws.statement: States act to keep any one power from dominating, so coalitions form against whoever grows too strong.

sources.text: Balance of power, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the definition, internal and external balancing, and Britain as balancer.
Political Realism in International Relations, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Morgenthau, Waltz, anarchy, and the balance of power.

laws.name: The Democratic Peace Theory
laws.statement: Democracies almost never go to war with one another, one of the strongest regularities in international relations.

sources.text: Democratic peace theory, Wikipedia. — the dyadic claim, the normative and institutional explanations, and the criticisms.
Doyle, 'Kant, Liberal Legacies, and Foreign Affairs,' Philosophy and Public Affairs 12 (1983). — the modern revival tying the pattern to Kant.

laws.name: Deterrence Theory
laws.statement: You prevent an attack by making its expected cost outweigh any gain, so the adversary chooses restraint.

sources.text: Deterrence theory, Wikipedia. — the typology of punishment and denial, the rationality assumption, and the criticisms.
Snyder, Deterrence and Defense: Toward a Theory of National Security (Princeton University Press, 1961). — the distinction between deterrence by denial and by punishment.

laws.name: The Madman Theory
laws.statement: Seem unhinged enough to do the unthinkable, and adversaries may back down from threats a rational leader could never make credible.

sources.text: Madman theory, Wikipedia. — the strategy, the Nixon-Haldeman origin, and the disputed effectiveness.
'Madman or Mad Genius? The International Benefits and Domestic Costs of the Madman Strategy' (McManus), Belfer Center. — the scholarly analysis of its failure modes and costs.

laws.name: The Domino Theory
laws.statement: Let one country fall to an ideology and its neighbours topple in turn, like a row of dominoes.

sources.text: Domino theory, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — Eisenhower's 1954 formulation, the Vietnam justification, and the theory's later discrediting.
Domino theory, Wikipedia. — the falling-domino principle, the containment antecedent, and the debate over its validity.

laws.name: Self-Organized Criticality
laws.statement: Some systems tune themselves to the brink of a phase transition, where a single grain can trigger an avalanche of any size.

sources.text: Bak, Tang & Wiesenfeld, 'Self-organized criticality: An explanation of the 1/f noise,' Physical Review Letters 59, 381 (1987). — the founding paper and the sandpile.
Self-organized criticality, Wikipedia. — the self-tuning critical state, the sandpile model, and the criticisms.

laws.name: The Small-World Phenomenon
laws.statement: In a vast, mostly clustered social network, any two people are linked by a surprisingly short chain of acquaintances.

sources.text: Small-world experiment, Wikipedia. — Milgram's completion figures, the five-and-a-half-to-six median, Kleinfeld's critique, and the Karinthy origin.
Backstrom, Boldi, Rosa, Ugander & Vigna, 'Four Degrees of Separation' (2012), arXiv:1111.4570. — the Facebook study finding an average distance of about four.

laws.name: Preferential Attachment
laws.statement: New links in a growing network attach preferentially to nodes that already have many, so the well-connected grow fastest.

sources.text: Barabási & Albert, 'Emergence of scaling in random networks,' Science 286:509-512 (1999). — the model and the two mechanisms, growth and preferential attachment.
Broido & Clauset, 'Scale-free networks are rare,' Nature Communications 10:411 (2019). — the empirical challenge to the ubiquity of scale-free structure.

laws.name: The Power-Law Distribution
laws.statement: A few events are enormous and almost all are tiny, and the frequency of an event falls as a power of its size.

sources.text: Clauset, Shalizi & Newman, 'Power-law distributions in empirical data,' SIAM Review 51(4):661-703 (2009), arXiv:0706.1062. — the rigorous testing framework and the mixed verdict on claimed power laws.
Power law, Wikipedia. — scale invariance, heavy tails, log-log signature, and the caveat that a log-log line is insufficient evidence.

laws.name: More Is Different
aliases: The autonomy of the special sciences
laws.statement: Assemble enough parts and entirely new laws emerge that knowing the pieces alone would never let you predict.

sources.text: Anderson, 'More Is Different,' Science 177(4047):393-396 (1972). — the constructionist critique, broken symmetry, and the hierarchy of the sciences.
Philip W. Anderson, Wikipedia. — the essay, his Nobel Prize, and his role in founding the Santa Fe Institute.

laws.name: The Edge of Chaos
aliases: Life at the edge of chaos
laws.statement: Poised between rigid order and pure randomness, a system finds the narrow band where rich, adaptive behaviour is possible.

sources.text: Mitchell, Crutchfield & Hraber, 'Dynamics, Computation, and the Edge of Chaos: A Re-Examination' (1993), arXiv:adap-org/9306003. — the challenge to the computation-at-the-edge claim.
Edge of chaos, Wikipedia. — Packard coining the phrase, Langton's lambda and cellular automata, and the re-examination critique.

laws.name: The Law of Requisite Variety
laws.statement: To control a system, a regulator must command at least as much variety as the disturbances it has to counter.

sources.text: Variety (cybernetics), Wikipedia. — Ashby's definition of variety, the law, the information-theoretic link, and Beer's restatement.
Good regulator theorem, Wikipedia. — Conant & Ashby's 1970 result and its statement and interpretation.

laws.name: The Strength of Weak Ties
laws.statement: Acquaintances, not close friends, are often the ones who bring you genuinely new information.

sources.text: Granovetter, 'The Strength of Weak Ties,' American Journal of Sociology 78(6):1360-1380 (1973). — the bridging argument, tie strength, and the forbidden triad.
Rajkumar, Saint-Jacques, Bojinov, Brynjolfsson & Aral, 'A Causal Test of the Strength of Weak Ties,' Science 377:1304-1310 (2022). — the large-scale LinkedIn experiment and the inverted-U finding.

laws.name: The Adjacent Possible
laws.statement: At any moment a system can only reach what lies one step away, and each step taken opens up new steps that did not exist before.

sources.text: Tria, Loreto, Servedio & Strogatz, 'The dynamics of correlated novelties,' Scientific Reports 4:5890 (2014). — the urn-with-triggering model of expansion into the adjacent possible.
Stuart Kauffman, Wikipedia. — Kauffman's development of the adjacent possible and its role in his account of the biosphere and innovation.

laws.name: Cascading Failure
laws.statement: One component fails, its load falls on the rest, and the overload topples them in turn until much of the system is gone.

sources.text: Motter & Lai, 'Cascade-based attacks on complex networks,' Physical Review E 66:065102(R) (2002). — the load-and-capacity model of overload cascades.

Buldyrev, Parshani, Paul, Stanley & Havlin, 'Catastrophic cascade of failures in interdependent networks,' Nature 464:1025-1028 (2010), arXiv:0907.1182. — the interdependent-network amplification of cascades.

laws.name: The Butterfly Effect
laws.statement: In a chaotic system, a difference too small to measure grows until it swamps any long-range prediction.

sources.text: Lorenz, 'Deterministic Nonperiodic Flow,' Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences 20(2):130-141 (1963). — the founding paper of chaos theory and sensitive dependence.
Butterfly effect, Wikipedia. — sensitive dependence, the Lorenz system, and the murky provenance of the phrase.

laws.name: Stigmergy
laws.statement: Agents coordinate not by talking but by leaving traces in a shared environment that prompt the next action.

sources.text: Stigmergy, Wikipedia. — the definition, Grassé's coining, sematectonic versus sign-based, and applications from ants to human collaboration.
Grassé, 'La reconstruction du nid et les coordinations interindividuelles... La théorie de la stigmergie,' Insectes Sociaux 6:41-80 (1959). — the original coining paper on termite nest-building.

laws.name: The Coupon Collector's Problem
laws.statement: Collecting the whole set takes far longer than the last few items, because the final ones almost never turn up.

sources.text: Coupon collector's problem, Wikipedia. — the n-times-harmonic expectation, the geometric mechanism, the variance bound, and the Erdős-Rényi Gumbel limit.
Coupon Collector Problem, Brilliant Math & Science Wiki. — the expected value and the per-stage geometric derivation.

laws.name: Condorcet's Jury Theorem
laws.statement: If each voter is more likely right than wrong, a larger majority is almost certain to reach the correct verdict.

sources.text: Jury Theorems, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the statement, the competence and independence assumptions, and the criticisms.
Condorcet's jury theorem, Wikipedia. — the p-above-half result, the incompetent-crowd flip, and the correlated-votes and heterogeneity caveats.

laws.name: May's Theorem
laws.statement: For a choice between just two options, simple majority rule is the only method that treats voters and options fairly and responds the right way to a switched vote.

sources.text: May's theorem, Wikipedia. — the three conditions, the biconditional characterisation, and the two-alternative scope.
Social Choice Theory, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — May's axioms and the contrast with Arrow's impossibility theorem.

laws.name: The Revelation Principle
laws.statement: Anything a clever mechanism can achieve, a simple honest one can achieve too, where telling the truth is the best strategy.

sources.text: Revelation principle, Wikipedia. — the statement, the dominant-strategy and Bayesian versions, and the attributions.
Mechanism design, Wikipedia. — the Bayesian revelation-principle formulation and the 2007 Nobel to Hurwicz, Maskin, and Myerson.

laws.name: The Ellsberg Paradox
laws.statement: People will pay to avoid unknown odds, preferring a known gamble even when it cannot be squared with any consistent belief.

sources.text: Ellsberg paradox, Wikipedia. — the three-colour urn, the preference reversals, and the sure-thing-principle violation.
Ellsberg, 'Risk, Ambiguity, and the Savage Axioms,' Quarterly Journal of Economics 75(4):643-669 (1961). — the original statement and the ambiguity concept.

laws.name: The Marginal Value Theorem
laws.statement: A forager should quit a depleting patch the moment its return rate falls to the average for the whole habitat.

sources.text: Charnov, 'Optimal foraging, the marginal value theorem,' Theoretical Population Biology 9(2):129-136 (1976). — the decision rule and the tangent construction.
Marginal value theorem, Wikipedia. — the statement, the graphical solution, the predictions, and the evidence.

laws.name: Fisher's Fundamental Theorem of Natural Selection
laws.statement: Selection lifts a population's fitness at a rate equal to the additive genetic variance in fitness it has to work with.

sources.text: Fisher's fundamental theorem of natural selection, Wikipedia. — the statement, the misunderstanding that fitness always rises, and Price's partial-change clarification.
Price, 'Fisher's fundamental theorem made clear,' Annals of Human Genetics 36(2):129-140 (1972). — the demonstration that the theorem is exact but partial.

laws.name: The Rule of 72
laws.statement: To find how many years money takes to double, divide 72 by the annual percentage rate.

sources.text: Pacioli, L. (1494). "Summa de Arithmetica, Geometria, Proportioni et Proportionalita" — the earliest known statement of the doubling rule. Smithsonian Libraries scan.
Rule of 72, Wikipedia. — the formula, the ln(2) basis, why 72 is chosen, and the rule-of-70 and tripling variants.
The Rule of 72, Stanford University EE204. — the derivation from ln(2) and the accuracy across interest rates.

laws.name: The Taylor Rule
laws.statement: A central bank should raise its interest rate by more than one point for each point of inflation, adjusting also for economic slack.

sources.text: Taylor, 'Discretion versus policy rules in practice,' Carnegie-Rochester Conference Series on Public Policy 39:195-214 (1993). — the original rule and calibration.
Bernanke, 'The Taylor Rule: A benchmark for monetary policy?', Brookings Institution (2015). — the rule as description and benchmark, and the rules-versus-discretion debate.

laws.name: Tobin's q
laws.statement: When the market values a firm's capital above what it costs to replace, it pays to build more; below that, it does not.

sources.text: The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences 1981 (James Tobin), NobelPrize.org. — the award and the description of Tobin's q.
Hayashi, 'Tobin's Marginal q and Average q: A Neoclassical Interpretation,' Econometrica 50(1):213-224 (1982). — the conditions under which average q equals marginal q.

laws.name: The Iron Law of Wages
laws.statement: Real wages are dragged back toward bare subsistence, because higher pay only breeds more workers to compete it away.

sources.text: Iron law of wages, Wikipedia. — Lassalle's coinage, the Ricardo and Malthus roots, Marx's criticism, and the demographic-transition refutation.
Marx, 'Critique of the Gotha Programme' (1875), part II. — Marx's rejection of the iron law as Lassalle's and its Malthusian basis.

laws.name: The Bohr Model
laws.statement: Electrons circle the nucleus only in fixed, quantized orbits, jumping between them by emitting or absorbing a single photon.

sources.text: Bohr model, Wikipedia. — the quantized orbits, the minus 13.6 eV levels and 0.529 angstrom radius, and the model's failures.
Niels Bohr, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the 1913 model, its explanation of the hydrogen spectrum, and the 1922 Nobel Prize.

laws.name: The Schwarzschild Radius
laws.statement: Compress any mass inside this radius and not even light can escape, and it becomes a black hole.

sources.text: Schwarzschild radius, Wikipedia. — the formula, the Sun and Earth values, the event horizon, and the coordinate-versus-true singularity.
Karl Schwarzschild, Wikipedia. — the 1916 solution of Einstein's field equations and its wartime origin.

laws.name: Kepler's Third Law
laws.statement: The square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of its distance from the Sun.

sources.text: Kepler, J. (1619). "Harmonices Mundi, Libri V" — Book V, where the period-distance relation appears. Smithsonian Libraries scan.
Kepler's laws of planetary motion, Wikipedia. — the harmonic law, the Newtonian form with the total mass, and the three laws in context.
Astronomia nova, Wikipedia. — the 1609 work grounding the first two laws in Tycho Brahe's observations of Mars.

laws.name: Carnot's Theorem
laws.statement: No heat engine between two temperatures can beat the efficiency of a reversible one, set only by those two temperatures.

sources.text: Carnot's theorem (thermodynamics), Wikipedia. — the maximum-efficiency statement, the one-minus-temperature-ratio formula, and the caloric-theory origin.
Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire, Wikipedia. — Carnot's 1824 work and its foundational role in thermodynamics.

laws.name: The Eddington Limit
laws.statement: A star or accreting object can shine only so brightly before its own light blows its outer layers away.

sources.text: Eddington luminosity, Wikipedia. — the radiation-gravity balance, the formula and per-solar-mass value, and the super-Eddington puzzle.
Arthur Eddington, Wikipedia. — the stellar-structure context in which the limit was developed.

The review "Breaking the limit: Super-Eddington accretion onto black holes and neutron stars" (arXiv:1903.06844), defining the limit as the point where outward radiation force equals gravity — supports the definition and numerical scaling.

laws.name: The Compton Effect
laws.statement: An X-ray bouncing off an electron comes away with a longer wavelength, as if two particles had collided.

sources.text: Compton scattering, Wikipedia. — the wavelength-shift formula, the angle-only dependence, the 1923 experiment, and the particle-nature significance.
Compton effect, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the definition, the formula, and the demonstration of light's particle nature.

laws.name: The Equipartition Theorem
laws.statement: In a system at temperature T, every way of holding energy that counts quadratically gets the same average share, half of kT.

sources.text: Equipartition theorem, Wikipedia. — the half-kT rule, the heat-capacity consequences, and the frozen-out-modes and ultraviolet-catastrophe failures.
Equipartition of energy, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the half-kT-per-degree-of-freedom statement and the monatomic and solid heat capacities.

laws.name: The Virial Theorem
laws.statement: In a stable, gravitationally bound system, the average kinetic energy is exactly half the magnitude of the potential energy.

sources.text: Virial theorem, Wikipedia. — the general and power-law forms, the etymology and Clausius 1870, and Zwicky's dark-matter application.
Virial theorem, Encyclopedia of Mathematics. — the 2T equals minus the virial statement, the power-law form, and the bounded-domain condition.

laws.name: Graham's Law of Effusion
laws.statement: Lighter gases escape through a tiny hole faster, at a rate set by one over the square root of their molar mass.

sources.text: Graham's law, Wikipedia. — the inverse-square-root-of-molar-mass relation, the kinetic-theory basis, and the uranium-enrichment application.
Graham's Laws of Diffusion and Effusion, Chemistry LibreTexts. — the effusion-versus-diffusion distinction and the derivation from molecular speeds.

laws.name: Kin Selection
laws.statement: Helping a relative reproduce can spread your own genes, so evolution can favour altruism toward kin.

sources.text: Kin selection, Wikipedia. — inclusive fitness, Hamilton's rule, the eusociality debate, and the green-beard distinction.
Nowak, Tarnita & Wilson, 'The evolution of eusociality,' Nature 466:1057-1062 (2010). — the challenge to inclusive-fitness theory that drew a large rebuttal.

laws.name: The Selfish Gene
laws.statement: Look at evolution from the gene's point of view, and organisms are survival machines built to copy their genes.

sources.text: Dawkins, R. (1976). "The Selfish Gene" — the book that put the gene's-eye view to a general readership. DOI resolves to the Routledge edition of the same work.
The Selfish Gene, Wikipedia. — the gene-centred view, replicators and vehicles, the meme, and the metaphor clarification.
Gene-centered view of evolution, Wikipedia. — the replicator concept, Williams 1966 as precursor, and the levels-of-selection debate.

laws.name: Punctuated Equilibrium
laws.statement: In the fossil record, species mostly stay unchanged for ages, then shift rapidly during brief bursts of speciation.

sources.text: Eldredge, N. & Gould, S. J. (1972). "Punctuated Equilibria: An Alternative to Phyletic Gradualism" — the chapter that proposed it, deposited by the American Museum of Natural History.
Punctuated equilibrium, Wikipedia. — the stasis-and-punctuation hypothesis, the Mayr foundation, and the saltation and creationist misreadings.
Punctuated Equilibria, TalkOrigins Archive. — the clarification that it is neither saltational nor anti-Darwinian.

laws.name: Sexual Selection
laws.statement: Traits can evolve because they win mates rather than aid survival, which is why the peacock has its tail.

sources.text: Darwin, C. (1871). "The Descent of Man, and Selection in Relation to Sex" — where sexual selection was set out at length, scanned by the Biodiversity Heritage Library.
Sexual selection, Wikipedia. — the two mechanisms, Darwin's 1871 account, and the runaway, good-genes, and handicap theories.
Bateman's principle, Wikipedia. — the investment asymmetry, anisogamy, and the disputed founding study.

laws.name: Batesian Mimicry
laws.statement: A harmless species evolves to look like a dangerous one, borrowing a warning it never earned.

sources.text: Batesian mimicry, Wikipedia. — the palatable-mimic definition, Bates's 1862 paper, aposematism, and frequency dependence.
Ritland & Brower, 'The viceroy butterfly is not a Batesian mimic,' Nature 350:497-498 (1991). — the reclassification of the viceroy as unpalatable.

laws.name: Müllerian Mimicry
laws.statement: Two genuinely dangerous species come to look alike, sharing the cost of teaching predators to stay away.

sources.text: Müllerian mimicry, Wikipedia. — the mutual, shared-signal definition, Müller's 1878 model, and mimicry rings.
Mimicry: Müllerian mimicry, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the cost-sharing of predator education across species with a shared warning pattern.

laws.name: The Theory of Island Biogeography
aliases: The equilibrium theory of insular zoogeography
laws.statement: The number of species on an island settles where the rate of new arrivals balances the rate of extinctions.

sources.text: The Theory of Island Biogeography, Wikipedia. — the immigration-extinction equilibrium, area and distance, turnover, and the SLOSS legacy.
Equilibrium Theory of Island Biogeography: A Review, USDA Forest Service. — the graphical equilibrium model and the Simberloff-Wilson experiment.

laws.name: The Latitudinal Diversity Gradient
laws.statement: Life is richest near the equator and thins toward the poles, but no one is sure exactly why.

sources.text: Latitudinal gradients in species diversity, Wikipedia. — the tropics-to-poles pattern, the competing hypotheses, the explicit lack of consensus, and the exceptions.
Hillebrand, 'On the generality of the latitudinal diversity gradient,' The American Naturalist 163(2):192-211 (2004). — the meta-analysis confirming the pattern and its scale dependence.

laws.name: r/K Selection Theory
laws.statement: Some species bet on many cheap offspring in a boom-and-bust world; others on a few well-tended ones near the limit.

sources.text: r/K selection theory, Wikipedia. — the r and K contrast, the logistic-equation origin, and the theory's decline and misuse.
Pianka, 'On r- and K-Selection,' The American Naturalist 104(940):592-597 (1970). — the life-history elaboration of the framework.

laws.name: The Metabolic Theory of Ecology
laws.statement: How fast an organism burns energy, set by its size and temperature, may govern the pace of ecology from cells to ecosystems.

sources.text: Brown, Gillooly, Allen, Savage & West, 'Toward a Metabolic Theory of Ecology,' Ecology 85(7):1771-1789 (2004). — the founding synthesis and the size-and-temperature scaling.
Metabolic theory of ecology, Wikipedia. — the size-and-temperature equation, the WBE network model, and the disputed exponent and Glazier critique.

laws.name: Taylor's Law
laws.statement: Across sampled populations, the variance in a species' abundance grows as a power of its mean abundance.

sources.text: Taylor's law, Wikipedia. — the variance-equals-a-times-mean-to-the-b form, the aggregation interpretation, and the broad generality and contested mechanism.
Cohen, Xu & Brunborg, 'Fluctuation Scaling, Taylor's Law, and Crime,' PLoS ONE (2013). — the connection to fluctuation scaling beyond ecology.

laws.name: The Error Catastrophe
laws.statement: Push a replicator's mutation rate past a critical threshold and its genetic information dissolves into noise.

sources.text: Error threshold (evolution), Wikipedia. — the error threshold, the master sequence and quasispecies, Eigen's paradox, and the genome-length limit.
'Lethal Mutagenesis of RNA Viruses and Approved Drugs with Antiviral Mutagenic Activity,' Viruses (2022). — RNA viruses near the threshold and the antiviral application.

laws.name: Bateson's Rule
laws.statement: When an extra limb sprouts beside a normal one, the pair come out as mirror images of each other.

sources.text: William Bateson, Wikipedia. — the 1894 'Materials for the Study of Variation', the coining of genetics, and his morphological work.
French, Bryant & Bryant, 'Pattern regulation in epimorphic fields,' Science 193:969-981 (1976). — the polar coordinate model explaining mirror-symmetric supernumerary limbs.

laws.name: Universal Grammar
laws.statement: The capacity for language is innate, and all human languages share a deep structure wired into the mind.

sources.text: Dąbrowska, 'What exactly is Universal Grammar, and has anyone seen it?', Frontiers in Psychology 6:852 (2015). — the definition, the innateness claim, and the disagreement over its contents.
Evans & Levinson, 'The myth of language universals,' Behavioral and Brain Sciences 32(5):429-492 (2009). — the typological challenge to proposed universals.

laws.name: The Poverty of the Stimulus
laws.statement: Children learn a grammar richer than anything their limited, uncorrected input could have taught them.

sources.text: Poverty of the stimulus, Wikipedia. — the underdetermination argument, structure-dependence, the no-negative-evidence point, and the criticisms.
Pullum & Scholz, 'Empirical assessment of stimulus poverty arguments,' The Linguistic Review 19:9-50 (2002). — the challenge that the crucial input is attested in corpora.

laws.name: The Critical Period Hypothesis
laws.statement: There is a window in early life when language is learned effortlessly, and it narrows with age.

sources.text: Critical period hypothesis, Wikipedia. — the Penfield-Roberts and Lenneberg origins and the first-versus-second-language and critical-versus-sensitive distinctions.
Hartshorne, Tenenbaum & Pinker, 'A critical period for second language acquisition,' Cognition 177:263-277 (2018). — the large study placing the grammar-learning decline near age seventeen.

laws.name: The Cooperative Principle
laws.statement: We assume our conversational partner is cooperating, and from that assumption we infer what they really mean.

sources.text: Paul Grice, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the cooperative principle, the maxims, implicature and cancellability, and the 1967 lectures.
Cooperative principle, Wikipedia. — the exact wording, the four maxims, flouting versus violating, and the Malagasy criticism.

laws.name: The Great Vowel Shift
laws.statement: Between about 1400 and 1700 English long vowels all rose, which is why the spelling no longer matches the sound.

sources.text: Great Vowel Shift, Wikipedia. — the raising and diphthongisation of the long vowels, the spelling consequence, and the unsettled causes.
Great Vowel Shift, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the dating, the examples, and Jespersen's coinage of the term.

laws.name: The Comparative Method
