laws.statement: Compare related languages for regular sound correspondences, and you can prove common descent and rebuild their lost ancestor.

sources.text: Comparative method, Wikipedia. — the reliance on regular correspondences, the staged procedure, the history, and the limitations.
Laryngeal theory, Wikipedia. — Saussure's 1879 prediction and its confirmation by the decipherment of Hittite.

laws.name: The Neogrammarian Hypothesis
laws.statement: Sound change is regular and exceptionless, hitting every word that meets its conditions, so apparent exceptions have other causes.

sources.text: Neogrammarian, Wikipedia. — the exceptionlessness principle, the two pillars, the Leipzig figures, and the lexical-diffusion criticism.
Verner's law, Wikipedia. — the accent-conditioned regularity that vindicated the Neogrammarian principle.

laws.name: Grassmann's Law
laws.statement: When two aspirated consonants fall in successive syllables, the first one loses its aspiration.

sources.text: Grassmann's law, Wikipedia. — the deaspiration rule, the Greek examples, the Grimm's-law-exceptions connection, and the independence debate.
Hermann Grassmann, Wikipedia. — that the mathematician of exterior algebra turned to Sanskrit and formulated the sound law.

laws.name: The Sonority Hierarchy
laws.statement: Sounds rank by how open and resonant they are, and a syllable rises to a sonority peak at its vowel and falls away.

sources.text: Sonority sequencing principle, Wikipedia. — the nucleus as sonority peak, the rise-and-fall requirement, and the plant-versus-lpant contrast.
Sonority hierarchy, Wikipedia. — the ranking of sound classes, the s-cluster exceptions, and the phonetic-correlate debate.

laws.name: The Arbitrariness of the Sign
laws.statement: There is no natural bond between a word's sound and its meaning; the link is pure convention.

sources.text: Course in General Linguistics, Wikipedia. — arbitrariness as the first principle, signifier and signified, value as difference, and the posthumous compilation.

Ćwiek et al., 'The bouba/kiki effect is robust across cultures and writing systems,' Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B (2022). — the cross-cultural sound-symbolism challenge to strict arbitrariness.

laws.name: Markedness
laws.statement: In a pair of forms, one is the plain default and the other is the special, more complex, rarer case.

sources.text: Markedness, Wikipedia. — the marked-unmarked distinction, the correlated properties, the Prague School origin, and the Optimality Theory connection.
Haspelmath, 'Against markedness (and what to replace it with),' Journal of Linguistics 42(1):25-70 (2006). — the argument that the term conflates many senses and should be replaced by frequency.

laws.name: Wackernagel's Law
laws.statement: Unstressed little words lean on the first word of a clause and settle into second position.

sources.text: Wackernagel's law, Wikipedia. — the second-position requirement, the prosodic motivation, and the Greek, Latin, and South Slavic examples.
Wackernagel, 'On a law of Indo-European word order' (1892), Language Science Press translation (2020). — the original statement of the law.

laws.name: The Brevity Law
laws.statement: The more often a word is used, the shorter it tends to be.

sources.text: Brevity law, Wikipedia. — the frequency-length relation, the Zipf origin, the least-effort framing, and the animal-communication extensions.
Bentz & Ferrer-i-Cancho, 'Zipf's law of abbreviation as a language universal.' — the negative frequency-length correlation across 986 languages.

laws.name: The Turing Machine
laws.statement: A head reading and writing symbols on an endless tape, following a finite table of rules, can compute anything computable.

sources.text: Turing, A. M. (1936-37). "On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem." Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society s2-42(1), 230-265 — the paper defining the machine.
Turing machine, Wikipedia. — the tape-head-states model, the universal machine, and Turing-completeness.
The Church-Turing Thesis, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the 1936 paper, the equivalence with lambda calculus, and the thesis.

laws.name: The Lambda Calculus
laws.statement: Build all of computation out of nothing but functions that take arguments and are applied to them.

sources.text: The Lambda Calculus, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the term-forming rules, beta-reduction, Turing-completeness, and Curry-Howard.
Lambda calculus, Wikipedia. — the syntax, reduction rules, Church encodings, and typed-versus-untyped distinction.

laws.name: The Entscheidungsproblem
laws.statement: Hilbert asked for an algorithm to decide whether any logical statement is valid; in 1936 it was proved impossible.

sources.text: The Rise and Fall of the Entscheidungsproblem, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the 1928 formulation, the 1936 negative solution, and the semi-decidability nuance.
Entscheidungsproblem, Wikipedia. — Hilbert and Ackermann, the Church and Turing proofs, and the link to the birth of computer science.

laws.name: The Cook-Levin Theorem
laws.statement: Boolean satisfiability is NP-complete, so every problem whose answer is easy to check reduces to it.

sources.text: Cook-Levin theorem, Wikipedia. — SAT as the first NP-complete problem, the reduction, and the P-versus-NP connection.
Stephen A. Cook, A.M. Turing Award, ACM. — Cook's 1971 result and the 1982 Turing Award.

laws.name: The Time Hierarchy Theorem
laws.statement: Give a computer strictly more time and it can solve strictly more problems.

sources.text: Time hierarchy theorem, Wikipedia. — the strict-containment statement, the P-inside-EXPTIME consequence, and the diagonalisation proof.
Hartmanis & Stearns, 'On the Computational Complexity of Algorithms,' Transactions of the AMS 117:285-306 (1965). — the founding paper of complexity theory.

laws.name: The Pumping Lemma
aliases: The pumping lemma for regular languages
laws.statement: Every long enough string in a regular language has a middle part you can repeat and still stay in the language.

sources.text: Pumping lemma for regular languages, Wikipedia. — the three conditions, the non-regularity proof method, and the necessary-not-sufficient point.
Pumping lemma for context-free languages, Wikipedia. — the five-part decomposition and the two-part pumping for context-free languages.

laws.name: The Master Theorem
laws.statement: For a divide-and-conquer algorithm, compare the work of splitting to the work of recursing to read off its running time.

sources.text: Master theorem (analysis of algorithms), Wikipedia. — the recurrence form, the three cases and critical exponent, and the Akra-Bazzi generalisation.
'A Best Possible General Form of the Master Theorem for Divide-and-Conquer Recurrences' (2025), arXiv:2507.16064. — a modern treatment of the theorem and its cases.

laws.name: The FLP Impossibility
laws.statement: In a fully asynchronous system, no deterministic protocol can guarantee agreement if even one process might crash.

sources.text: Fischer, Lynch & Paterson, 'Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process,' Journal of the ACM 32(2):374-382 (1985). — the impossibility result and its conditions.
Consensus (computer science), Wikipedia. — the consensus properties, the FLP result, and the partial-synchrony, randomisation, and failure-detector circumventions.

laws.name: The Dining Philosophers Problem
laws.statement: Five philosophers share five forks, each needing both neighbours' forks to eat, and a naive protocol leaves them all stuck.

sources.text: Dining philosophers problem, Wikipedia. — the setup, the deadlock via circular wait, and the resource-ordering and arbitrator solutions.
Deadlock (computer science), Wikipedia. — the four Coffman conditions from Coffman, Elphick, and Shoshani's 1971 'System Deadlocks'.

laws.name: The Shannon-Hartley Theorem
laws.statement: A noisy channel of a given bandwidth can carry error-free information only up to a hard limit set by its signal-to-noise ratio.

sources.text: Shannon-Hartley theorem, Wikipedia. — the capacity formula, the reliability threshold, the AWGN assumption, and the non-constructive proof.
Shannon, 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication,' Bell System Technical Journal (1948). — the founding theory of channel capacity.

laws.name: The Stable Marriage Problem
laws.statement: Given two groups ranking each other, you can always pair them so no two would rather abandon their partners for each other.

sources.text: Gale-Shapley algorithm, Wikipedia. — the stable-matching and blocking-pair definitions, the existence guarantee, and proposer-optimality.
The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences 2012, NobelPrize.org. — the award to Roth and Shapley for stable allocations and market design.

laws.name: The Traveling Salesman Problem
laws.statement: Find the shortest route that visits every city once and returns home; it is easy to state and famously hard to solve.

sources.text: Travelling salesman problem, Wikipedia. — the definition, NP-hardness, Held-Karp, and the heuristics and exact solvers.
Christofides algorithm, Wikipedia. — the one-and-a-half approximation for metric TSP.

laws.name: The Ski Rental Problem
laws.statement: Not knowing how long you'll keep skiing, rent until the rentals equal the purchase price, then buy.

sources.text: Ski rental problem, Wikipedia. — the rent-or-buy setup, the break-even two-competitive result, and the randomised optimum.
Karlin, Manasse, Rudolph & Sleator, 'Competitive Snoopy Caching,' Algorithmica (1988). — the rent-or-buy analysis equivalent to ski rental.

laws.name: Euclid's Theorem
laws.statement: There are infinitely many prime numbers, however far up the number line you look.

sources.text: Euclid's theorem, Wikipedia. — the infinitude of primes, Euclid's construction, and the constructive-not-contradiction point.
Meštrović, 'Euclid's theorem on the infinitude of primes: a historical survey of its proofs,' arXiv:1202.3670. — the Book IX Proposition 20 attribution and the many proofs.

laws.name: Fermat's Little Theorem
laws.statement: For a prime p and any integer a, a raised to the p leaves the same remainder as a itself when divided by p.

sources.text: Fermat's little theorem, Wikipedia. — the congruence, the Fermat 1640 and Euler 1736 history, and the Carmichael-number caveat.
Fermat's Little Theorem, Wolfram MathWorld. — the statement, Euler's generalisation, and the smallest Carmichael number 561.

laws.name: The Chinese Remainder Theorem
laws.statement: If you know a number's remainders on division by several coprime moduli, those remainders pin it down uniquely.

sources.text: Chinese remainder theorem, Wikipedia. — the statement for coprime moduli, the Sunzi puzzle answer 23, and Qin Jiushao's general algorithm.
Chinese Remainder Theorem, Wolfram MathWorld. — the simultaneous-congruence statement and the ring-isomorphism form.

laws.name: The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
laws.statement: Every polynomial equation of degree one or more has a root among the complex numbers.

sources.text: Fundamental theorem of algebra, Wikipedia. — the complex-root statement, algebraic closure, the analysis requirement, and the d'Alembert and Gauss history.
Fundamental Theorem of Algebra, Wolfram MathWorld. — the existence of a complex root and complete factorisation into linear factors.

laws.name: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
laws.statement: Differentiation and integration are inverse operations; each undoes the other.

sources.text: Fundamental theorem of calculus, Wikipedia. — the two parts, the inverse relationship of differentiation and integration, and the Newton-Leibniz and Stokes context.
Fundamental Theorems of Calculus, Wolfram MathWorld. — the first and second fundamental theorems and antiderivative evaluation.

laws.name: The Intermediate Value Theorem
laws.statement: A continuous function that takes two values also takes every value in between.

sources.text: Intermediate value theorem, Wikipedia. — the statement, Bolzano's 1817 sign-change form, the completeness dependence, and the connectedness generalisation.
Intermediate Value Theorem, Wolfram MathWorld. — the continuous-function statement and its role in guaranteeing roots.

laws.name: The Brouwer Fixed-Point Theorem
laws.statement: Any continuous way of stirring a disc back into itself must leave at least one point exactly where it started.

sources.text: Brouwer fixed-point theorem, Wikipedia. — the self-map statement, the coffee and map illustrations, the no-retraction proof, and the Brouwer 1911 attribution.
Brouwer Fixed Point Theorem, Wolfram MathWorld. — the continuous-self-map statement and the convex-compact setting.

laws.name: The Hairy Ball Theorem
aliases: You can't comb a hairy ball flat
laws.statement: You cannot comb the hair on a ball flat without leaving at least one cowlick.

sources.text: Hairy ball theorem, Wikipedia. — the no-nonzero-tangent-field statement, the Euler-characteristic obstruction, the windless-point consequence, and the Brouwer 1912 attribution.
Hairy Ball Theorem, Wolfram MathWorld. — the even-dimensional sphere statement and the impossibility of combing the hair flat.

laws.name: The Riemann Hypothesis
laws.statement: Every nontrivial zero of the Riemann zeta function lies exactly on the critical line, half.

sources.text: Riemann hypothesis, Wikipedia. — the critical-line statement, the 1859 origin, Hilbert's eighth problem and Clay Millennium status, and Hardy's 1914 result.
The Riemann Hypothesis, Clay Mathematics Institute. — the official Millennium Prize Problem statement and its million-dollar prize.

laws.name: The Continuum Hypothesis
laws.statement: There is no size of infinity strictly between the counting numbers and the real number line.

sources.text: Continuum hypothesis, Wikipedia. — the no-intermediate-cardinal statement, Cantor's origin, Hilbert's first problem, and the Godel 1940 and Cohen 1963 independence results.
Continuum Hypothesis, Wolfram MathWorld. — the cardinality statement and its independence from Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory.

laws.name: The Collatz Conjecture
laws.statement: Halve it if even, triple it and add one if odd, and every number falls back to one.

sources.text: Collatz conjecture, Wikipedia. — the 3n+1 rule, the every-number-reaches-one claim, Erdos's remark, Tao's 2019 result, and the computational verification bound.
Collatz Problem, Wolfram MathWorld. — the hailstone map, the conjecture's statement, and its status as an unsolved problem.

laws.name: Flow
laws.statement: Fully absorbed in a task that matches your skill, you lose yourself and time seems to vanish.

sources.text: Flow (psychology), Wikipedia. — the definition, Csikszentmihalyi and the 1990 book, the challenge-skill balance with anxiety and boredom, the characteristics, and the flow-channel application.
Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi: The Father of Flow, PositivePsychology.com. — the conditions and characteristics of flow and its place in positive psychology.

laws.name: The Straw Man
laws.statement: Beat a distorted, feeble version of your opponent's argument and pretend you've defeated the real one.

sources.text: Straw man, Wikipedia. — the definition as refuting a distorted proxy of the opponent's argument, the metaphor, the forms including nutpicking, and steelmanning as the antidote.
Fallacies, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the straw man as a fallacy of relevance based on caricaturing an argument.

laws.name: The Ad Hominem
laws.statement: Attack the person making an argument instead of answering the argument itself.

sources.text: Ad hominem, Wikipedia. — the Latin meaning and attack-the-person definition, the abusive, circumstantial, tu quoque, and poisoning-the-well forms, the relevance nuance, and the history of the term.
Fallacies, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the ad hominem among the informal fallacies and the conditions under which attacking a person is or is not relevant.

laws.name: The False Dilemma
laws.statement: Present only two options as if they were the only ones, when in fact more exist.

sources.text: False dilemma, Wikipedia. — the definition and alternate names, the true-versus-false dichotomy distinction via contradictories and contraries, and the black-and-white-thinking connection.
What Is the Either-Or Fallacy?, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the presentation of only two options while ignoring others and its use to polarise debate.

laws.name: Begging the Question
laws.statement: Assume the very thing you are trying to prove, so the argument proves nothing.

sources.text: Begging the question, Wikipedia. — the definition and Latin term petitio principii, the opium example, the Aristotelian origin, the circular-reasoning link, and the modern raises-the-question misusage.
Logical Fallacy: Begging the Question, The Fallacy Files. — the circular structure in which the premises assume the conclusion.

laws.name: The Slippery Slope
aliases: The thin end of the wedge
laws.statement: Claim one small step must lead, unstoppably, to some disastrous end, without showing why.

sources.text: Slippery slope, Wikipedia. — the definition, the unsupported-chain point, that well-supported versions can be valid, and the causal and conceptual types with the sorites connection.
Fallacies, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the slippery slope as depending on the strength of the probabilities linking each step.

laws.name: The Appeal to Authority
laws.statement: Cite an authority's say-so as proof, even when they are no expert or the point is theirs to assert.

sources.text: Argument from authority, Wikipedia. — the definition and Latin term, when it is fallacious versus a legitimate inductive appeal, fallacious forms, and the Locke origin.

Ad Verecundiam (Argument from Authority), Lander University Introduction to Logic. — the requirement that the authority's expertise be relevant to the question and the fallacious appeal outside the field.

laws.name: The Genetic Fallacy
laws.statement: Judge a claim by where it came from rather than by whether it is actually true.

sources.text: Genetic fallacy, Wikipedia. — the definition of judging by origin rather than merit, that genetic means genesis, both directions, the relation to ad hominem and appeal to authority, and the Cohen and Nagel 1934 coinage.
Genetic Fallacy - Definition & Examples, LogicalFallacies.org. — judging a claim by its source, the relevance nuance, and ad hominem and appeal to authority as special cases.

laws.name: The Motte-and-Bailey
laws.statement: Advance a bold claim, retreat to a modest one when challenged, then quietly reclaim the bold one.

sources.text: Motte-and-bailey fallacy, Wikipedia. — the definition and retreat-and-advance dynamic, the castle metaphor, Shackel's 2005 coinage, and its classification as a form of equivocation.
Shackel, The Vacuity of Postmodernist Methodology, Metaphilosophy (2005). — the original motte-and-bailey doctrine and its analysis.

laws.name: The No True Scotsman
laws.statement: When a counterexample refutes your generalization, redefine the category so it no longer counts.

sources.text: No true Scotsman, Wikipedia. — the definition as ad hoc redefinition and appeal to purity, the porridge example, Antony Flew's origin, and the ad-hoc-rescue mechanism.
Logical Fallacy: The No-True-Scotsman Fallacy, The Fallacy Files. — the conversion of a refutable generalization into an unfalsifiable tautology.

laws.name: The Red Herring
laws.statement: Throw in something irrelevant to distract from the real question rather than answer it.

sources.text: Red herring, Wikipedia. — the definition as an irrelevant distraction, both the literary and fallacy senses, the ignoratio elenchi relation, and the Cobbett 1807 etymology with the debunked fish-training story.
The Lure of the Red Herring, Michael Quinion, World Wide Words. — the Cobbett origin of the figurative usage and the dubiousness of the hound-training practice.

laws.name: The Appeal to Nature
laws.statement: Assume something is good because it is natural, or bad because it is unnatural.

sources.text: Appeal to nature, Wikipedia. — the definition that natural is treated as good and unnatural as bad, the natural-can-be-harmful counterpoint, the vagueness of natural, the relation to the naturalistic fallacy, and the all-natural marketing example.
The Appeal to Nature Fallacy: Why Natural Isn't Necessarily Better, Effectiviology. — that naturalness does not entail goodness and the difficulty of defining natural.

laws.name: The Texas Sharpshooter Fallacy
laws.statement: Fire wildly, then draw the bullseye around the tightest cluster and call yourself a marksman.

sources.text: Texas sharpshooter fallacy, Wikipedia. — the definition, the barn and painted-target metaphor, the clustering-illusion and multiple-comparisons connections, and the disease-cluster example.
Texas Sharpshooter Fallacy, Logically Fallacious. — inferring a pattern from random data by drawing the target after the shots.

laws.name: The Fallacy Fallacy
laws.statement: A bad argument for a claim does not prove the claim false; the conclusion may still be true.

sources.text: Argument from fallacy, Wikipedia. — the definition, the alternate names, the point that a fallacious argument can have a true conclusion, the cat example, and the invalid denying-the-antecedent structure.
Logical Fallacy: Fallacy Fallacy, The Fallacy Files. — that a fallacious argument says nothing about the truth or falsity of its conclusion.

laws.name: Schrödinger's Cat
laws.statement: A cat in a sealed box, its fate tied to a quantum event, is somehow both alive and dead until observed.

sources.text: Schrödinger's cat, Wikipedia. — the 1935 origin, the box setup, the superposition of alive and dead, the reductio targeting the measurement problem, and the many-worlds and decoherence resolutions.
Schrödinger's cat, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the thought experiment, the superposition, and its objection to the Copenhagen interpretation.

laws.name: The Brain in a Vat
laws.statement: If a disembodied brain in a vat were fed the same signals as yours, it could not tell that its whole world was a fake.

sources.text: Brain in a vat, Wikipedia. — the setup of a brain fed simulated signals, its descent from Descartes's evil demon, the skeptical argument, the Matrix comparison, and Putnam's self-refutation reply.
The Brain in a Vat Argument, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the skeptical scenario, its relation to Cartesian doubt, and Putnam's semantic-externalism response.

laws.name: The Experience Machine
laws.statement: Offered a machine that could give you any blissful experience you wanted for life, most people would refuse to plug in.

sources.text: Experience machine, Wikipedia. — Nozick's 1974 thought experiment, the tank-and-electrodes setup, the argument against hedonism, the reasons not to plug in, and the status-quo-bias objection.
Hedonism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the experience machine as the standard objection to hedonistic theories of value.

laws.name: The Beetle in a Box
laws.statement: If everyone had a box no one else could look into, the word for what is inside could not get its meaning from the thing itself.

sources.text: Private language argument, Wikipedia. — the beetle-in-a-box passage at Investigations §293, the unseeable boxes, the object dropping out as irrelevant, and the argument that sensation words get meaning from public use.
Ludwig Wittgenstein, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the Philosophical Investigations, the private language argument, and meaning as use.

laws.name: Maxwell's Demon
laws.statement: A tiny gatekeeper sorting fast molecules from slow ones seems able to create order from disorder and cheat the second law of thermodynamics.

sources.text: Maxwell's demon, Wikipedia. — Maxwell's 1867 thought experiment, the sorting door and apparent second-law violation, Szilard's engine, and the Landauer-Bennett resolution via the cost of information erasure.
Landauer's principle, Wikipedia. — the principle that erasing one bit of information dissipates at least kT ln 2 of heat, and its role in resolving the demon paradox.

laws.name: Twin Earth
laws.statement: On a planet identical to ours except that water is a different chemical, the word water would mean something different, though nothing in anyone's head has changed.

sources.text: Twin Earth thought experiment, Wikipedia. — Putnam's 1975 scenario, the H2O-versus-XYZ setup, the identical mental states with different reference, and the conclusion that meanings are not in the head.
Externalism About the Mind, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Putnam's Twin Earth argument and the thesis of semantic externalism about meaning and content.

laws.name: The Utility Monster
laws.statement: If one being gained far more happiness from each resource than anyone else, strict utilitarianism would tell everyone to feed it everything.

sources.text: Utility monster, Wikipedia. — Nozick's 1974 thought experiment, the being that converts resources into utility more efficiently than others, and the objection to utilitarian aggregation and distribution.
Robert Nozick, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Nozick's critique of utilitarianism and the separateness of persons underlying the utility-monster objection.

laws.name: The Philosophical Zombie
laws.statement: A being physically identical to you but with no inner experience at all seems at least conceivable, and that alone threatens the view that mind is nothing but matter.

sources.text: Philosophical zombie, Wikipedia. — the definition of a p-zombie as a non-conscious physical duplicate, Kirk's coinage of the term, Chalmers's conceivability argument against physicalism, and Dennett's rejection.
Zombies, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the zombie thought experiment, the conceivability-to-possibility argument, and the main physicalist responses.

laws.name: The Gettier Problem
laws.statement: You can have a justified true belief and still not know, if it is true only by luck.

sources.text: Gettier, E. L. (1963). "Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?" Analysis 23(6), 121-123 — the three-page paper that opened the problem.

Gettier problem, Wikipedia. — Gettier's 1963 paper, the refutation of justified true belief as knowledge, the role of luck, the stopped-clock and false-premise cases, and the search for a fourth condition.

The Analysis of Knowledge, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the justified-true-belief analysis, Gettier's counterexamples, and the main responses including no-false-lemmas and anti-luck conditions.

laws.name: Laplace's Demon
laws.statement: An intellect knowing the position and motion of every particle could calculate the entire future and past of the universe.

sources.text: Laplace's demon, Wikipedia. — Laplace's 1814 formulation, the intellect knowing every particle's state, the expression of causal determinism, and the quantum and chaos-theory challenges.
Causal Determinism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the doctrine of determinism that Laplace's demon expresses and its relation to prediction and the laws of physics.

laws.name: The Violinist Argument
laws.statement: Even if you woke up plugged into a stranger whose life depended on your body, you would not be obligated to stay attached.

sources.text: A Defense of Abortion, Wikipedia. — Thomson's 1971 paper, the kidnapped-and-plugged-to-the-violinist setup, the grant of fetal personhood, the right-to-life-versus-use-of-body argument, and the responsibility objection and Samaritan distinction.
Abortion, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Thomson's violinist argument, the bodily-autonomy reasoning, and its place in the philosophical debate over abortion.

laws.name: The Teletransportation Paradox
laws.statement: If a machine scanned you, destroyed the original, and built an exact copy on Mars, it is unclear whether the person who steps out is you or merely a replica.

sources.text: Teletransportation paradox, Wikipedia. — Parfit's 1984 formulation, the scan-destroy-reconstruct-on-Mars setup, the non-destructive branching variant, and the conclusion that psychological continuity, Relation R, is what matters.
Personal Identity, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the psychological-continuity theory, duplication thought experiments, and Parfit's view that identity itself has no practical importance.

laws.name: The Drowning Child
laws.statement: If you would ruin your clothes to save a drowning child at your feet, you cannot consistently refuse to give to save a dying child far away.

sources.text: Famine, Affluence, and Morality, Wikipedia. — Singer's 1972 paper, the shallow-pond and muddy-clothes setup, the comparable-moral-importance principle, the distance-is-irrelevant analogy to global poverty, the effective-altruism connection, and the demandingness objection.
Study Guide: Peter Singer's Famine, Affluence, and Morality, utilitarianism.net. — the strong and moderate versions of the principle and the argument's structure.

laws.name: The Allegory of the Cave
laws.statement: Prisoners chained to face a wall mistake the shadows cast on it for the whole of reality.

sources.text: Allegory of the cave, Wikipedia. — the Republic Book VII setting, the Socrates-Glaucon dialogue, the chained prisoners and shadows, the ascent to sunlight, the sun as the Form of the Good, and the hostile return.
Myth of the cave, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — Plato's cave allegory, the ascent to comprehend the Form of the Good, and its place in the theory of Forms.

laws.name: The Ring of Gyges
laws.statement: If a ring made you invisible and unpunishable, would you still act justly, or would anyone in your place turn to injustice?

sources.text: Ring of Gyges, Wikipedia. — the Republic Book II setting, Glaucon's challenge, the shepherd Gyges and the invisibility ring, the seizing of the throne, the just-and-unjust-alike claim, and Plato's defence of justice as intrinsically good.
Why be Moral? Plato's Ring of Gyges Thought Experiment, 1000-Word Philosophy. — the impunity challenge, justice practised only as a lesser evil, and the intrinsic-value response.

laws.name: Pascal's Wager
laws.statement: Since believing in God risks little but may win infinite reward, a rational gambler should bet on God.

sources.text: Pascal's wager, Wikipedia. — Pascal, the Pensées published 1670, the finite-cost-versus-infinite-reward decision matrix, the act-as-if-to-believe remedy, and the many-gods and inauthentic-belief objections.
Pascal's Wager, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the wager's decision-theoretic structure, its status as an early contribution to decision theory, and the main objections.

laws.name: Buridan's Ass
laws.statement: A donkey placed exactly between two identical piles of hay, with no reason to prefer either, would starve unable to choose.

sources.text: Buridan's ass, Wikipedia. — the equidistant-hay setup and starvation through indecision, the satirical naming after Jean Buridan, the Aristotle and al-Ghazali antecedents, and the Leibniz sufficient-reason response.
John Buridan, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Buridan's account of free choice and moral determinism and the note that the donkey example is not found in his writings but was a later parody.

laws.name: The Inverted Spectrum
laws.statement: Two people might see colours swapped, your red being their green, and neither could ever tell from behaviour or words.

sources.text: Inverted spectrum, Wikipedia. — the Locke antecedent, the systematic and behaviourally undetectable inversion, the anti-functionalism argument about qualia, and the color-space asymmetry objection.
Inverted Qualia, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the inversion scenario, its use against functionalism, and objections including the asymmetry of colour space.

laws.name: Molyneux's Problem
laws.statement: A person born blind who knows a cube and a sphere by touch, if suddenly given sight, could not at first tell which is which by looking.

sources.text: Molyneux's problem, Wikipedia. — Molyneux's question to Locke, the cube-and-sphere setup, the empiricist no answer, the empiricism-versus-nativism stakes, and the modern Project Prakash tests.
Molyneux's Problem, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the problem's formulation in Locke's Essay, Locke's and Molyneux's reasoning, and its philosophical stakes.

laws.name: The Swampman
laws.statement: If lightning by freak chance assembled an exact copy of you, its thoughts would mean nothing, because it has no history.

sources.text: Swampman, Wikipedia. — Davidson's 1987 paper, the lightning-strike molecular-duplicate setup, the argument that content depends on causal history, and the claim that Swampman lacks genuine meaning and memory.

Donald Davidson, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the Swampman example, its use in arguing that mental content depends on causal-historical relations, and the note that Davidson did not elaborate it.

laws.name: The Lottery Paradox
laws.statement: It seems rational to believe each ticket will lose, yet believing that of every ticket means believing no ticket wins.

sources.text: Lottery paradox, Wikipedia. — Kyburg's 1961 statement, the fair-lottery setup, the three inconsistent principles and the conjunction-closure contradiction, the high-probability-not-sufficient point, and the preface-paradox link.
Epistemic Paradoxes, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the lottery paradox in relation to knowledge, closure, and the reluctance to say one knows a ticket will lose.

laws.name: The Repugnant Conclusion
laws.statement: Adding up welfare implies that a vast crowd of barely-worth-living lives can be better than a smaller world of flourishing ones.

sources.text: Parfit, D. "The Mere Addition Paradox", chapter 19 of Reasons and Persons (1984) — where the repugnant conclusion is drawn.

The Repugnant Conclusion, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Parfit's 1984 formulation and exact statement, the total-utilitarian mechanism, the search for Theory X, and the Arrhenius impossibility results.
Mere addition paradox, Wikipedia. — the A, A+, B−, B argument leading to the repugnant conclusion and the contrast between total and average utilitarianism.

laws.name: The China Brain
laws.statement: If a billion people each played the part of one neuron, the whole nation would replicate a brain, yet surely feel nothing.

sources.text: China brain, Wikipedia. — Block's Troubles with Functionalism (1978), the population-of-China-as-a-brain setup with people as neurons, the absent qualia objection to functionalism, and the functionalist replies.
Functionalism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Block's Chinese nation, the absent and inverted qualia objections, and functionalism's problem of qualia.

laws.name: Pascal's Mugging
laws.statement: A con artist promising an astronomically large reward can, on pure expected value, talk you out of your wallet however unlikely the promise.

sources.text: Pascal's mugging, Wikipedia. — the Yudkowsky origin and Bostrom's 2009 Analysis dialogue, the mugger and tiny-probability-times-vast-reward structure, the Pascal's Wager analogy with finite stakes, and the expected-utility breakdown or fanaticism.
Nick Bostrom, Pascal's Mugging, Analysis 69(3), 2009. — the original dialogue in which Pascal admits he sees no flaw in the mugger's expected-value mathematics.

laws.name: The Last Man
laws.statement: If the last person alive destroyed every living thing before dying, harming no one, our sense that it is still wrong suggests nature has value in itself.

sources.text: Routley, R. (1973). "Is There a Need for a New, an Environmental, Ethic?", Proceedings of the XVth World Congress of Philosophy — the paper introducing the last man argument. DOI resolves to the reprint in The Ethics of the Environment.

Environmental Ethics, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Routley's 1973 last man argument, the destruction of nature harming no human interest, the challenge to anthropocentrism, and the intrinsic value of nature.
Richard Sylvan [Routley], Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Routley's 1973 paper Is There a Need for a New, an Environmental, Ethic, and the last man thought experiment against human chauvinism.

laws.name: The Two Envelopes Problem
laws.statement: A flawed calculation says the other envelope is always worth more, so you should switch forever.

sources.text: Two envelopes problem, Wikipedia. — the two-envelopes and twice-the-amount setup, the 1.25A switching argument, the infinite-switching absurdity, the equivocation resolution, and the subtler unbounded-prior variant.
Infinity, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the two envelopes as a tacitly infinite decision problem and the treatment of the infinite-expectation case.

laws.name: The Boy or Girl Paradox
laws.statement: Told a family of two has at least one boy, the chance both are boys is one in three, not one in two.

sources.text: Boy or girl paradox, Wikipedia. — Gardner's 1959 popularisation, the boy-boy/boy-girl/girl-boy/girl-girl sample space, the one-half and one-third answers, the procedure-dependence and Gardner's admission of ambiguity, and the boy-born-on-Tuesday variant.
The Two-Child Paradox: Dichotomy and Ambiguity, Peter Lynch (University College Dublin). — an academic treatment of the paradox and its dependence on how the information is obtained.

laws.name: The Sleeping Beauty Problem
laws.statement: Woken with no way to know how many times, what should Beauty believe about a coin flip, one half or one third?

sources.text: Sleeping Beauty problem, Wikipedia. — the coin-flip and memory-erasure setup, the credence-in-heads question, the thirder position of Elga and the halfer position of Lewis, and the unresolved debate over self-locating belief.
Adam Elga, Self-locating Belief and the Sleeping Beauty Problem, Analysis 60(2), 2000. — the original argument for the thirder answer of one third.

laws.name: The German Tank Problem
laws.statement: From a handful of captured serial numbers you can estimate how many tanks the enemy built, and do it startlingly well.

sources.text: German tank problem, Wikipedia. — the serial-number estimation setup, the wartime origin using gearbox and other numbers, the minimum-variance unbiased estimator m plus m over k minus one, and the comparison of statistical (about 246 per month) versus intelligence (about 1,400) versus actual (245) figures.
Lessons from the German Tank Problem, S. J. Miller et al. (Williams College). — an academic treatment of the estimator and its statistical basis.

laws.name: The Bertrand Paradox
laws.statement: Asked the chance a random chord is longer than a triangle's side, three natural methods give three different answers.

sources.text: Bertrand paradox (probability), Wikipedia. — Bertrand's 1889 formulation, the random-chord-versus-triangle-side question, the three methods giving one third, one half, and one quarter, the principle-of-indifference lesson, and Jaynes's invariance resolution.
Bertrand's Paradox, Random Services (K. Siegrist, University of Alabama in Huntsville). — the three constructions of a random chord and their differing probabilities.

laws.name: The Unexpected Hanging Paradox
laws.statement: A prisoner proves a surprise hanging is impossible, then is surprised anyway, exactly as promised.

sources.text: Unexpected hanging paradox, Wikipedia. — the surprise-hanging setup, the backward-induction elimination from Friday to Monday, the ironic surprise outcome, the Gardner and Quine discussions, and the absence of a canonical resolution.
Epistemic Paradoxes, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the surprise-examination paradox and its relation to the preface and knower paradoxes and to problems of foreknowledge.

laws.name: The Raven Paradox
laws.statement: Observing a green apple, which is a non-black non-raven, seems to confirm that all ravens are black.

sources.text: Raven paradox, Wikipedia. — Hempel's 1940s formulation, Nicod's criterion, the contrapositive equivalence and equivalence condition, the green-apple and white-shoe conclusion, the indoor-ornithology absurdity, and the Bayesian negligible-confirmation resolution.
Carl Hempel, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the raven paradox within Hempel's Studies in the Logic of Confirmation and its place in confirmation theory.

laws.name: The Grue Paradox
laws.statement: The same green emeralds that support all emeralds are green equally support that they are grue, which predicts blue.

sources.text: New riddle of induction, Wikipedia. — Goodman's 1955 Fact, Fiction, and Forecast, the definitions of grue and bleen, the equal confirmation of all emeralds are grue predicting blue, the projectibility problem, entrenchment, and the symmetry point.
Nelson Goodman, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the new riddle of induction, grue, projectibility, and Goodman's appeal to entrenchment.

laws.name: The Berry Paradox
laws.statement: The smallest number not describable in under sixty letters is just described, in under sixty letters.

sources.text: Berry paradox, Wikipedia. — the smallest-integer-not-definable formulation, the Berry and Russell attribution and 1908 publication, the finite-phrases contradiction, the ill-defined-definability resolution, and the links to Richard's paradox, Tarski, and Chaitin.
Berry Paradox, Wolfram MathWorld. — Russell's syllable formulation and the paradox's basis in the vague notion of definability.

laws.name: The Allais Paradox
laws.statement: People who take a sure million over a gamble will still gamble when both options become uncertain, defying expected utility.

sources.text: Allais paradox, Wikipedia. — Allais's 1953 problem, the two pairs of gambles with the standard payoffs, the common pattern of choosing 1A and 2B, the violation of the independence axiom, the certainty effect, and the prospect-theory connection.

The Allais paradox: what it became, what it really was, what it now suggests to us, Philippe Mongin (HEC Paris), Economics and Philosophy. — the 1953 origin and the paradox's relation to expected utility theory.

laws.name: Hilbert's Hotel
aliases: Hilbert's paradox of the Grand Hotel
laws.statement: A hotel with infinitely many rooms, every one occupied, can still make room for a new guest.

sources.text: Hilbert's paradox of the Grand Hotel, Wikipedia. — Hilbert's 1920s lecture and Gamow's 1947 popularisation, the shift n to n plus one for one guest and n to two n for infinitely many, the infinite-coaches extension, and the cardinality lesson about aleph-null.
Helge Kragh, The True (?) Story of Hilbert's Infinite Hotel (arXiv). — the historical origin of the thought experiment in Hilbert's lectures.

laws.name: The Potato Paradox
laws.statement: Potatoes that are 99 percent water, dried to 98 percent water, lose half their weight, not one percent.

sources.text: Potato paradox, Wikipedia. — the hundred-kilogram, ninety-nine-to-ninety-eight-percent-water setup, the fifty-kilogram answer, the constant one-kilogram dry-mass reasoning going from one to two percent, and its status as a veridical paradox.
Potato Paradox, Wolfram MathWorld. — the puzzle and the dry-mass calculation yielding the halved weight.

laws.name: The Coastline Paradox
aliases: How long is the coast of Britain
laws.statement: The shorter your measuring stick, the longer a coastline becomes, so it has no single true length.

sources.text: Coastline paradox, Wikipedia. — the scale-dependence of measured length, Richardson's original observation and the Richardson effect, Mandelbrot's 1967 paper, the self-similarity mechanism, the fractal dimension between one and two with Britain's west coast at about one and a quarter, and the disagreement in published lengths.

Benoit Mandelbrot, How Long Is the Coast of Britain? Statistical Self-Similarity and Fractional Dimension, Science (1967). — the founding treatment of coastlines as self-similar curves with fractional dimension.

laws.name: The Reciprocity Norm
laws.statement: Give someone a favour, even an unasked one, and they feel an obligation to give one back.

sources.text: Reciprocity (social psychology), Wikipedia. — the norm of returning favours, the indebtedness even from uninvited favours, Cialdini's principle and free-sample examples, reciprocity of concessions, and the Gouldner and Regan sources.

Alvin W. Gouldner, The Norm of Reciprocity: A Preliminary Statement, American Sociological Review (1960). — reciprocity as a universal moral norm requiring one to help, and not harm, those who have helped one.

laws.name: The Scarcity Principle
laws.statement: People want a thing more when it is rare or slipping out of reach.

sources.text: Scarcity (social psychology), Wikipedia. — the higher value placed on scarce things, Cialdini's principle, the scarcity heuristic and reactance and loss-aversion mechanisms, marketing tactics, and the Worchel, Lee, and Adewole 1975 cookie experiment.
The gentle science of persuasion, part six: Scarcity, W. P. Carey News (Arizona State University). — Cialdini's account of scarcity and the desire for what is less available.

laws.name: Social Proof
laws.statement: Unsure what to do, people copy the crowd, trusting that others must know better.

sources.text: Social proof, Wikipedia. — the copying of others under the assumption they know better, Cialdini's coinage, informational social influence, the moderators of uncertainty, number, and similarity, and the classic conformity research.

Milgram, Bickman, and Berkowitz, Note on the Drawing Power of Crowds of Different Size, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (1969). — the street experiment showing larger crowds drew more passers-by to look up.

laws.name: The Ben Franklin Effect
laws.statement: Doing someone a favour makes you like them more, not the other way round.

sources.text: Ben Franklin effect, Wikipedia. — the definition that doing a favour increases liking, the Franklin autobiography book-borrowing anecdote and maxim, the cognitive-dissonance explanation, the Jecker and Landy 1969 study, and the reverse harm effect.
Benjamin Franklin effect, The Decision Lab. — the phenomenon and its explanation via cognitive dissonance and attitude change.

laws.name: The Foot-in-the-Door Technique
laws.statement: Agree to a small request first, and you become far more likely to grant a big one later.

sources.text: Foot-in-the-door technique, Wikipedia. — the small-then-large request tactic, the Freedman and Fraser 1966 billboard study with the roughly three-quarters versus one-in-six result, the self-perception and consistency mechanisms, and the contrast with door-in-the-face.
Freedman and Fraser, Compliance without pressure: The foot-in-the-door technique, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (1966). — the original demonstration of the effect.

laws.name: The Door-in-the-Face Technique
laws.statement: Ask for far too much first, get refused, then the real, smaller request suddenly seems reasonable.

sources.text: Door-in-the-face technique, Wikipedia. — the large-then-small request tactic, the Cialdini et al. 1975 counsellor and zoo study with the roughly fifty percent versus control result, the reciprocal-concessions and perceptual-contrast mechanisms, and the contrast with foot-in-the-door.
Does the Door-in-the-Face Technique Really Work?, Psychology Today. — the tactic's basis in reciprocal concessions and its moderating conditions.

laws.name: The Pratfall Effect
laws.statement: A small blunder makes a highly competent person more likable, but makes an average one less so.

sources.text: Pratfall effect, Wikipedia. — the competence-dependent effect of blunders on likability, the Aronson, Willerman, and Floyd 1966 coffee-spill study, the humanising mechanism, and the self-esteem and gender moderators.
Why admitting a weakness makes people like you more, Association for Psychological Science. — the pratfall effect and the appeal of relatable imperfection.

laws.name: The Illusion of Transparency
laws.statement: People believe their inner nerves, feelings, and lies show on the outside far more than they really do.

sources.text: Illusion of transparency, Wikipedia. — the overestimation of how visible one's internal states are, the Gilovich, Savitsky, and Medvec 1998 origin, the public-speaking-anxiety application, and the link to the spotlight effect.
Illusion of Transparency, The Decision Lab. — the definition, the anchoring and egocentric mechanism, and the concealed-emotion and lie-detection findings.

laws.name: The False-Consensus Effect
laws.statement: People assume their own views and habits are far more common than they really are.

sources.text: False consensus effect, Wikipedia. — the overestimation of how widely one's views are shared, the Ross, Greene, and House 1977 study, the selective-exposure and motivated-projection mechanisms, and the false-uniqueness contrast.
The False Consensus Effect, SimplyPsychology. — the definition, the mechanisms of selective exposure, motivation, and ambiguity resolution, and the tendency to judge dissenters.

laws.name: Diffusion of Responsibility
laws.statement: The more people who are present, the less any single person feels responsible for acting.

sources.text: Diffusion of responsibility, Wikipedia. — the division of responsibility among those present, the connection to the bystander effect, the Darley and Latané seizure research, the Genovese case with its later-documented exaggeration, and social loafing.
Bystander effect: Diffusion of Responsibility, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — diffusion of responsibility as the process underlying the bystander effect.

laws.name: Deindividuation
aliases: Loss of self in the crowd
laws.statement: Submerged in a crowd and stripped of identity, people do things they never would alone.

sources.text: Deindividuation, Wikipedia. — the loss of self-awareness and accountability in groups, the Festinger, Pepitone, and Newcomb 1952 coinage, Le Bon's roots, Zimbardo's factors, the reduced-restraint mechanism, and the SIDE model.
Deindividuation: From Le Bon to the social identity model of deindividuation effects, Cogent Psychology. — the history of the concept and the modern social identity reinterpretation.

laws.name: Groupthink
laws.statement: When a group prizes harmony over honest appraisal, it talks itself into bad decisions.

sources.text: Groupthink, Wikipedia. — the consensus-seeking definition, Janis's development in Victims of Groupthink (1972), Whyte's 1952 coinage and the Orwell allusion, the eight symptoms and antecedent conditions, the Bay of Pigs and Challenger cases, the remedies, and the mixed empirical support.
Groupthink, EBSCO Research Starters. — Janis's theory, the symptoms and antecedents, and the criticism that empirical support is limited.

laws.name: The Overjustification Effect
laws.statement: Pay people for something they already loved doing, and their inner motivation for it can wither.

sources.text: Overjustification effect, Wikipedia. — the undermining of intrinsic motivation by expected external rewards, the Lepper, Greene, and Nisbett 1973 Good Player Award study, Deci's 1971 puzzle study, the self-perception and cognitive-evaluation mechanisms, the boundary conditions, and the Deci-Koestner-Ryan versus Cameron-Pierce debate.
Overjustification Effect, The Decision Lab. — the effect, its mechanisms, and its boundary conditions.

laws.name: The Giffen Good
laws.statement: A staple so central to the poor that they buy more of it as its price rises.

sources.text: Giffen good, Wikipedia. — the upward-sloping demand definition, the Giffen and Marshall attribution, the income-versus-substitution mechanism and three conditions, the disputed potato example, the Jensen and Miller China study, and the contrast with Veblen goods.
Jensen and Miller, Giffen Behavior and Subsistence Consumption, American Economic Review (2008). — field evidence of Giffen behaviour for rice and wheat among poor households in China.

laws.name: The Veblen Good
laws.statement: A luxury wanted more precisely because it costs more, since the high price is the point.

sources.text: Veblen good, Wikipedia. — the demand rising with price definition, Veblen and conspicuous consumption in The Theory of the Leisure Class (1899), Leibenstein's 1950 coinage, the status-signalling mechanism, the contrast with Giffen goods, and the snob and bandwagon effects.
Harvey Leibenstein, Bandwagon, Snob, and Veblen Effects in the Theory of Consumers' Demand, Quarterly Journal of Economics (1950). — the formal distinction of the Veblen, snob, and bandwagon effects.

laws.name: The Principal-Agent Problem
laws.statement: When one person acts for another whose interests differ and whose watching is imperfect, the agent may serve themselves.

sources.text: Principal-agent problem, Wikipedia. — the conflict of interest and information asymmetry between principal and agent, moral hazard and adverse selection, agency costs, the shareholders-versus-managers example, the Ross 1973 and Jensen and Meckling 1976 contributions, and the incentive-alignment and monitoring solutions.

Jensen and Meckling, Theory of the Firm: Managerial Behavior, Agency Costs and Ownership Structure, Journal of Financial Economics (1976). — the foundational analysis of agency costs and ownership structure.

laws.name: Rent-Seeking
laws.statement: Grabbing a bigger slice of the pie by working the system, instead of baking a bigger pie.

sources.text: Rent-seeking, Wikipedia. — the capture of existing wealth without creating new wealth, the economic-rent concept, the Tullock 1967 analysis and Krueger 1974 coinage, the lobbying and licensing examples, the deadweight-loss harm, and the public-choice connection.
Rent Seeking, The Concise Encyclopedia of Economics (Econlib). — the definition, the economic-rent concept, and the wastefulness of seeking transfers rather than creating value.

laws.name: Dutch Disease
laws.statement: A resource boom can hollow out a country's factories and farms by driving up its currency.

sources.text: Dutch disease, Wikipedia. — the booming-resource-sector-harms-tradables definition, The Economist 1977 coinage and the Groningen origin, the currency-appreciation and resource-movement mechanism, the Corden and Neary 1982 model, the deindustrialization consequences, and the resource-curse connection.
40 Years of Dutch Disease Literature: Lessons for Developing Countries, PMC (National Library of Medicine). — an academic review of the Dutch disease mechanism and remedies.

laws.name: The Resource Curse
laws.statement: Countries rich in oil and minerals often grow slower, govern worse, and stay poorer than resource-poor ones.

sources.text: Resource curse, Wikipedia. — the paradox that resource-rich countries often underperform, Auty's 1993 coinage, the mechanisms of Dutch disease, volatility, rent-seeking and weak institutions, the rentier state and conflict, the Sachs and Warner evidence, and the institutions-matter nuance with Norway and Botswana.
Jeffrey Sachs and Andrew Warner, Natural Resource Abundance and Economic Growth, NBER Working Paper No. 5398 (1995). — the empirical negative relationship between resource dependence and growth.

laws.name: The Cantillon Effect
laws.statement: New money helps whoever spends it first, before prices rise, and hurts those who get it last.

sources.text: Cantillon effect, Wikipedia. — the uneven distributional effects of new money, the benefit to first recipients, the non-neutrality of money, the gold-inflow example, and the modern quantitative-easing and inequality interpretation.
Richard Cantillon, Wikipedia. — Cantillon and his Essay on the Nature of Trade in General, written around 1730 and published in 1755, and his originating analysis of money's non-neutrality.

laws.name: Diminishing Marginal Utility
aliases: The Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility
laws.statement: Each extra slice of cake gives you a little less pleasure than the one before.

sources.text: Marginal utility, Wikipedia. — the declining additional satisfaction from successive units, marginal versus total utility and satiation, the marginalist origins and Gossen's first law, the diamond-water paradox resolution, and the demand-curve and diminishing-marginal-utility-of-income implications.
Paradox of value (diamond-water paradox), EBSCO Research Starters. — the resolution of the diamond-water paradox through marginal utility.

laws.name: The Money Illusion
laws.statement: People judge money by its face value and forget that inflation quietly shrinks what it buys.

sources.text: Money illusion, Wikipedia. — the confusion of nominal for real value, the Fisher and Keynes attribution, the wage-and-inflation example, the Shafir, Diamond, and Tversky 1997 evidence, the nominal-rigidity implication, and the rational-versus-behavioural debate.
Shafir, Diamond, and Tversky, Money Illusion, Quarterly Journal of Economics (1997). — experimental evidence that people exhibit money illusion.

laws.name: The Fisher Effect
laws.statement: When expected inflation rises, nominal interest rates rise with it, leaving the real return unchanged.

sources.text: Fisher equation, Wikipedia. — the relationship among nominal and real interest rates and inflation, the equation one plus the nominal rate equals one plus the real rate times one plus inflation, and its attribution to Irving Fisher.
Fisher hypothesis, Wikipedia. — the hypothesis that the real rate is independent of monetary factors, so nominal rates adjust one-for-one with expected inflation.

laws.name: The Paradox of Thrift
laws.statement: If everyone saves more at once in a slump, incomes fall and total saving may not rise at all.

sources.text: Paradox of thrift, Wikipedia. — the proposition that collective saving reduces aggregate demand, output, and total saving, the Keynes and General Theory attribution, the fallacy-of-composition mechanism, the below-full-employment condition, the classical loanable-funds criticism, and the Mandeville antecedent.
Government austerity policy and the paradox of thrift, CORE Economics (The Economy). — the paradox in the context of recession, aggregate demand, and austerity.

laws.name: The Liquidity Trap
laws.statement: When interest rates hit zero, printing more money just gets hoarded and monetary policy stops working.

sources.text: Liquidity trap, Wikipedia. — the near-zero-rate impotence of monetary policy, the Keynes 1936 origin and Hicks IS-LM formalisation, the elastic-money-demand mechanism, the Japan and 2008 examples, the fiscal-policy and quantitative-easing responses, and the monetarist debate.
Liquidity Trap: definition, examples and explanation, Economics Help. — the liquidity trap, its mechanism, and policy responses.

laws.name: Agenda-Setting Theory
laws.statement: The news may not tell you what to think, but it is stunningly good at telling you what to think about.

sources.text: Agenda-setting theory, Wikipedia. — the what-to-think-about formulation from Cohen, the McCombs and Shaw Chapel Hill 1968 study published 1972, the salience-transfer mechanism, the first and second levels, and the links to priming, framing, and gatekeeping.
Agenda-setting theory, EBSCO Research Starters. — the theory's origin, the transfer of salience, and its influence in political communication.

laws.name: Cultivation Theory
laws.statement: The more television you watch, the more your sense of reality drifts toward the world as television shows it.

sources.text: Cultivation theory, Wikipedia. — the claim that heavy television viewing shapes perceptions of reality, Gerbner and the Cultural Indicators project at Annenberg, the mean world syndrome, heavy versus light viewers, mainstreaming and resonance, the gradual cumulative mechanism, and the criticism over causality and small effects.
Gerbner's Cultivation Theory in Media Communication, SimplyPsychology. — the theory, the mean world syndrome, mainstreaming, resonance, and its critiques.

laws.name: The Spiral of Silence
laws.statement: Fearing isolation, people who sense they hold the minority view fall silent, making the majority seem even larger.

sources.text: Spiral of silence, Wikipedia. — the fear-of-isolation-driven silencing of the perceived minority, Noelle-Neumann's origin, the quasi-statistical sense and media role, the spiral feedback loop, the hard-core exception, and the cross-cultural and empirical debate.
Spiral of silence, EBSCO Research Starters. — the theory, its mechanisms, and its critiques.

laws.name: The Two-Step Flow of Communication
laws.statement: Media ideas reach most people not directly but through opinion leaders who pass them on.

sources.text: Two-step flow of communication, Wikipedia. — the flow from media to opinion leaders to the public, the Lazarsfeld Erie County study and Katz and Lazarsfeld's Personal Influence, the opinion-leader concept, the challenge to the hypodermic-needle model, and the multi-step-flow refinement.
Two-step flow model of communication, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — interpersonal influence versus direct media effects and the role of opinion leaders.

laws.name: The Hypodermic Needle Model
laws.statement: The old idea that media messages inject powerful, uniform effects straight into a passive audience.

sources.text: Hypodermic needle model, Wikipedia. — the direct, uniform, powerful effects on a passive audience, the magic-bullet and transmission-belt names, the propaganda-era context, the War of the Worlds association and its exaggeration, the supersession by limited-effects research, and its status as a retrospective strawman.
Hypodermic Needle Theory (Magic Bullet Theory), EBSCO Research Starters. — the direct-effects model, its propaganda-era context, and its refutation.

laws.name: Uses and Gratifications Theory
laws.statement: Ask not what media do to people, but what people actively do with media to meet their needs.

sources.text: Uses and gratifications theory, Wikipedia. — the active-audience focus on what people do with media, the contrast with passive-audience models, Herzog and Katz, Blumler, and Gurevitch, the gratification categories, the active-audience assumptions, and the criticisms.
Uses and Gratifications Theory, Introduction to Communication Inquiry and Theory (Montgomery College). — the active audience, the gratifications sought, and the approach's assumptions.

laws.name: The Knowledge Gap Hypothesis
laws.statement: As more information floods a society, the educated absorb it faster, so the knowledge gap widens rather than closes.

sources.text: Knowledge gap hypothesis, Wikipedia. — the claim that increased information widens knowledge gaps by status, the Tichenor, Donohue, and Olien 1970 origin, the mechanisms, the widening-inequality point, the gap-narrowing conditions, and the digital-divide connection.
Tichenor, Donohue, and Olien, Mass Media Flow and Differential Growth in Knowledge, Public Opinion Quarterly (1970). — the original statement of the hypothesis.

laws.name: The Third-Person Effect
laws.statement: People think persuasive media sway everyone else far more than they sway themselves.

sources.text: Third-person effect, Wikipedia. — the perception that media affect others more than oneself, Davison's 1983 origin, the perceptual and behavioural components, the reversal into a first-person effect for desirable content, and the self-enhancement mechanism.
W. Phillips Davison, The Third-Person Effect in Communication, Public Opinion Quarterly (1983). — the original statement of the effect.

laws.name: The Hostile Media Effect
laws.statement: Opposing partisans watch the same neutral news report and each side is sure it is biased against them.

sources.text: Hostile media effect, Wikipedia. — opposing partisans perceiving identical neutral coverage as biased against them, the Vallone, Ross, and Lepper 1985 Beirut study, the selective-perception and motivated-reasoning mechanism, the perception-not-reality point, and the relative hostile media effect.
Hostile Media Effect, Oxford Bibliographies (Communication). — the phenomenon, the founding study, and the research literature.

laws.name: The Elaboration Likelihood Model
laws.statement: Persuasion travels one of two roads: careful thought about the argument, or a quick reaction to surface cues.

sources.text: Elaboration likelihood model, Wikipedia. — the dual-process theory of Petty and Cacioppo, the central and peripheral routes and their outcomes, and motivation and ability as the determinants of elaboration.
Elaboration Likelihood Model, SimplyPsychology. — the two routes to persuasion, their characteristics, and the role of motivation and ability.

laws.name: The Sleeper Effect
laws.statement: A message from a doubtful source can grow more persuasive over time, once you forget who said it.

sources.text: Sleeper effect, Wikipedia. — the delayed increase in persuasion with a discounting cue, the Hovland wartime army-film origin, the dissociation discounting-cue mechanism, and the fragility and reliability conditions from Gruder and Pratkanis.

Pratkanis, Greenwald, Leippe, and Baumgardner, In Search of Reliable Persuasion Effects: The Sleeper Effect, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (1988). — the conditions under which the sleeper effect reliably occurs.

laws.name: Parasocial Interaction
laws.statement: The one-sided sense of friendship a viewer feels toward a media figure who does not know they exist.

sources.text: Parasocial interaction, Wikipedia. — the one-sided relationship with a media persona, the interaction-versus-relationship distinction, Horton and Wohl's 1956 intimacy-at-a-distance origin, the direct-address mechanism, the social-media relevance, and its status as a normal phenomenon.
Parasocial interaction, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the semblance of interpersonal exchange with performers, the 1956 origin, and the mechanism and effects.

laws.name: The Filter Bubble
laws.statement: Algorithms feed you what you already agree with, quietly walling you off from views you would dislike.

sources.text: Filter bubble, Wikipedia. — the algorithmic personalisation that isolates users from disagreeable information, Pariser's 2011 coinage, the mechanism and the different-results example, the echo-chamber distinction, the polarisation and misinformation concerns, and the mixed and contested evidence.
Axel Bruns, Filter Bubbles and Echo Chambers: Debunking the Myths. — the argument that filter-bubble and echo-chamber effects are overstated.

laws.name: The Shepard Tone
laws.statement: A tone that seems to rise forever yet never actually gets any higher.

sources.text: Shepard tone, Wikipedia. — the illusion of an endlessly rising or falling tone, Shepard's 1964 origin and the Risset glissando, the octave-spaced sine waves and bell-shaped envelope, the pitch-class circularity, and the film and game uses.
Listening to the Shepard-Risset Glissando, Frontiers in Psychology (PMC). — the Shepard-Risset glissando and its perceptual and emotional effects.

laws.name: The Tritone Paradox
laws.statement: The same pair of ambiguous tones rises for some listeners and falls for others, depending on where they grew up.

sources.text: Tritone paradox, Wikipedia. — the ambiguous tritone pair heard as ascending or descending by different listeners, the use of Shepard-type octave-ambiguous tones, Deutsch's 1986 discovery, and the correlation with linguistic and geographical background.
Diana Deutsch, The Tritone Paradox (philomel.com). — the illusion, the octave-ambiguous tones, and the finding that perceived direction correlates with linguistic background.

laws.name: The Rubber Hand Illusion
laws.statement: Watch a fake hand stroked in time with your hidden one, and your brain starts to feel the rubber hand is yours.

sources.text: Rubber hand illusion, Wikipedia. — the feeling that a fake hand is one's own, the hidden-hand and synchronous-stroking procedure, the synchronous-versus-asynchronous finding, proprioceptive drift, the threat response, the Botvinick and Cohen 1998 origin, and the multisensory-integration significance.
Botvinick and Cohen, Rubber hands feel touch that eyes see, Nature (1998). — the original report of the illusion.

laws.name: The Ventriloquist Effect
laws.statement: We hear a sound as coming from wherever we see its likely source, so the voice seems to come from the moving puppet.

sources.text: Visual capture, Wikipedia. — the ventriloquist effect as the shifting of perceived sound location toward a visual source, the ventriloquism-act and cinema examples, and the visual-capture framing.

Bruns, The Ventriloquist Illusion as a Tool to Study Multisensory Processing, Frontiers in Integrative Neuroscience (2019). — the definition, the reliability-weighted integration mechanism, and the ventriloquism aftereffect.

laws.name: The Phi Phenomenon
laws.statement: Flash two lights in quick succession and the eye sees a single light moving, motion present in neither frame.

sources.text: Phi phenomenon, Wikipedia. — the apparent motion from successive stationary stimuli, Wertheimer's 1912 study and the founding of Gestalt psychology, the beta-movement-versus-strict-phi distinction and its common conflation, and the film-motion significance.
Phi phenomenon, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the illusion of movement between alternating stationary objects and its Gestalt significance.

laws.name: The Café Wall Illusion
laws.statement: Rows of offset dark and light tiles make the perfectly straight lines between them look sloped.

sources.text: Cafe wall illusion, Wikipedia. — the parallel lines appearing sloped, the offset-tiles and intermediate-grey-mortar setup, the Gregory and Heard 1979 naming and the Bristol café, the Munsterberg antecedent, and the border-contrast mechanism with the essential mortar.
Gregory and Heard, Border locking and the Café Wall illusion, Perception (1979). — the original description and the border-locking account.

laws.name: Troxler's Fading
laws.statement: Fix your gaze and hold it still, and unchanging things in the corner of your eye quietly fade from view.

sources.text: Troxler's fading, Wikipedia. — the fading of unchanging peripheral stimuli under steady fixation, Troxler's 1804 identification, the neural-adaptation and fixational-eye-movement mechanism, the filling-in, the retinal-stabilisation connection, and the lilac chaser demonstration.
Troxler Effect, The Illusions Index (University of Glasgow). — the phenomenon, its conditions, and the role of adaptation and eye movements.

laws.name: The McCollough Effect
laws.statement: Stare at colored stripes for minutes and black-and-white stripes look tinted for hours, days, even weeks afterward.

sources.text: McCollough effect, Wikipedia. — the orientation-contingent colour aftereffect, the induction procedure and complementary result, McCollough's 1965 Science paper, the remarkably long duration, and the cortical, debated mechanism.
McCollough Effect, The Illusions Index (University of Glasgow). — the aftereffect, its induction, and its persistence.

laws.name: The Ponzo Illusion
laws.statement: Two identical bars laid across converging railway tracks look unequal, the upper one seeming larger.

sources.text: Ponzo illusion, Wikipedia. — identical bars across converging lines appearing different sizes, the Mario Ponzo attribution around 1911, the perspective and size-constancy explanation, the framing alternative, and the moon-illusion connection.
Ponzo illusion, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the illusion and its explanation via linear perspective and size constancy.

laws.name: The Kanizsa Triangle
laws.statement: Three notched circles conjure a bright white triangle with crisp edges that are not actually there.

sources.text: Illusory contours, Wikipedia. — the perception of edges and a shape without physical contours, the three-notched-circle arrangement and brighter illusory triangle, Kanizsa's 1955 work, modal and amodal completion, and the V1 and V2 neural responses.
Kanizsa Triangle, The Illusions Index (University of Glasgow). — the illusory-contour figure and its constructive-perception interpretation.

laws.name: The Motion Aftereffect
laws.statement: Stare at a waterfall, then at the rocks beside it, and the still rocks seem to drift upward.

sources.text: Motion aftereffect, Wikipedia. — the illusion of reverse motion after adaptation, the waterfall-illusion name, Addams's 1834 Falls of Foyers description and the Aristotle antecedent, the direction-selective-neuron adaptation mechanism, the motion-without-displacement paradox, and the MT or V5 localisation.
Waterfall Illusion, The Illusions Index (University of Glasgow). — the motion aftereffect, its mechanism, and the paradoxical motion-without-displacement percept.

laws.name: The Stroop Effect
laws.statement: Naming the ink colour of a word is slow and error-prone when the word spells a different colour.

sources.text: Stroop effect, Wikipedia. — the interference in naming the ink colour of mismatched colour words, Stroop's 1935 study, the incongruent-condition slowdown, the automaticity-of-reading and related explanations, and its use to measure attention and cognitive control.
Stroop Effect: Definition, Experiment and Examples, SimplyPsychology. — the effect, the classic task, and the automaticity explanation.

laws.name: The Müller-Lyer Illusion
laws.statement: Two equal lines look unequal when tipped with arrow fins: the one with outward fins seems longer.

sources.text: Muller-Lyer illusion, Wikipedia. — the equal lines appearing unequal with the outward-finned line looking longer, Müller-Lyer's 1889 origin, Gregory's perspective and size-constancy explanation and the alternatives, and the Segall cross-cultural carpentered-world finding and its debate.
Muller-Lyer Illusion, The Illusions Index (University of Glasgow). — the illusion, the competing explanations, and its role in debates about perception.

laws.name: Ethos, Pathos, Logos
laws.statement: Persuasion works through three appeals: the speaker's character, the audience's emotion, and the argument's logic.

sources.text: Modes of persuasion, Wikipedia. — Aristotle's three artistic proofs ethos (character/credibility), pathos (emotion), and logos (logic/reason) from the Rhetoric, the inartistic-versus-artistic-proof distinction, and kairos sometimes added as a later fourth appeal.
Rhetoric, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — Aristotle's Rhetoric and the appeals to character, emotion, and reason as the means of persuasion.

laws.name: Kairos
laws.statement: Persuasion depends not just on what is said but on saying it at the right, opportune moment.

sources.text: Kairos, Wikipedia. — the ancient Greek sense of the right or opportune moment, its role in classical rhetoric, the contrast with chronos, and its later theological and modern uses.
Caerus, Wikipedia. — the personification of opportunity, depicted with a forelock and bald behind so the moment can be seized only as it approaches, the Roman counterpart of the Greek Kairos.

laws.name: The Toulmin Model
laws.statement: A real argument breaks into a claim, the grounds for it, and the warrant that links them.

sources.text: Stephen Toulmin, Wikipedia. — Toulmin's The Uses of Argument (1958), his critique of formal logic for practical reasoning, and the argument model with claim, grounds/data, warrant, backing, qualifier, and rebuttal.
The Toulmin Model of Argument, Purdue Online Writing Lab (OWL). — the six components of the Toulmin model and their roles in analysing arguments.

laws.name: The Socratic Method
laws.statement: Truth is pursued not by lecturing but by relentless questions that expose contradictions in what one believes.

sources.text: Socratic method, Wikipedia. — the cooperative question-and-answer method named after Socrates, the elenchus or refutation, Socratic irony, the aporia in which dialogues often end, and modern uses in law and therapy.
Socrates, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Socrates, his method of questioning as portrayed in Plato's dialogues, and the interpretive issues surrounding the historical Socrates.

laws.name: The Principle of Charity
laws.statement: Interpret others by assuming their statements are rational and true, taking the strongest reading available.

sources.text: Principle of charity, Wikipedia. — the norm of interpreting a speaker's statements in the most rational, strongest form, Neil Wilson's 1959 coinage, its use by Quine and Davidson, and its contrast with the straw man.
Donald Davidson, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Davidson's principle of charity as a precondition of radical interpretation and the interdependence of meaning and belief.

laws.name: Reductio ad Absurdum
laws.statement: To refute a claim, assume it true and show it leads to something absurd or contradictory.

sources.text: Reductio ad absurdum, Wikipedia. — the argument form that refutes a claim by showing it leads to an absurd or contradictory conclusion, its use as proof by contradiction, the square-root-of-two and infinitude-of-primes examples, and its Greek and Aristotelian roots.
Reductio ad absurdum, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the method of disproving a proposition by deriving an absurd or contradictory consequence from it.

laws.name: The Burden of Proof
laws.statement: Whoever makes a claim bears the duty to prove it; disbelief needs no proof of its own.

sources.text: Burden of proof (philosophy), Wikipedia. — the onus probandi resting on the party who asserts a claim, the maxim incumbit ei qui dicit, the argument from ignorance and shifting the burden, and Russell's teapot, Sagan's standard, and Hitchens's razor.
Burden of proof, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the obligation to prove a disputed assertion and its role and standards in law.

laws.name: The Golden Mean
laws.statement: Virtue lies in the middle: each is a mean between too much and too little of a thing.

sources.text: Golden mean (philosophy), Wikipedia. — Aristotle's doctrine of virtue as the mean between excess and deficiency, examples such as courage between cowardice and rashness, the mean as relative to us, and acts that admit of no mean.
Aristotle's Ethics, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the doctrine of the mean, the role of practical wisdom (phronesis), and the structure of Aristotle's account of moral virtue.

laws.name: The Principle of Sufficient Reason
laws.statement: Nothing is so without a reason: everything that is has a sufficient reason why it is so.

sources.text: Principle of Sufficient Reason, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Yitzhak Y. Melamed and Martin Lin). — the principle that everything must have a reason, cause, or ground, Leibniz as main formulator with antecedents, the pairing with the principle of contradiction, the cosmological argument, Schopenhauer's fourfold root, and challenges from necessitarianism and quantum indeterminacy.
Principle of sufficient reason, Wikipedia. — the principle that every contingent fact has a sufficient reason, its association with Leibniz, and its precursors and debates.

laws.name: The Law of Noncontradiction
laws.statement: A proposition and its negation cannot both be true at the same time and in the same respect.

sources.text: Law of noncontradiction, Wikipedia. — the principle that a proposition and its negation cannot both be true at the same time and in the same respect, its symbolic form, Aristotle's Metaphysics formulations and firmest-principle status, the three laws of thought, and the distinction from excluded middle.
