Dialetheism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the view that there are true contradictions, its coinage by Priest and Routley, and its rejection of the universal law of noncontradiction alongside paraconsistent logic.

laws.name: The Principle of Explosion
laws.statement: From a single contradiction, absolutely anything can be proved: one falsehood makes everything derivable.

sources.text: Principle of explosion, Wikipedia. — the law that any statement can be proved from a contradiction, the Latin terms ex falso quodlibet and ex contradictione quodlibet, the trivialisation consequence, the disjunction-introduction and disjunctive-syllogism derivation, the paraconsistent response, and the William of Soissons attribution.
Paraconsistent Logic, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the definition of a paraconsistent consequence relation as one that is not explosive, and its connection to dialetheism.

laws.name: The Steel Man
laws.statement: Before you refute an argument, rebuild it into the strongest version its holder could give.

sources.text: Straw man, Wikipedia (Steelmanning section). — the steel man as the opposite of the straw man, defined as applying the rhetorical principle of charity by addressing the strongest form of the other person's argument, and the rationale that countering the strongest form yields a stronger position.

steelman, Wiktionary. — the definition and etymology of steelman as a deliberate inverse of straw man, an improvement of a position that is harder to defeat than the one originally stated, with a 2011 origin noted.

laws.name: The Rule of Three
laws.statement: Things grouped in threes are more satisfying, memorable, and persuasive than other numbers.

sources.text: Rule of three (writing), Wikipedia. — the principle that a trio of elements is more satisfying and memorable than other numbers because three is the smallest number to create a pattern with brevity and rhythm, its roots in oral storytelling, and the comic triple.
Tricolon, Wikipedia. — the rhetorical figure of three parallel elements and the ascending tricolon crescens, with examples such as veni, vidi, vici.

laws.name: The Circle of Fifths
laws.statement: Arrange the twelve tones by perfect fifths and they close into a circle mapping every key.

sources.text: Circle of fifths, Wikipedia. — the arrangement of the twelve pitch classes by ascending perfect fifths clockwise and fourths counterclockwise, the twelve-fifth closure in equal temperament, the sharps-clockwise and flats-counterclockwise key signatures, relative minors, enharmonic equivalence, and the Diletsky and Heinichen history.
Circle of fifths, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the circle of fifths, its arrangement of keys, and the outer major and inner relative-minor rings.

laws.name: Equal Temperament
laws.statement: Split the octave into twelve identical steps and every key sounds equally, imperfectly, in tune.

sources.text: 12 equal temperament, Wikipedia. — the division of the octave into twelve equal semitones at the ratio of the twelfth root of two, the cent, the only-octave-pure trade-off enabling all keys, the 700-cent fifth and 400-cent third deviations, and the distribution of the Pythagorean comma.
Equal temperament, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — equal temperament as dividing the octave into twelve equal semitones, with only the octave acoustically pure, enabling keyboard playing in all keys.

laws.name: The Harmonic Series
laws.statement: A vibrating string sounds not one note but a whole ladder of integer-multiple frequencies at once.

sources.text: Harmonic series (music), Wikipedia. — the sequence of integer-multiple frequencies produced by a vibrating string or air column, the fundamental and overtones, the mapping of low harmonics onto octave, fifth, fourth, and third, the timbre link, and the basis of consonance and just intonation.
Harmonic, Wikipedia. — the definition of a harmonic as an integer multiple of the fundamental, the harmonic-versus-overtone distinction, and modes of vibration with nodes and antinodes.

laws.name: Consonance and Dissonance
laws.statement: Some tone combinations sound stable and at rest, others tense and demanding resolution.

sources.text: Consonance and dissonance, Wikipedia. — the stability-versus-tension definition, the association of consonance with simple frequency ratios traced to Pythagoras, Helmholtz's beating and roughness account with the critical band, and the historical and cultural variability of the distinction.
Consonance and dissonance, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — consonance as an impression of stability and repose and dissonance as tension, and the small-integer-ratio basis of the perfect consonances.

laws.name: Just Intonation
laws.statement: Tune every interval to a simple whole-number ratio and the chords ring pure, but only in one key.

sources.text: Just intonation, Wikipedia. — tuning by ratios of small whole numbers (octave 2:1, fifth 3:2, third 5:4, minor third 6:5), the alignment with overtones and beatless purity, the syntonic comma 81:80, the limitation on free modulation, and uses by a cappella, string, and barbershop ensembles.
Just intonation, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — just intonation as tuning from pure natural thirds and fifths, and its impracticality for polyphonic keyboard music.

laws.name: The Pythagorean Comma
laws.statement: Twelve pure fifths overshoot seven octaves by a tiny gap that no keyboard can hide.

sources.text: Pythagorean comma, Wikipedia. — the interval by which twelve pure fifths exceed seven octaves, the ratio 531441:524288 (3^12:2^19) of about 23.46 cents, the failure of the circle of fifths to close, and the distribution of the comma in equal temperament by narrowing each fifth.
Syntonic comma, Wikipedia. — the distinct comma of 81:80 between a Pythagorean and a just major third, distinguished from the Pythagorean comma.

laws.name: The Missing Fundamental
laws.statement: Remove the bass note itself and the ear still hears its pitch, inferred from the overtones.

sources.text: Missing fundamental, Wikipedia. — the perception of the fundamental's pitch when only its higher harmonics are present, the greatest-common-divisor periodicity mechanism and temporal autocorrelation account, and the telephone and small-loudspeaker applications.

The Ohm-Seebeck Dispute, Hermann von Helmholtz, and the Origins of Physiological Acoustics, British Journal for the History of Science. — the nineteenth-century debate over pitch and the missing fundamental among Seebeck, Ohm, and Helmholtz.

laws.name: Helmholtz Resonance
laws.statement: Blow across a bottle and the air in its neck bounces on the air within like a spring.

sources.text: Helmholtz resonance, Wikipedia. — the resonance of air in a cavity with an open neck modelled as the neck air (a mass) on the cavity air (a spring), the blown-bottle example, the frequency formula and its dependence on neck area, volume, and length, the Helmholtz attribution, and applications from bass-reflex speakers to instrument bodies.
Helmholtz resonator, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the Helmholtz resonator, its resonant frequency, and Helmholtz's use of resonators to analyse the components of complex sounds.

laws.name: The Precedence Effect
aliases: The law of the first wavefront
laws.statement: When a sound and its echoes arrive close together, we locate it by the first to reach us.

sources.text: Precedence effect, Wikipedia. — the localization of fused sounds to the first-arriving wavefront with suppression of later reflections, the signal-dependent time window, the Haas effect and its level tolerance, the echo threshold, the Wallach-Newman-Rosenzweig coinage, and applications in rooms and sound reinforcement.
Haas Effect, Sound On Sound glossary. — the Haas effect, the delayed copy that is not heard as a separate echo, and its use in stereo and sound reinforcement.

laws.name: Beats
laws.statement: Two tones a little apart in pitch throb together, waxing and waning at their frequency difference.

sources.text: Beat (acoustics), Wikipedia. — the periodic loudness variation from two nearby frequencies, the beat frequency equal to their difference, the superposition explanation with a carrier at the average frequency and an envelope at half the difference, tuning by eliminating beats, and the transition to roughness and separate tones.
Beats, OpenStax University Physics Volume 1 (17.6). — beats as interference producing a tone at the average frequency that pulsates at the difference frequency, and their use in tuning.

laws.name: The Critical Band
laws.statement: The ear hears in overlapping frequency bands; tones sharing a band interfere, tones in different bands do not.

sources.text: Critical band, Wikipedia. — the auditory-filter bandwidth within which a second tone masks or roughens a first, the basilar-membrane basis, within-band interaction, the growth of bandwidth with frequency, and Fletcher's introduction of the concept.
Bark scale, Wikipedia. — Zwicker's Bark scale of twenty-four critical bands and its role in loudness and masking models.

laws.name: The Rule of Thirds
laws.statement: Divide the frame into thirds and place what matters on the lines, not dead center.

sources.text: Rule of thirds, Wikipedia. — the three-by-three grid, placement of elements on the lines and at the intersections or power points, the tension-and-interest rationale versus centering, John Thomas Smith's 1797 coinage, and the guideline status and relation to the golden ratio.
Who Wrote the Rule of Thirds?, B&H eXplora. — the attribution of the term to John Thomas Smith's 1797 Remarks on Rural Scenery and the rule's use in composition.

laws.name: Form Follows Function
laws.statement: The shape of a thing should grow from what it is meant to do.

sources.text: Form follows function, Wikipedia. — the principle that form should relate to intended function, Louis Sullivan's coinage of form ever follows function in his 1896 essay, the natural inspiration and Greenough influence, Frank Lloyd Wright's form and function are one, the modernist association, and Sullivan's own use of ornament.
The Tall Office Building Artistically Considered (excerpt), Grantmakers in the Arts. — Sullivan's 1896 essay containing the pervading-law passage and the words form ever follows function.

laws.name: The Coandă Effect
laws.statement: A jet of fluid tends to cling to a nearby surface and follow it instead of flying straight.

sources.text: Coandă effect, Wikipedia. — the tendency of a fluid jet to stay attached to a nearby surface, the entrainment and lower-pressure mechanism, the note that the spoon demonstration is dominated by surface tension, the Henri Coandă attribution, and applications in aircraft, fluidics, and ventilation.
Coandă effect, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the tendency of a fluid jet to follow a nearby curved surface via entrainment and a lower-pressure region.

laws.name: The Venturi Effect
laws.statement: Squeeze a flow through a narrow throat and it speeds up while its pressure drops.

sources.text: Venturi effect, Wikipedia. — the pressure reduction when fluid speeds up through a constriction, the continuity-and-Bernoulli basis, the Giovanni Battista Venturi attribution and 1797 publication, the Venturi meter and flow measurement, and applications in carburetors, atomizers, and aspirators.
Venturi tube, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the Venturi tube in which fluid speeds up and pressure drops in the throat, its use in flow measurement and as a pump, and the Bernoulli basis.

laws.name: The Kármán Vortex Street
laws.statement: Flow past a blunt body sheds spinning eddies from alternating sides in a staggered trailing wake.

sources.text: Kármán vortex street, Wikipedia. — the repeating pattern of alternating vortices shed from a bluff body, the Reynolds-number range, the Strouhal number, the von Kármán attribution, and examples including singing wires, oscillating structures, and cloud streets, with the Tacoma Narrows flutter clarification.
Vortex shedding, Wikipedia. — the process of alternating vortex shedding from a bluff body, its Reynolds-number dependence, and vortex-induced vibration of structures.

laws.name: The Rayleigh-Taylor Instability
laws.statement: Rest a heavy fluid on a light one and the boundary breaks into fingers and mushrooming plumes.
laws.namedAfter: Lord Rayleigh and G. I. Taylor

sources.text: Rayleigh-Taylor instability, Wikipedia. — the instability of an interface when a lighter fluid pushes a heavier one, the heavy-over-light and accelerating conditions, the mushroom spikes and bubbles, the Rayleigh and Taylor attributions, and examples from oil and water to mushroom clouds and the Crab Nebula.

Rayleigh-Taylor instability and mixing, Scholarpedia. — the instability arising when the density gradient opposes the pressure gradient, Rayleigh's 1883 static analysis and Taylor's 1950 accelerating case, and the turbulent mixing it drives.

laws.name: The Kelvin-Helmholtz Instability
laws.statement: Where two fluids slide past each other at different speeds, the boundary curls into breaking waves.
laws.namedAfter: Lord Kelvin and Hermann von Helmholtz

sources.text: Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, Wikipedia. — the instability from velocity shear across an interface, the roll-up into spiral vortices and billows, the Kelvin and Helmholtz attributions, the wind-over-water origin, the fluctus clouds and planetary and solar examples, and the distinction from the density-driven Rayleigh-Taylor instability.
Fluctus (Kelvin-Helmholtz cloud feature), WhatsThisCloud. — the billow clouds formed when wind shear between cloud layers curls the interface into a succession of vortices.

laws.name: Cavitation
laws.statement: Drop a liquid's pressure enough and it boils cold into bubbles that implode with violent force.

sources.text: Cavitation, Wikipedia. — the formation of vapor cavities when local pressure drops below the vapor pressure and their violent collapse, the distinction from boiling, occurrence on propellers and pumps, erosion by shock waves and microjets, the inertial and acoustic types, and examples from the pistol shrimp to sonoluminescence.

Cavitation, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — cavities forming when pressure falls to the vapor pressure and collapsing at higher pressure, with erosion, pitting, noise, and reduced efficiency in pumps, turbines, and propellers.

laws.name: The Marangoni Effect
laws.statement: A difference in surface tension drives liquid to flow from the slack surface toward the taut one.

sources.text: Marangoni effect, Wikipedia. — the flow along an interface from lower to higher surface tension, the temperature and concentration causes, the Carlo Marangoni and Gibbs attributions, and applications in thin films, welding, crystal growth, and wafer drying.

Tears of wine, Wikipedia. — the tears-of-wine mechanism in which faster alcohol evaporation raises the surface tension of a climbing film, drawing up liquid that collects and falls, with James Thomson's earlier explanation.

laws.name: The Leidenfrost Effect
laws.statement: On a surface far hotter than boiling, a water droplet rides its own vapor and lingers.

sources.text: Leidenfrost effect, Wikipedia. — the insulating vapor layer that levitates a liquid on a surface far above its boiling point, the dancing droplets lasting longer, the Leidenfrost point (around 193 degrees Celsius for water), the low-conductivity vapor mechanism, and the Johann Gottlob Leidenfrost 1756 attribution.
Leidenfrost Effect and Leidenfrost Point, Nuclear Power. — the film-boiling basis of the effect, the Leidenfrost point, and its relevance to cooling, quenching, and the boiling crisis.

laws.name: The Tyndall Effect
laws.statement: Fine suspended particles scatter a light beam sideways, making its path glow visibly through the haze.

sources.text: Tyndall effect, Wikipedia. — the scattering of light by colloidal particles making a beam visible, the colloid-versus-true-solution test, the stronger scattering of blue wavelengths and relation to Rayleigh scattering by particle size, the John Tyndall attribution, and examples from beams in fog to bluish smoke.
Tyndall effect, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the scattering of a light beam by a medium with small suspended particles such as smoke or dust, named after John Tyndall.

laws.name: Surface Tension
laws.statement: A liquid's surface behaves like a stretched elastic skin, pulling itself to the smallest possible area.

sources.text: Surface tension, Wikipedia. — the tendency of a liquid surface to minimize its area, the cohesion and unbalanced-force mechanism, the force-per-length and energy-per-area units with water about 0.0728 newtons per metre, the water-strider and droplet examples, and the surfactant and temperature effects.

Surface tension, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — surface tension as the property of a liquid surface acting like a stretched elastic membrane, its cohesive origin, the ~0.07275 joules per square metre value for water, and its decrease with temperature.

laws.name: Terminal Velocity
laws.statement: A falling body speeds up only until drag matches gravity, then falls at a steady maximum speed.

sources.text: Terminal velocity, Wikipedia. — the maximum speed when drag and buoyancy balance gravity giving zero net force, the drag-increases-with-speed mechanism, the dependence on mass, area, drag coefficient, and fluid density, the square-law drag and terminal-velocity formula, and skydiver figures.

Terminal velocity, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the steady speed of a body falling through a fluid when air resistance equals its weight and acceleration is zero, with the parachutist and raindrop examples.

laws.name: Capillary Action
laws.statement: Liquid climbs a narrow tube on its own, drawn up by its attraction to the walls.

sources.text: Capillary action, Wikipedia. — the flow of a liquid through narrow spaces without or against external forces, the adhesion, cohesion, and surface-tension mechanism, Jurin's inverse-radius law, the water and mercury menisci, and examples including wicking and a contributing role in plants.
Capillarity, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the rise or depression of a liquid in a small passage, the dependence on wetting, and the higher rise in narrower tubes.

laws.name: The Brazil Nut Effect
laws.statement: Shake a mix of grains and the biggest pieces climb to the top, like Brazil nuts in the tin.

sources.text: Granular convection, Wikipedia. — the Brazil nut effect in which shaking makes larger particles rise, the naming from mixed nuts, the percolation and convection mechanisms, its status as an unsolved problem, the reverse Brazil nut effect, and relevance to industrial mixing.

Reversing the Brazil-nut effect: competition between percolation and condensation, Physical Review Letters. — the existence of the reverse Brazil nut effect and its dependence on particle density and conditions.

laws.name: Lagrange Points
laws.statement: Five points hang in a two-body system where a small craft can ride along, holding its place.

sources.text: Lagrange point, Wikipedia. — the five points L1 to L5 in a two-body system, their geometry with collinear L1-L3 and triangular L4-L5, the unstable-versus-stable distinction and the ~24.96 mass-ratio condition, the Lagrange and Euler attributions, and uses including JWST at L2 and Jupiter Trojans at L4/L5.
What is a Lagrange Point?, NASA. — the collinear and triangular Lagrange points, the balance of gravitational and centripetal forces, and their use for spacecraft and observatories.

laws.name: The Hohmann Transfer Orbit
laws.statement: The cheapest way between two circular orbits is a single ellipse kissing them both, with two burns.

sources.text: Hohmann transfer orbit, Wikipedia. — the most fuel-efficient two-impulse transfer between two circular coplanar orbits via a tangent ellipse, the two-burn raise-then-circularize structure, the Walter Hohmann 1925 attribution, the bi-elliptic alternative for large ratios, and uses for geostationary and interplanetary transfers.
Hohmann Transfer, Orbital Mechanics & Astrodynamics. — the tangent-ellipse definition, the two tangential burns, and the delta-v analysis of the Hohmann transfer.

laws.name: Tidal Locking
laws.statement: Over time an orbiting body's spin matches its orbit, so it forever shows one face to its partner.

sources.text: Tidal locking, Wikipedia. — the state where rotation period equals orbital period so one face stays toward the partner, the Moon example, the tidal-bulge torque mechanism, the dark-side misconception, Pluto-Charon mutual locking, Mercury's 3:2 resonance, and the distance dependence of the timescale.
Tidal Locking, NASA. — the Moon's synchronous rotation keeping one face toward Earth and the tidal process that slowed its spin to match its orbit.

laws.name: The Oberth Effect
laws.statement: A rocket burn buys more energy when fired fast and deep in a gravity well than when slow.

sources.text: Oberth effect, Wikipedia. — the greater change in mechanical energy from firing an engine at higher speed, the kinetic-energy and exhaust reasoning, the Oberth maneuver burning at periapsis, the Hermann Oberth attribution, and that it does not violate energy conservation.
The Sun Diver: Combining solar sails with the Oberth effect, arXiv. — a study applying the Oberth effect, confirming that a burn deep in a gravity well at high speed maximizes the energy gain.

laws.name: The Hill Sphere
laws.statement: Around every planet is a bubble within which its gravity, not the Sun's, rules any moon.

sources.text: Hill sphere, Wikipedia. — the region where a body's gravity dominates over the primary's for retaining satellites, the radius formula scaling with distance and the cube root of the mass ratio, the Hill and Roche attribution, Earth's ~1.5 million km sphere, the relation to the L1 and L2 points, and the distinction from the Roche limit.
Roche limit, Wikipedia. — the distinct concept of the distance within which tidal forces break up a body, distinguished from the Hill (Roche) sphere.

laws.name: Gravity Assist
laws.statement: A spacecraft steals a sliver of a moving planet's motion to change its own speed for free.

sources.text: Gravity assist, Wikipedia. — the use of a planet's gravity and motion to change a spacecraft's speed and direction, the frame-dependent velocity change with conserved momentum, the behind-speeds-up and in-front-slows-down geometry, and mission examples including Voyager, Cassini, and MESSENGER, plus the powered Oberth combination.
Basics of Spaceflight: A Gravity Assist Primer, NASA. — how a gravity assist transfers orbital momentum from a planet to a spacecraft to increase or decrease its speed relative to the Sun.

laws.name: The Roche Lobe
laws.statement: Around each star in a pair is a teardrop of space it can hold; overflow it and matter spills to the other.

sources.text: Roche lobe, Wikipedia. — the teardrop region bound to each star in a binary meeting at the inner Lagrange point L1, the critical equipotential in the co-rotating frame, Roche-lobe overflow driving mass transfer, the accretion and interacting-binary consequences, and the Édouard Roche attribution.
Cataclysmic variable star, Wikipedia. — the accretion of matter from a Roche-lobe-filling companion onto a white dwarf, the accretion disk, and the resulting nova and related phenomena.

laws.name: Orbital Resonance
laws.statement: When orbits fall into whole-number ratios, bodies tug each other in rhythm, locking or clearing them.

sources.text: Orbital resonance, Wikipedia. — the periodic gravitational influence when orbital periods form small-integer ratios, mean-motion resonance, the stabilizing Laplace and Neptune-Pluto resonances, the destabilizing Kirkwood gaps and ring divisions, and the significance for system architecture and migration.
Orbital resonances of the Galilean moons, The Planetary Society. — the one-two-four Laplace resonance of Io, Europa, and Ganymede as a stable resonant configuration.

laws.name: The Oort Cloud
laws.statement: Far beyond the planets, a vast shell of icy bodies wraps the Sun and feeds long comets.

sources.text: Oort cloud, Wikipedia. — the roughly spherical shell of billions of icy planetesimals at thousands to ~100,000+ astronomical units, the inner Hills and outer regions, the ejection origin, the perturbation of long-period comets by passing stars and galactic tides, the Jan Oort 1950 attribution, and its hypothetical, unobserved status.
Oort Cloud Facts, NASA. — the distant spherical shell of icy bodies surrounding the solar system, the source of long-period comets arriving from all directions, and its enormous distance.

laws.name: The Kármán Line
laws.statement: The conventional edge of space sits about a hundred kilometres up, where wings stop working.

sources.text: Kármán line, Wikipedia. — the conventional 100 km (about 62 mile) boundary of space with no sharp physical significance, von Kármán's reasoning that above it the air is too thin for aerodynamic flight requiring orbital speed for lift, the von Kármán attribution, and the FAI 100 km versus US 80 km (50 mile) dispute.
Kármán line, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the Kármán line as the roughly 100 km conventional boundary between the atmosphere and space, named after Theodore von Kármán.

laws.name: Escape Velocity
laws.statement: Fling something upward fast enough and gravity never wins it back; for Earth that is 11 km/s.

sources.text: Escape velocity, Wikipedia. — the minimum unpowered speed to escape a body's gravity, the formula root of 2GM/r and the root-2 relation to orbital velocity, Earth's ~11.2 km/s and the Moon and Sun figures, the independence from the escaping object's mass, the decrease with altitude, and the black-hole connection.
Escape velocity, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the velocity needed to escape a gravitational centre without further acceleration, Earth's ~11.2 km/s, and the black-hole event-horizon case.

laws.name: The Goldilocks Zone
laws.statement: Around each star lies a band not too hot, not too cold, where water could stay liquid.

sources.text: Circumstellar habitable zone, Wikipedia. — the orbital range where surface liquid water is possible given a suitable atmosphere, the Goldilocks nickname, the too-hot and too-cold bounds, the dependence on stellar luminosity, Earth's position, and the caveats that the zone is not a guarantee and that subsurface oceans can exist outside it.
Habitable Zone, NASA. — the region around a star where liquid surface water could exist, essential for life as we know it, and its use in the search for habitable exoplanets.

laws.name: Retrograde Motion
laws.statement: A planet seems to pause and drift backward against the stars as Earth overtakes it.

sources.text: Apparent retrograde motion, Wikipedia. — the apparent westward motion of a planet against the stars, the prograde-versus-retrograde distinction, the relative-motion and overtaking cause with the highway analogy, the Ptolemaic epicycle versus Copernican heliocentric explanations, and the distinction from true retrograde motion.

Retrograde motion, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the apparent motion depending on the difference in orbital speeds of the planets, and the distinction of true retrograde rotation such as that of Venus and Uranus.

laws.name: The Maillard Reaction
laws.statement: Heat amino acids and sugars together and they brown into the flavors of searing and toasting.

sources.text: Maillard reaction, Wikipedia. — the non-enzymatic browning reaction between amino acids and reducing sugars producing melanoidins and flavour compounds, the carbonyl-amino mechanism, the ~140 to 165 degree Celsius range, the distinction from caramelization, the Louis-Camille Maillard 1912 attribution, and examples like seared steak and roasted coffee.
Maillard reaction, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the nonenzymatic browning when sugars and proteins are heated together, with reducing sugars reacting with the amino groups of proteins or amino acids.

laws.name: Caramelization
laws.statement: Heat sugar alone and it breaks apart, browning into caramel's colour and buttery flavour.

sources.text: Caramelization, Wikipedia. — the non-enzymatic, pyrolytic browning of sugar alone, the distinction from the Maillard reaction, the decomposition into many compounds including diacetyl and the caramelan/caramelen/caramelin pigments, and the sugar-specific temperatures with sucrose around 170 degrees Celsius.
Caramelization, The Science of Cooking. — the browning of sugar through thermal decomposition and its role in flavour and colour in cooking.

laws.name: Gelatinization
laws.statement: Heat starch in water and its granules swell, burst, and thicken the mixture into a sauce.

sources.text: Starch gelatinization, Wikipedia. — the swelling and loss of crystalline structure of starch granules heated in water, the water-penetration, crystalline-melting, amylose-leaching, and viscosity-increase mechanism, the roughly 55 to 85 degree range, amylose and amylopectin, and retrogradation.
Starch retrogradation, ScienceDirect Topics. — the recrystallization of gelatinized starch on cooling, distinct from gelatinization, and its role in bread staling and gel firming.

laws.name: Emulsion
laws.statement: Beat oil into water hard enough, with a binder, and the two unmixable liquids hold together.

sources.text: Emulsion, Wikipedia. — a mixture of immiscible liquids with one dispersed as droplets in the other, the oil-in-water and water-in-oil types, the amphiphilic emulsifiers that lower interfacial tension, the instability requiring energy to form, and food examples like milk, mayonnaise, and butter.

Emulsions: making oil and water mix, American Oil Chemists' Society (AOCS). — emulsions as droplets of one immiscible fluid in another, emulsifiers stabilizing droplets, and egg-yolk lecithin in mayonnaise and sauces.

laws.name: Protein Denaturation
laws.statement: Heat, acid, or whisking unravels a protein's folded shape while leaving its chain intact.

sources.text: Denaturation (biochemistry), Wikipedia. — the loss of a protein's folded structure under stresses like acid, base, salt, solvent, agitation, or heat, with the primary sequence and peptide bonds intact, the coagulation of egg white and curdling of milk, and often irreversible denaturation.
Ceviche, Wikipedia. — the citric-acid denaturation of raw fish that alters the protein structure and turns the flesh opaque and firm.

laws.name: Fermentation
laws.statement: Microbes eat sugars without air and leave behind alcohol, acids, and gas that preserve and flavour food.

sources.text: Fermentation, Wikipedia. — the anaerobic metabolic breakdown of sugars by microorganisms into products like ethanol, lactate, and carbon dioxide, ethanol and lactic-acid fermentation, and the food and preservation applications.

Fermentation in food processing, Wikipedia. — the use of fermentation to make beer, wine, bread, yogurt, cheese, sauerkraut, and other foods, its preservation and flavour roles, and Pasteur's link of yeast to fermentation.

laws.name: The Gluten Network
laws.statement: Wet wheat flour and knead it, and its proteins link into an elastic web that traps gas.

sources.text: Gluten, Wikipedia. — gluten as the elastic network of wheat's gliadin and glutenin proteins, the cross-linking by disulfide bonds on hydration and kneading, the trapping of carbon dioxide that makes dough rise, the protein-content effect on chewiness, and the celiac-disease immune response.

Gluten: The Protein Network That Makes Bread Possible, 123 Food Science. — the complementary roles of glutenin (elasticity) and gliadin (extensibility), gluten development by kneading, and the effects of protein content and fat.

laws.name: The Scoville Scale
laws.statement: Chili heat is graded in Scoville units, from a bland zero to millions for the fiercest peppers.

sources.text: Scoville scale, Wikipedia. — the measurement of pungency in Scoville Heat Units based on capsaicinoid concentration, Wilbur Scoville's 1912 organoleptic dilution test, its subjectivity and the modern HPLC method, and example values from bell pepper (0) to pure capsaicin (~16 million).
Scoville scale, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the system measuring the spiciness of chili peppers in Scoville Heat Units, Wilbur Scoville, and the subjectivity of the measurements.

laws.name: Umami
laws.statement: Beyond sweet, sour, salty, and bitter lies a fifth taste: the savoury depth of broth and cheese.

sources.text: Umami, Wikipedia. — umami as the fifth basic taste, the savoury character, the glutamate and inosinate/guanylate basis, the synergy effect, Kikunae Ikeda's 1908 discovery from kombu and development of MSG, the umami taste receptors, and umami-rich foods.
Umami, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — umami as the savoury fifth taste derived from glutamate, guanylate, and inosinate, and its taste receptor.

laws.name: Pasteurization
laws.statement: Gently heating milk kills its dangerous germs without boiling it or making it sterile.

sources.text: Pasteurization, Wikipedia. — the mild heat treatment that destroys pathogens and reduces spoilage organisms without full sterilization, the Louis Pasteur 1860s origin, the LTLT, HTST, and UHT methods and temperatures, the survival of spores, and the public-health impact on milk-borne disease.

Pasteurization, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — pasteurization as heat treatment destroying pathogenic microorganisms using lower temperatures than sterilization, its origin with Pasteur and wine, and its methods.

laws.name: Enzymatic Browning
laws.statement: A cut apple browns not from heat but from an enzyme reacting with air on the exposed flesh.

sources.text: Enzymatic browning, Wikipedia. — the enzyme-driven browning of cut fruits and vegetables at room temperature, distinct from the Maillard reaction and caramelization, the polyphenol oxidase oxidation of phenols to quinones and melanins, and prevention by acid, oxygen exclusion, and heat.
Polyphenol oxidase, Wikipedia. — the copper-containing enzyme that catalyzes the oxidation of phenols in enzymatic browning, and its role in the browning of produce and in tea, coffee, and cocoa.

laws.name: The Smoke Point
laws.statement: Every cooking oil has a temperature where it starts to break down and smoke bitterly.

sources.text: Smoke point, Wikipedia. — the temperature at which a heated oil begins to produce continuous bluish smoke and break down, releasing acrolein, the effect of free fatty acids and refining, the fact that it is not fixed and decreases with use, and the distinction from the flash and fire points.
Smoke point, what is it exactly?, Food Meets Science. — the smoke point as the onset of oil breakdown and smoking, acrolein, and the effects of composition and refining.

laws.name: Curing
laws.statement: Salt and nitrites draw the water from meat and starve its microbes, preserving it for months.

sources.text: Curing (food preservation), Wikipedia. — the preservation of meat and fish with salt, nitrates/nitrites, sugar, and smoke, the salt-osmosis lowering of water activity, nitrite's role against Clostridium botulinum and in the cured pink colour, dry and wet curing, and the nitrosamine and processed-meat health concerns.

Meat processing: Curing and smoking, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — curing by adding salt to reduce moisture and nitrite to prevent microbial growth and rancidity, enhancing safety, shelf life, colour, and flavour.

laws.name: Additive Color
laws.statement: Mix red, green, and blue light and you build up every colour, ending in white.

sources.text: Additive color, Wikipedia. — the mixing of coloured light with red, green, and blue primaries adding toward white, the secondary combinations, the contrast with subtractive color, the use in RGB displays, and the trichromatic basis via the Young-Helmholtz theory.
Additive and subtractive colour mixing, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — additive mixing of red, green, and blue light beginning from darkness and combining to white, and the three cone types.

laws.name: Subtractive Color
laws.statement: Pigments make colour by absorbing light, so mixing them all darkens toward black.

sources.text: Subtractive color, Wikipedia. — the mixing of colorants that absorb wavelengths from white light, the cyan, magenta, and yellow primaries and their combinations toward black, the RYB-versus-CMY distinction, CMYK printing and the reason for the black key ink, and the contrast with additive color.
Primary color, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the subtractive primaries cyan, magenta, and yellow, their wider colour range than red, yellow, blue, and mixing by absorption.

laws.name: Complementary Colors
laws.statement: Opposite each other on the colour wheel, complements cancel to grey and, side by side, intensify.

sources.text: Complementary colors, Wikipedia. — pairs of colours opposite on the wheel that cancel to a grayscale colour, the dependence on the colour model, the additive complements (red-cyan, green-magenta, blue-yellow) mixing to white, the traditional pairs (red-green, etc.), the afterimage link, and the high-contrast artistic use.

Complementary color, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — complementary colours as opposite pairs on the colour wheel, their mutual enhancement of intensity when juxtaposed, and Chevreul's law of simultaneous contrast.

laws.name: Color Constancy
laws.statement: A red apple looks red in sunlight, shade, or lamplight, though the light it reflects differs wildly.

sources.text: Color constancy, Wikipedia. — the relative constancy of perceived object colour under varying illumination, the reflectance-versus-illumination problem and discounting the illuminant, chromatic adaptation and context, Edwin Land's retinex theory, and the imperfection under monochromatic light.
The dress, Wikipedia. — the viral photograph seen as blue-and-black or white-and-gold, explained via color constancy and differing assumptions about the illumination.

laws.name: The Afterimage
laws.statement: Stare at a colour, look away, and a ghost of it lingers in the opposite hue.

sources.text: Afterimage, Wikipedia. — the lingering image after exposure, the negative afterimage in complementary colours with reversed brightness, the adaptation and opponent-process mechanism, the positive afterimage, and the flag demonstration.
Afterimage, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the visual illusion in which retinal impressions persist after a stimulus is removed, and the positive and negative (complementary) forms.

laws.name: Simultaneous Contrast
laws.statement: The same colour looks different against different surroundings, shifting toward the opposite of its neighbour.

sources.text: Contrast effect, Wikipedia. — simultaneous contrast in which a colour's appearance depends on its surroundings, the lightness and chromatic (complement-shift) aspects, the lateral-inhibition and opponent-process mechanism, and the distinction from successive contrast.
Law of simultaneous contrast, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — Chevreul's law of simultaneous contrast of colours, the mutual influence of juxtaposed colours, and their enhancement toward complements.

laws.name: The Purkinje Effect
laws.statement: As light fades to dusk, reds darken and blues brighten as the eye shifts to its rods.

sources.text: Purkinje effect, Wikipedia. — the shift of peak luminance sensitivity toward blue at low light, the reds-darken observation, the cone (~555 nm) and rod (~507 nm) peaks and rod insensitivity to red, the Purkyně 1819 attribution, and the red-light night-vision application.

How Does the Human Eye Perceive Light? Photopic and Scotopic Vision, AZoM. — the cone and rod systems, their peak sensitivities, and the transition between photopic and scotopic vision underlying the Purkinje shift.

laws.name: Trichromacy
laws.statement: Human colour vision runs on just three kinds of cone, so three primaries can recreate any hue.

sources.text: Trichromacy, Wikipedia. — the three independent colour channels from the three cone types, the S, M, and L cones and approximate peaks, the Young-Helmholtz theory, the basis for three-primary colour reproduction, metamerism as a consequence, and variations including colour blindness and tetrachromacy.
Young-Helmholtz theory, Wikipedia. — Thomas Young's 1802 proposal of three receptor types and Helmholtz's development of the trichromatic theory of colour vision.

laws.name: The Opponent-Process Theory
laws.statement: Colour is coded in opposing pairs, so we never see a reddish-green or a yellowish-blue.

sources.text: Opponent process, Wikipedia. — the three opponent channels red-green, blue-yellow, and black-white, the impossibility of reddish-green, the afterimage evidence, Ewald Hering's theory in opposition to trichromacy, and the reconciliation as opponent processing of cone signals in retinal ganglion cells and beyond.

Opponent Processing Theory of Color Vision, York University Centre for Vision Research. — the opponent channels, Hering's red-patch afterimage demonstration, and the excitation-inhibition opponent-neuron mechanism.

laws.name: Metamerism
laws.statement: Two colours built from different spectra can look identical, then diverge under different light.

sources.text: Metamerism (color), Wikipedia. — the matching of colours with different spectral power distributions, the trichromatic reduction to three tristimulus values, illuminant metameric failure with the clothing and paint examples, observer metamerism, and the basis for colour reproduction.

Metamerism: when colours seem to change in different light sources, RMIT Colour Theory. — metamerism as different spectra appearing to match, its trichromatic basis, and its practical challenges in colour matching.

laws.name: Color Temperature
laws.statement: Light's colour is rated in kelvins, where, oddly, low numbers are warm and high numbers cool.

sources.text: Color temperature, Wikipedia. — the colour of a light source described by comparison to a black-body radiator in kelvins, the counterintuitive warm-low and cool-high convention, the black-body colour progression, reference values, the white-balance and lighting applications, and correlated colour temperature.

Colour temperature, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — colour temperature as the colour of light emitted by a black body at a given temperature in kelvins, with higher temperatures richer in blue and poorer in red.

laws.name: Color Blindness
laws.statement: When a cone type is missing or altered, some colours become hard to tell apart, most often red and green.

sources.text: Color blindness, Wikipedia. — reduced colour discrimination from cone problems, red-green as the most common form, the protan, deutan, tritan, and monochromacy types and the dichromacy-versus-anomalous distinction, the X-linked genetics with ~8% of men and ~0.5% of women affected, the Ishihara test, and no cure.
Color blindness, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — colour vision deficiency from cone dysfunction, usually a weakened rather than absent colour sense, and its inheritance and types.

laws.name: Benham's Top
laws.statement: Spin a black-and-white patterned disc and most people see phantom colours that are not there.

sources.text: Fechner color effect, Wikipedia. — the illusory colours seen from a spinning black-and-white pattern, Benham's top and Charles Benham's marketing, Gustav Fechner's 1838 description, the incompletely understood temporal-response mechanism, and use in vision research and diagnostics.

Benham's Top, Michael Bach (optical illusions). — the black-and-white disc producing colour, the differing temporal responses of the colour channels, and the note that the mechanism is not fully understood.

laws.name: The Milgram Experiment
laws.statement: Ordinary people, ordered by an authority, kept delivering shocks they thought were harming a stranger.

sources.text: Milgram experiment, Wikipedia. — the obedience experiments by Stanley Milgram at Yale from 1961, the teacher, learner, and experimenter roles, the fake shocks up to 450 volts, the ~65% baseline obedience, the fixed prods, the Eichmann motivation, the agentic-state interpretation, and the ethical and methodological criticisms.
Milgram experiment, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — Milgram's obedience study, its setup and findings, and the ethical concerns it raised.

laws.name: The Stanford Prison Experiment
laws.statement: Students playing guards turned cruel in a mock prison, in a study now largely discredited.

sources.text: Stanford prison experiment, Wikipedia. — Zimbardo's 1971 mock-prison study, the random assignment and six-day termination, the situational claim, and the extensive modern criticisms including the coaching of guards, the biased sample, the faked breakdown, the demand characteristics, the lack of peer review, and the ethical problems.
Stanford Prison Experiment, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the study's design and dramatic results, Zimbardo's situational interpretation, and the disputes over its validity.

laws.name: The Little Albert Experiment
aliases: Watson and Rayner's conditioning of fear
laws.statement: By pairing a white rat with a frightening noise, researchers taught an infant to fear the rat and other furry things.

sources.text: Little Albert experiment, Wikipedia. — the 1920 Watson and Rayner study at Johns Hopkins, the conditioning of fear of a white rat by pairing it with a loud steel-bar noise, the generalization to other furry objects, the ethical problems and unremoved fear, the single-subject and methodological criticisms, and the disputed identity of Albert.
Little Albert experiment, Simply Psychology. — Watson and Rayner's conditioning of a fear response in an infant, the procedure and generalization, and the ethical concerns.

laws.name: Classical Conditioning
laws.statement: Pair a bell with food often enough and the bell alone will make the dog salivate.

sources.text: Classical conditioning, Wikipedia. — the pairing of a neutral stimulus with a biologically potent one so it elicits a similar response, Pavlov's dogs, the unconditioned and conditioned stimuli and responses, extinction and generalization, and the contrast with operant conditioning.
Conditioning, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — classical or Pavlovian conditioning as the association of stimuli, Pavlov's salivating dogs, and the conditioned response.

laws.name: Operant Conditioning
laws.statement: Behavior followed by reward tends to recur, and behavior followed by punishment tends to fade.

sources.text: Operant conditioning, Wikipedia. — the shaping of voluntary behavior by consequences, Skinner and Thorndike's law of effect, positive and negative reinforcement and punishment, shaping and extinction, the Skinner box, the schedules of reinforcement, and the contrast with classical conditioning.
Operant conditioning, Simply Psychology. — Skinner's reinforcement and punishment, the four contingencies, schedules of reinforcement, and the distinction from classical conditioning.

laws.name: The Bobo Doll Experiment
laws.statement: Children who watched an adult attack an inflatable doll went on to attack it the same way themselves.

sources.text: Bobo doll experiment, Wikipedia. — Bandura's early-1960s Stanford studies with Dorothea and Sheila Ross, children imitating an adult model's aggression toward the Bobo doll, the control conditions, the sex differences and same-sex modeling, observational learning and social learning theory, the learning-versus-performance distinction, and the criticisms of ecological validity and ethics.
Bobo doll experiment, Simply Psychology. — Bandura's demonstration of observational learning of aggression, the procedure, the findings on imitation and modeling, and the criticisms.

laws.name: The Marshmallow Test
laws.statement: A child offered one treat now or two if they wait reveals a capacity for delayed gratification, once thought to predict success.

sources.text: Stanford marshmallow experiment, Wikipedia. — Mischel's delay-of-gratification study, the one-now-or-two-later procedure and wait times, the cognitive strategies for resisting temptation, the 1990 follow-up linking waiting to later achievement, and the 2018 replication finding the effect much weaker and largely explained by background.
Marshmallow test, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — Mischel's delayed-gratification experiment, the procedure and the reported longitudinal associations, and the later reassessment.

laws.name: The Asch Conformity Experiments
laws.statement: Faced with a group unanimously giving an obviously wrong answer, many people go along with it.

sources.text: Asch conformity experiments, Wikipedia. — Solomon Asch's line-judgement studies around 1951, the confederates' unanimous wrong answers, the ~75% who conformed at least once and ~one-third of critical trials conforming versus under 1% control error, normative and informational influence, and the effects of a dissenting ally and group size.
Asch conformity experiments, Simply Psychology. — Asch's line studies, the procedure and conformity rates, the roles of unanimity and group size, and normative versus informational influence.

laws.name: The Harlow Experiments
laws.statement: Infant monkeys clung to a soft cloth mother that gave no food over a wire one that did, showing comfort matters more than feeding.

sources.text: Harry Harlow, Wikipedia. — the surrogate-mother studies with infant rhesus monkeys preferring the cloth over the wire mother, the conclusion that contact comfort drives attachment over feeding, the influence on attachment theory, the isolation and deprivation studies, and the ethical and animal-welfare criticisms.
Harlow's monkey experiments, Simply Psychology. — the cloth and wire surrogate mothers, contact comfort, the secure-base behavior, the deprivation studies, and the ethical concerns.

laws.name: The Robbers Cave Experiment
laws.statement: Two groups of boys at a summer camp turned hostile when made to compete, then reconciled only when forced to cooperate on shared goals.

sources.text: Realistic conflict theory, Wikipedia. — the Sherifs' 1954 Robbers Cave study, the three phases of in-group formation, friction from competition, and integration through superordinate goals, realistic conflict theory, and the criticisms of manipulation, sample, ethics, and the failed 1953 pilot.

Robbers Cave experiment, Simply Psychology. — the Sherifs' summer-camp study, the Rattlers and Eagles, the competition-driven hostility, the resolution through superordinate goals, and the criticisms.

laws.name: The Rosenhan Experiment
aliases: On Being Sane in Insane Places
laws.statement: Healthy people who faked a single symptom were admitted to psychiatric hospitals and diagnosed as mentally ill.

sources.text: Rosenhan experiment, Wikipedia. — Rosenhan's 1973 On Being Sane in Insane Places, the eight pseudopatients reporting empty, hollow, thud, the admissions and schizophrenia diagnoses, the ~19-day stays and in-remission discharges, the reverse second experiment, the conclusion on diagnostic unreliability, and the Spitzer critique and Cahalan's fabrication doubts.
On Being Sane in Insane Places, D. L. Rosenhan, Science, 1973. — the original report of the pseudopatient study and its conclusions about psychiatric diagnosis.

laws.name: The Skinner Box
laws.statement: A small chamber with a lever and a food dispenser lets an animal's behavior be shaped and measured by its consequences.

sources.text: Operant conditioning chamber, Wikipedia. — the Skinner box developed by B. F. Skinner in the 1930s, the lever for rats and key for pigeons, the food and water dispensers, the electrified grid and signaling lights and speakers, the study of reinforcement schedules, the cumulative recorder, Skinner's dislike of the name, and the distinction from the air crib.
B. F. Skinner, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — Skinner's operant conditioning chamber and its role in the experimental analysis of behavior and the study of reinforcement.

laws.name: Learned Helplessness
laws.statement: An animal or person repeatedly subjected to unavoidable harm stops trying to escape, even when escape becomes possible.

sources.text: Seligman, M. E. P. & Maier, S. F. (1967). "Failure to escape traumatic shock." Journal of Experimental Psychology 74(1), 1-9 — the original experiments.

Learned helplessness, Wikipedia. — Seligman and Maier's ~1967 dog experiments with inescapable shock and the shuttle-box escape failure, the expectation of uncontrollability, the yoked-control design, the depression model, the 1978 attributional reformulation, and the 2016 Maier and Seligman revision that passivity is the default and control is learned.
Learned helplessness, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the concept of passivity following uncontrollable aversive events, Seligman's experiments, and its application to depression.

laws.name: The Double-Slit Experiment
laws.statement: Send particles one at a time through two slits and they still build an interference pattern, as if each passed through both.

sources.text: Double-slit experiment, Wikipedia. — Young's interference work around 1801 to 1803, the single-particle quantum version building an interference pattern, wave-particle duality and the wavefunction, the which-path measurement destroying interference, complementarity, Feynman's 'only mystery', and that the effect is independent of any conscious observer.

The double-slit experiment, Physics World. — the history from Young through Jönsson 1961, Merli, Missiroli and Pozzi 1974, and Tonomura's 1989 single-electron build-up, and the 2002 vote for the most beautiful experiment in physics.

laws.name: The Michelson-Morley Experiment
laws.statement: The famous failed search for the aether found no change in the speed of light whichever way the Earth moved.

sources.text: Michelson-Morley experiment, Wikipedia. — the 1887 Cleveland experiment by Michelson and Morley, the interferometer on a stone floating in mercury, the search for motion through the luminiferous aether, the null result and its being called the most famous failed experiment, the link to the constancy of light and special relativity, and Dayton Miller's disputed later claims.
Michelson-Morley experiment, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the aether-drift experiment, the interferometer method, the null result, and its significance for relativity.

laws.name: The Millikan Oil-Drop Experiment
laws.statement: By balancing gravity against an electric field on tiny oil droplets, the experiment measured the charge of a single electron.

sources.text: Oil drop experiment, Wikipedia. — Millikan and Fletcher's 1909 to 1913 measurement of the elementary charge by balancing gravity and an electric field on charged oil droplets, the quantization of charge, the value close to 1.6e-19 C, the 1923 Nobel Prize, and the controversies over data selection and Fletcher's credit.

August, 1913: Robert Millikan Reports His Oil Drop Results, American Physical Society. — the oil-drop method, Fletcher's role, the measured value and its slight discrepancy from the air-viscosity value, and the notebook data-selection debate.

laws.name: The Rutherford Gold Foil Experiment
laws.statement: A few alpha particles fired at a thin gold foil bounced almost straight back, revealing the atom's tiny dense nucleus.

sources.text: Rutherford scattering experiments, Wikipedia. — the Geiger-Marsden experiments under Rutherford at Manchester from about 1908 to 1913, the alpha particles on gold foil, the one-in-eight-thousand large-angle deflections, the failure of the plum pudding model, Rutherford's 1911 nuclear model, and the tissue-paper recollection.
Rutherford model, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the gold foil scattering, the discovery of the nucleus, and the nuclear model of the atom.

laws.name: The Cavendish Experiment
laws.statement: Using a delicate torsion balance, Cavendish measured the faint gravitational pull between lead spheres and so weighed the Earth.

sources.text: Cavendish experiment, Wikipedia. — Henry Cavendish's 1797 to 1798 torsion-balance experiment using Michell's apparatus, the measurement of gravitational attraction between lead spheres, the mean density of the Earth of about 5.448 times water, the 5.48 published slip caught by Baily, and that the gravitational constant was a later formulation derived from his data.
Cavendish experiment, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — Cavendish's determination of the Earth's density with a torsion balance and its role in measuring gravity.

laws.name: The Foucault Pendulum
laws.statement: A freely swinging pendulum slowly turns its plane of swing, visibly proving the Earth rotates beneath it.

sources.text: Foucault pendulum, Wikipedia. — Léon Foucault's 1851 demonstration at the Paris Observatory and the Panthéon, the swing plane rotating relative to the ground as the Earth turns beneath it, the sine-of-latitude rate, the roughly 32-hour Paris period, and the Coriolis-force description.
Foucault pendulum, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the pendulum as a demonstration of the Earth's rotation, the latitude dependence, and Foucault's 1851 experiment.

laws.name: The Stern-Gerlach Experiment
laws.statement: A beam of atoms passing through an uneven magnetic field split into two discrete spots, revealing quantized angular momentum.

sources.text: Stern-Gerlach experiment, Wikipedia. — the 1922 Frankfurt experiment by Stern and Gerlach, the silver beam splitting into two spots in an inhomogeneous magnetic field, space quantization, the later understanding as electron spin with spin proposed only in 1925, and Stern's 1943 Nobel Prize for the molecular-ray method.

How the Stern-Gerlach experiment made physicists believe in quantum mechanics, Physics World. — the setup and two-spot result, the demonstration of quantized angular momentum, and the historical interpretation.

laws.name: Eratosthenes' Measurement of the Earth
aliases: Eratosthenes' measurement of the Earth's circumference
Eratosthenes and the size of the Earth
laws.statement: From the different noon shadows in two cities, Eratosthenes estimated the circumference of the whole Earth with geometry.

sources.text: Eratosthenes, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — Eratosthenes of Cyrene as director of the Library of Alexandria, his measurement of the Earth's circumference from the solstice shadows at Alexandria and Syene, the one-fiftieth angle, and the result near 250,000 stadia.

Eratosthenes Measures Earth, American Physical Society. — the method using the gnomon shadow and the well at Syene, the ~7.2 degree angle and 5,000 stadia, the ~250,000 to 252,000 stadia result, and the uncertainty in the length of the stadion.

laws.name: The Franck-Hertz Experiment
laws.statement: Electrons driven through mercury vapour lost energy only in fixed jumps, proving atoms absorb energy in discrete quanta.

sources.text: Franck-Hertz experiment, Wikipedia. — the 1914 experiment by Franck and Hertz accelerating electrons through mercury vapour, the current drops at regular ~4.9 volt intervals, the inelastic collisions exciting mercury and the ~254 nm ultraviolet emission, the confirmation of quantized atomic energy levels and the Bohr model, and the 1925 Nobel Prize.
The Nobel Prize in Physics 1925, NobelPrize.org. — the award to James Franck and Gustav Hertz for their discovery of the laws governing the impact of an electron upon an atom.

laws.name: The Eddington Eclipse Experiment
laws.statement: During a solar eclipse, starlight was seen to bend around the Sun by just the amount Einstein's gravity predicted.

sources.text: Eddington experiment, Wikipedia. — the 29 May 1919 eclipse expeditions to Sobral and Príncipe organized by Dyson and Eddington, the test of general relativity by the deflection of Hyades starlight, the ~0.87 arcsecond Newtonian versus ~1.75 arcsecond Einstein predictions, the confirmation and Einstein's fame, and the debate over the discarded Sobral plates.

Bending space-time: a commentary on Dyson, Eddington and Davidson (1920), Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A. — the 1919 measurement of the deflection of light by the Sun and a modern assessment of the data and its later reanalysis.

laws.name: Galileo's Inclined Plane
laws.statement: By rolling balls down a ramp to slow their fall, Galileo found the distance grows as the square of the time.

sources.text: Two New Sciences, Wikipedia. — Galileo's 1638 work presenting the inclined plane experiments, the times-squared law of naturally accelerated motion, the water-clock timing, and the independence of the fall rate from weight.
Galileo's Leaning Tower of Pisa experiment, Wikipedia. — the documented inclined plane work versus the apocryphal Leaning Tower story from Viviani's later biography.

laws.name: Thomson's Cathode Ray Experiment
laws.statement: By deflecting cathode rays with electric and magnetic fields, Thomson found particles far lighter than any atom: the electron.

sources.text: J. J. Thomson, Wikipedia. — Thomson's 1897 cathode ray experiments at the Cavendish Laboratory, the deflection by electric and magnetic fields, the charge-to-mass ratio about a thousand times that of the hydrogen ion, the corpuscles as a universal constituent of matter, the discovery of the electron and the plum pudding model, and the 1906 Nobel Prize.
The Nobel Prize in Physics 1906, NobelPrize.org. — the award to J. J. Thomson for his investigations on the conduction of electricity by gases.

laws.name: The Davisson-Germer Experiment
laws.statement: Electrons fired at a nickel crystal diffracted like waves, confirming that matter itself has a wavelength.

sources.text: Davisson-Germer experiment, Wikipedia. — the 1927 experiment at Bell Labs firing electrons at a nickel crystal, the diffraction peaks confirming the wave nature of electrons, the match to de Broglie's 1924 matter-wave hypothesis, the accidental recrystallization of the nickel, and Davisson's shared 1937 Nobel Prize with George Paget Thomson.
The Nobel Prize in Physics 1937, NobelPrize.org. — the award to Clinton Davisson and George Paget Thomson for their experimental discovery of the diffraction of electrons by crystals.

laws.name: Mendel's Pea Experiments
laws.statement: By breeding pea plants and counting their traits, Mendel uncovered the hidden rules by which inheritance works.

sources.text: Gregor Mendel, Wikipedia. — Mendel's pea plant experiments from 1856 to 1863 at Brno, the seven contrasting traits, the dominant and recessive forms and the 3:1 F2 ratio, the laws of segregation and independent assortment, the presentation in 1865 and publication in 1866, the rediscovery around 1900, and Fisher's 1936 statistical critique.
Gregor Mendel, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — Mendel's hybridization experiments with peas, the two laws of inheritance, and their significance for genetics.

laws.name: The Miller-Urey Experiment
laws.statement: Sparks through a flask of simple gases produced amino acids, showing life's building blocks can form from lifeless chemistry.

sources.text: Miller-Urey experiment, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — Stanley Miller and Harold Urey's 1952 to 1953 experiment, the sealed apparatus with water and a methane, ammonia, and hydrogen atmosphere energized by sparks, the production of amino acids, the support for the primordial soup hypothesis, and the debate over the early atmosphere.

'Lost' Miller-Urey experiment created more of life's building blocks, ScienceDaily. — the 2008 reanalysis of Miller's preserved vials finding many more amino acids, including from a volcanic-vapour variant.

laws.name: The Hershey-Chase Experiment
laws.statement: By tagging a virus's DNA and protein separately, Hershey and Chase showed it is the DNA that carries heredity.

sources.text: Hershey-Chase experiment, Wikipedia. — the 1952 experiments at Cold Spring Harbor using T2 phage on E. coli, the phosphorus-32 labelling of DNA and sulfur-35 labelling of protein, the Waring blender and centrifugation, the finding that DNA enters the cell, the confirmation of DNA as the genetic material, and Hershey's shared 1969 Nobel Prize.

The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1969, NobelPrize.org. — the award to Delbrück, Hershey, and Luria for their discoveries concerning the replication mechanism and the genetic structure of viruses.

laws.name: The Meselson-Stahl Experiment
aliases: The most beautiful experiment in biology
laws.statement: By weighing DNA made with heavy then light nitrogen, the experiment showed each new helix keeps one old strand.

sources.text: Meselson-Stahl experiment, Wikipedia. — the 1957 to 1958 Caltech experiment testing the semiconservative, conservative, and dispersive models, the heavy nitrogen-15 to light nitrogen-14 switch, cesium chloride density-gradient centrifugation, the intermediate band after one generation confirming semiconservative replication, and the 'most beautiful experiment in biology' description.
The Meselson-Stahl Experiment (1957-1958), Embryo Project Encyclopedia. — the design and results of the experiment and its confirmation of semiconservative DNA replication.

laws.name: Griffith's Experiment
laws.statement: Dead virulent bacteria could turn live harmless ones deadly, revealing that heredity can pass between organisms.

sources.text: Griffith's experiment, Wikipedia. — Frederick Griffith's 1928 experiment with virulent smooth and harmless rough Streptococcus pneumoniae, the four mouse conditions, the recovery of living virulent bacteria from the dead-smooth-plus-live-rough mixture, the discovery of transformation and the transforming principle, and its later identification as DNA.
Frederick Griffith, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — Griffith's transformation experiment and its significance for the study of heredity.

laws.name: The Avery-MacLeod-McCarty Experiment
laws.statement: By destroying each candidate molecule in turn, they showed the substance that carries heredity is DNA.
laws.namedAfter: Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, and Maclyn McCarty

sources.text: Avery, O. et al. (1944). “Studies on the chemical nature of the substance inducing transformation of pneumococcal types.” Journal of Experimental Medicine, vol. 79. — the paper identifying DNA as the transforming principle.

Avery-MacLeod-McCarty experiment, Wikipedia. — the 1944 Rockefeller experiments identifying the chemical nature of Griffith's transforming principle, the enzyme-elimination method destroying protein, RNA, and DNA, the finding that only destroying DNA abolished transformation, the initial skepticism, and confirmation by Hershey-Chase.
1944: DNA is Transforming Principle, National Human Genome Research Institute. — Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty's identification of DNA as the transforming principle and its significance.

laws.name: Redi's Experiment
laws.statement: By covering some meat and leaving other meat open, Redi showed maggots come from flies, not from rot itself.

sources.text: Francesco Redi, Wikipedia. — Redi's 1668 Experiments on the Generation of Insects, the jars of meat left open, sealed, and covered with gauze, the appearance of maggots only where flies could reach, the conclusion that maggots come from flies' eggs, and its status as an early controlled experiment challenging spontaneous generation.
Francesco Redi, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — Redi as an experimenter and parasitologist, his meat-and-flies experiment, and its challenge to spontaneous generation.

laws.name: Pasteur's Swan-Neck Flask Experiment
laws.statement: Broth in a curved-neck flask stayed sterile as long as dust could not reach it, disproving spontaneous generation.

sources.text: Spontaneous Generation, Microbiology (OpenStax), Biology LibreTexts. — Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiments around 1859 to 1861, the sterilized broth kept sterile while the curved neck trapped dust, the growth when contaminated, and the disproof of spontaneous generation for microorganisms.
Spontaneous Generation, Microbiology (Lumen Learning). — the swan-neck flask method, Pasteur's disproof of spontaneous generation, and its support for germ theory.

laws.name: Wöhler's Urea Synthesis
laws.statement: Wöhler made urea, a compound of living things, from an inorganic salt, unsettling the idea of a vital force.

sources.text: Wöhler synthesis, Wikipedia. — Friedrich Wöhler's 1828 synthesis of urea from ammonium cyanate, the isomerism of the two compounds, the traditional link to the challenge of vitalism, the letter to Berzelius, and the modern view that the one-stroke death of vitalism is a mythologized oversimplification.
Friedrich Wöhler Quotes, Today in Science History. — the letter to Berzelius stating he could make urea without the use of kidneys of any animal, be it man or dog.

laws.name: Lavoisier and Combustion
laws.statement: By weighing what he burned, Lavoisier showed burning is combining with oxygen and that mass is conserved.

sources.text: Antoine Lavoisier, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — Lavoisier's combustion experiments, the oxygen theory replacing phlogiston, metals gaining weight by combining with oxygen, the law of conservation of mass, the naming of oxygen and hydrogen, the 1789 treatise, and his standing as the father of modern chemistry.

Antoine Lavoisier, Wikipedia. — the quantitative combustion experiments, the mercury calx experiment, the overturning of phlogiston, conservation of mass, the independent isolation of oxygen by Scheele and Priestley, and Lavoisier's execution in 1794.

laws.name: Photo 51
laws.statement: A single X-ray image of DNA revealed its telltale helical cross, a key clue to the double helix.

sources.text: Photo 51, Wikipedia. — the 2 May 1952 X-ray diffraction image of the B-form of DNA taken by Raymond Gosling under Rosalind Franklin at King's College London, the X-shaped helical signature, its role in Watson and Crick's 1953 model, Wilkins showing it to Watson, the 1962 Nobel Prize, and the credit controversy.

What Rosalind Franklin truly contributed to the discovery of DNA's structure, Cobb and Comfort, Nature (2023). — a reassessment arguing Franklin was an equal contributor who understood the significance of her data, complicating the simpler victim narrative.

laws.name: The Luria-Delbrück Experiment
laws.statement: Wild swings in how many resistant bacteria appeared proved that mutations arise at random, before any selection.

sources.text: Luria-Delbrück experiment, Wikipedia. — the 1943 fluctuation test by Luria and Delbrück, the induced-versus-spontaneous question for phage resistance, the parallel cultures and jackpot fluctuations showing random pre-existing mutation, the Luria-Delbrück distribution, and its foundational role in bacterial genetics.

The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1969, NobelPrize.org. — the award to Delbrück, Hershey, and Luria for their discoveries concerning the replication mechanism and the genetic structure of viruses.

laws.name: Mendeleev's Periodic Table
laws.statement: Mendeleev arranged the elements so their properties repeated, and left gaps that predicted undiscovered ones.

sources.text: Mendeleev's predicted elements, Wikipedia. — Mendeleev's 1869 periodic table ordered by atomic weight, the periodic law, the gaps left for eka-aluminium, eka-boron, and eka-silicon predicted and later found as gallium, scandium, and germanium, and the priority of Newlands and Lothar Meyer.

Henry Moseley and the Periodic Table of the Elements, NIST. — Moseley's 1913 demonstration that the elements should be ordered by atomic number rather than atomic weight, resolving the anomalies in Mendeleev's table.

laws.name: Piaget's Stages of Cognitive Development
laws.statement: Children's thinking develops through four distinct stages, each a new way of understanding the world.

sources.text: Piaget's theory of cognitive development, Wikipedia. — Jean Piaget's four stages (sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational) with their approximate ages and features, the concepts of schemas, assimilation, accommodation, equilibration, object permanence, egocentrism, and conservation, and the criticisms that he underestimated children and that development is more continuous.
Piaget's Theory and Stages of Cognitive Development, Simply Psychology. — the four stages, the key concepts, the constructivist view, and the main criticisms of the theory.

laws.name: The Zone of Proximal Development
laws.statement: There is a range of tasks a learner cannot yet do alone but can do with guidance, where learning best happens.

sources.text: Zone of Proximal Development, Simply Psychology. — Vygotsky's definition as the distance between the actual developmental level and the potential level under guidance, the more knowledgeable other, scaffolding and its coinage by Wood, Bruner, and Ross, and the contrast with Piaget.

Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development: Instructional Implications and Teachers' Professional Development, ERIC. — the zone of proximal development in sociocultural theory and its implications for instruction.

laws.name: Erikson's Stages of Psychosocial Development
laws.statement: Life unfolds through eight stages, each posing a crisis whose resolution shapes a person's strengths.

sources.text: Erikson's stages of psychosocial development, Wikipedia. — Erik Erikson's eight lifespan stages, each with its psychosocial crisis and resulting virtue, from trust versus mistrust to integrity versus despair, the coinage of identity crisis, the contrast with Freud, and the criticisms of testability and cultural bias.
Erik Erikson's Stages of Psychosocial Development Explained, PositivePsychology.com. — the eight stages, the crises and virtues, and the significance and criticisms of the theory.

laws.name: Kohlberg's Stages of Moral Development
laws.statement: Moral reasoning develops through six stages, from avoiding punishment to following universal principles.

sources.text: Lawrence Kohlberg's stages of moral development, Wikipedia. — Kohlberg's six stages in three levels (preconventional, conventional, postconventional) building on Piaget, the focus on reasoning over conclusions, the Heinz dilemma, and the criticisms including Gilligan's ethics-of-care critique, cultural bias, the rarity of stage six, and the reasoning-behavior gap.
Kohlberg's Stages of Moral Development, Simply Psychology. — the three levels and six stages, the moral-dilemma method, and the main criticisms of the theory.

laws.name: Bloom's Taxonomy
laws.statement: Learning objectives climb from remembering facts to creating new work, in a ladder of thinking skills.

sources.text: Bloom's taxonomy, Wikipedia. — the 1956 Taxonomy of Educational Objectives under Benjamin Bloom, the original six cognitive levels (knowledge, comprehension, application, analysis, synthesis, evaluation), the 2001 Anderson and Krathwohl revision to verbs with create at the top, the three domains, and the criticisms of the strict hierarchy and the later pyramid.

Bloom's Taxonomy of Educational Objectives, University of Illinois Chicago Center for the Advancement of Teaching Excellence. — the cognitive levels, their use in writing objectives, and the revised taxonomy.

laws.name: Attachment Theory
laws.statement: Infants are born to form a close bond with a caregiver, a secure base that shapes their development.

sources.text: Attachment theory, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the innate need to form a close bond with a caregiver, the secure base, Bowlby's evolutionary account and internal working models, Ainsworth's Strange Situation and attachment patterns, and the cultural and determinism criticisms.

John Bowlby's Attachment Theory, Simply Psychology. — Bowlby and Ainsworth, attachment as an evolved survival mechanism, the secure base and internal working models, the attachment patterns including the later disorganized type, and the maternal-deprivation critique.

laws.name: Theory of Mind
laws.statement: To understand others, we grasp that they have beliefs and desires of their own, which may differ from ours.

sources.text: Premack, D. & Woodruff, G. (1978). "Does the chimpanzee have a theory of mind?" Behavioral and Brain Sciences 1(4), 515-526 — the paper that named it.

Sally-Anne test, Wikipedia. — the false-belief task for theory of mind, its development from Wimmer and Perner and adaptation by Baron-Cohen, Leslie, and Frith, the passing age around four, and the autism findings and mindblindness hypothesis.

Does the chimpanzee have a theory of mind? 30 years later, Call and Tomasello, Trends in Cognitive Sciences (2008). — the origin of the term with Premack and Woodruff and an assessment of theory of mind in chimpanzees.

laws.name: Gardner's Multiple Intelligences
laws.statement: Gardner argued intelligence is not one thing but several, from linguistic to musical to interpersonal.

sources.text: Theory of multiple intelligences, Wikipedia. — Gardner's 1983 Frames of Mind, the original seven intelligences and the later naturalistic and possible existential ones, the popularity in education, and the criticisms that the intelligences lack empirical support, are not independent, and are hard to test.
Frames of Mind: The Theory of Multiple Intelligences, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — Gardner's proposal of multiple intelligences and its influence on education.

laws.name: The Strange Situation
laws.statement: By watching how an infant reacts to leaving and reunion, the procedure reveals the quality of its attachment.

sources.text: Ainsworth, M. D. S. & Bell, S. M. (1970). "Attachment, Exploration, and Separation: Illustrated by the Behavior of One-Year-Olds in a Strange Situation." Child Development 41(1), p. 49 — the procedure's introduction.

Strange situation, Wikipedia. — Ainsworth and Wittig's procedure from around 1969 to 1970, the eight episodes of separation and reunion, the focus on reunion behavior, the secure, avoidant, and resistant patterns, the later disorganized pattern from Main and Solomon, and the cultural and validity criticisms.
Mary Ainsworth Strange Situation Experiment, Simply Psychology. — the procedure, the attachment classifications, and the significance and criticisms of the method.

laws.name: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs
laws.statement: Human needs rise in levels, from food and safety at the base to self-fulfillment at the summit.

sources.text: Maslow, A. H. (1943). "A Theory of Human Motivation." Psychological Review 50(4), 370-396 — where the hierarchy was set out.

Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs, Simply Psychology. — Maslow's 1943 and 1954 work, the five-level hierarchy from physiological to self-actualization, the later cognitive, aesthetic, and self-transcendence levels, deficiency versus growth needs, the pyramid created by others, and the criticisms of empirical support, strict ordering, and cultural bias.
Maslow's hierarchy of needs, EBSCO Research Starters. — the levels of the hierarchy, the theory of motivation, and its applications and criticisms.

laws.name: The Big Five Personality Traits
laws.statement: Personality can be described along five broad dimensions, from openness to conscientiousness to neuroticism.

sources.text: Big Five personality traits, Wikipedia. — the five dimensions (openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism), the lexical hypothesis and factor-analytic history from Allport and Odbert through Costa and McCrae, the traits as continua, their heritability and cross-cultural recurrence, and the HEXACO alternative and other criticisms.

An historical analysis of the lexical emergence of the Big Five personality adjective descriptors, Personality and Individual Differences (ScienceDirect). — the lexical origins and factor-analytic development of the Big Five model.

laws.name: Cognitive Load Theory
