laws.statement: Because working memory is tiny, teaching should avoid overloading it so knowledge can take root.

sources.text: Sweller, J. (1994). "Cognitive load theory, learning difficulty, and instructional design." Learning and Instruction 4(4), 295-312.

Cognitive load, Wikipedia. — Sweller's cognitive load theory from the late 1980s, the limited working memory and unlimited long-term memory storing schemas, the intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load types, the link to Miller's limited memory, the instructional effects, and the debate over germane load and load measurement.

The Evolution of Cognitive Load Theory and the Measurement of Its Intrinsic, Extraneous and Germane Loads: A Review. — the development of the three load types, the reconsideration of germane load, and the challenges of measuring cognitive load.

laws.name: Self-Determination Theory
laws.statement: People thrive when their needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness are met, and act best from genuine interest.

sources.text: Self-determination theory, Wikipedia. — Deci and Ryan's theory of motivation, the intrinsic-versus-extrinsic distinction, the basic needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness, the undermining or overjustification effect from Deci's experiments, and the theory's applications.
Self-determination theory: A quarter century of human motivation research, American Psychological Association. — the development and evidence for self-determination theory and its basic needs.

laws.name: The Social Contract
laws.statement: Governments are legitimate only by the consent of the governed, as if founded on an agreement among them.

sources.text: Contractarianism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the social contract tradition, the grounding of political obligation in agreement and consent, Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau, and Rawls's twentieth-century revival with the original position.

Social Contract Theory, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the definition of social contract theory, the views of Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau, and the tacit-consent, feminist (Pateman), and racial (Mills) criticisms.

laws.name: The Categorical Imperative
laws.statement: Act only on a rule you could will everyone to follow, and treat people as ends, never merely as means.

sources.text: Kant, I. (1785). "Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals", in Practical Philosophy, ed. Mary Gregor (Cambridge Edition of the Works of Immanuel Kant) — the work in which the imperative is formulated.

Kant's Moral Philosophy, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the categorical imperative as the supreme principle of morality in the 1785 Groundwork, the contrast with hypothetical imperatives, the Formulas of Universal Law, Humanity, Autonomy, and the Kingdom of Ends, the grounding of human dignity, and the criticisms of rigidity.

Categorical imperative, Wikipedia. — Kant's formulations, the categorical-versus-hypothetical distinction, the treatment of persons as ends, and the criticisms including the lying-to-a-murderer objection.

laws.name: The Harm Principle
laws.statement: The only justification for using power over someone against their will is to prevent harm to others.

sources.text: Harm principle, Wikipedia. — Mill's principle from On Liberty that power may be used over a person against their will only to prevent harm to others, the self-regarding versus other-regarding distinction, the opposition to paternalism and legal moralism, and Feinberg's offense principle and the difficulty of defining harm.

John Stuart Mill's Moral, Social and Political Philosophy, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Mill's harm principle in On Liberty, its defense of individual liberty and free expression, and its interpretation.

laws.name: The General Will
laws.statement: Legitimate law expresses the general will, the community's shared aim at the common good, not just the sum of private interests.

sources.text: Jean Jacques Rousseau, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the general will in The Social Contract, its aim at the common good, the distinction from the will of all, the compatibility with freedom, the forced to be free passage in Book I chapter 7, and the interpretive debates over the concept.

General will, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the general will and popular sovereignty, its influence on the French Revolution and the Declaration of the Rights of Man, and the authoritarianism criticisms of Talmon and Constant.

laws.name: Natural Rights
laws.statement: Some rights belong to people by their very nature, universal and inalienable, prior to any government.

sources.text: Natural rights, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — rights inherent in human beings by their nature, universal and inalienable, contrasted with legal or positive rights, Locke's life, liberty, and property, the influence on the American and French declarations, and the later turn to human rights.

Human Rights, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the tradition of natural rights, their grounding and inalienability, the criticisms including Bentham's rejection, and the relationship to modern human rights.

laws.name: The Separation of Powers
laws.statement: Dividing government into legislative, executive, and judicial branches keeps any one from holding all the power.

sources.text: Separation of powers, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the division of government into legislative, executive, and judicial branches, Montesquieu's formulation in The Spirit of the Laws, the influence on the U.S. Constitution, and the note that the doctrine has lost rigidity and that systems vary, with parliamentary systems fusing executive and legislature.
Montesquieu, The Spirit of the Laws (1748), National Constitution Center. — Montesquieu's description of the three powers and his warning that combining them ends liberty.

laws.name: The State of Nature
laws.statement: Imagining people without any government is a way to reason about why we have one and what it owes us.

sources.text: State of nature, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the real or hypothetical condition before political association, its use in social contract theory, and the differing views of Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau, with the state of nature as heuristic rather than historical.
Noble savage, Wikipedia. — documentation that the phrase noble savage was not used by Rousseau but attributed to him later, clarifying his actual view of the state of nature.

laws.name: The Difference Principle
laws.statement: Inequalities are just only if they work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged members of society.

sources.text: John Rawls, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Rawls's theory of justice as fairness in A Theory of Justice, the two principles including the difference principle that inequalities must most benefit the least advantaged, the original position and maximin reasoning, and Nozick's entitlement critique.
Original Position, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the veil of ignorance, maximin reasoning, and the choice of the two principles of justice including the difference principle.

laws.name: Negative and Positive Liberty
laws.statement: Freedom can mean being left alone by others, or being master of oneself, and the two can pull apart.

sources.text: Positive and Negative Liberty, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Berlin's 1958 distinction between negative liberty as absence of constraint and positive liberty as self-mastery, the two guiding questions, Berlin's worry that positive liberty licenses coercion, and MacCallum's triadic critique.

Positive liberty, Wikipedia. — positive liberty as self-mastery and the possession of the power and resources to act, its contrast with negative liberty, and Berlin's warnings linking it to Rousseau's forced to be free.

laws.name: The Noble Lie
laws.statement: Plato imagined rulers spreading a useful myth to bind citizens together and reconcile them to their place.

sources.text: Noble lie, Wikipedia. — Plato's gennaion pseudos in Republic Book III, the myth of the metals with gold, silver, and bronze and iron and the autochthony myth, its purpose of unity and social order, the translation debate, and Popper's critique.
The Open Society and Its Enemies, Wikipedia. — Karl Popper's attack on Plato's noble lie as authoritarian manipulation and its likeness to modern myths of blood and soil.

laws.name: The Invisible Hand
laws.statement: People pursuing their own gain are led, as if by an invisible hand, to promote the good of society.

sources.text: Invisible hand, Wikipedia. — Adam Smith's metaphor, its rare use across his works and single strictly economic instance in The Wealth of Nations, the idea of self-interest promoting the public good, and the criticisms of over-interpretation, Smith's support for government roles, and market failures.
Adam Smith's Invisible Hands, Econ Journal Watch. — the sparse and varied usage of the phrase across Smith's works and its later over-interpretation.

laws.name: The Original Position
laws.statement: To find just principles, imagine choosing them without knowing who in society you will turn out to be.

sources.text: Rawls, J. (1971). "A Theory of Justice" — the work in which the original position and the veil of ignorance are set out.

Original Position, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Rawls's hypothetical device for choosing principles of justice, the veil of ignorance that hides the parties' identities, the maximin reasoning and the two principles, and the criticisms from Harsanyi and Sandel.
John Rawls, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — justice as fairness, the original position and veil of ignorance, and their role in deriving Rawls's two principles of justice.

laws.name: The Marketplace of Ideas
laws.statement: Let ideas compete freely, the thinking goes, and the true or best ones will win out.

sources.text: Marketplace of Ideas, The First Amendment Encyclopedia (Middle Tennessee State University). — the marketplace of ideas as a rationale for free expression, its roots in Milton and Mill and Holmes's Abrams dissent, its role in First Amendment law, and its criticisms.

Marketplace of ideas, Wikipedia. — the metaphor and its intellectual roots, Holmes's free-trade-in-ideas dissent and the later coinage of the exact phrase, and the criticisms concerning market failures and unequal access.

laws.name: Anomie
laws.statement: When shared norms weaken or break down, people lose their moral bearings and society drifts toward disorder.

sources.text: Anomie, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — anomie as a condition of instability from the breakdown of standards and values, Durkheim's development of the concept, its link to deviance and suicide, and Merton's continuum of adaptations.

Anomie, Wikipedia. — the Greek origin and normlessness sense, Durkheim's use in The Division of Labour and Suicide and anomic suicide, Merton's 1938 strain theory and five modes of adaptation, and the anomie-versus-anomia distinction.

laws.name: The Looking-Glass Self
laws.statement: We come to see ourselves as we imagine others see us, forming our self-image in their reflected gaze.

sources.text: Looking-glass self, Wikipedia. — Cooley's 1902 concept from Human Nature and the Social Order, the self formed from imagining how we appear to and are judged by others, the three elements of appearance, judgment, and self-feeling, and its place in symbolic interactionism.
Looking-glass self, Encyclopedia.com. — the looking-glass self as the social formation of self-concept through the imagined appraisals of others, and Cooley's three principal elements.

laws.name: Social Capital
laws.statement: The networks, norms, and trust that connect people are a resource, letting groups get things done together.

sources.text: Putnam, R. (1995). “Bowling Alone: America's Declining Social Capital.” Journal of Democracy, vol. 6. — the essay that put the term into general use; Bourdieu and Coleman developed it earlier in sociology.

Social capital, Wikipedia. — the networks, norms, and trust that make social relationships a resource, the versions of Bourdieu, Coleman, and Putnam, bonding versus bridging social capital, the applications, and the criticisms of divergent definitions, measurement, and the dark side.
Bowling Alone: America's Declining Social Capital, Journal of Democracy. — Robert Putnam's argument that American civic engagement and social capital have declined, and his account of the concept.

laws.name: The Protestant Ethic
aliases: The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism
laws.statement: Weber argued that a religious ethic of disciplined work and thrift helped give rise to modern capitalism.

sources.text: Weber, M. (2005). “The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism.” — the English translation of the 1904-05 essays.

The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism, Wikipedia. — Weber's 1904 to 1905 thesis that ascetic Protestantism and Calvinist predestination, the calling, and worldly asceticism fostered the spirit of capitalism, the iron cage, and the criticisms from Tawney and others that capitalism predated Protestantism.
The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — Weber's argument linking Protestant asceticism to capitalism and its significance and debates.

laws.name: Conspicuous Consumption
laws.statement: People buy costly, visible luxuries less to use them than to display their wealth and status to others.

sources.text: Conspicuous consumption, Wikipedia. — Veblen's 1899 The Theory of the Leisure Class, the display of wealth and status through visible spending, conspicuous leisure and pecuniary emulation, and the connection to status signaling and inequality.
Veblen good, Wikipedia. — the Veblen good whose demand rises as its price rises because the high price signals status, named after Veblen and distinguished from the Giffen good.

laws.name: Cultural Hegemony
laws.statement: The ruling class stays on top not just by force but by making its worldview feel like plain common sense.

sources.text: Cultural hegemony, Wikipedia. — Gramsci's concept from the Prison Notebooks, the domination of society by a ruling class shaping its culture so its worldview becomes accepted common sense, rule by consent versus coercion, civil society, organic intellectuals, and counter-hegemony.

Antonio Gramsci, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Gramsci's theory of hegemony, the state as coercion plus consent, civil society, organic intellectuals, and the war of position, and the fragmentary nature of the Prison Notebooks.

laws.name: The Iron Cage
laws.statement: Modern life traps us in a rationalized order of rules and efficiency that is hard to escape.

sources.text: Iron cage, Wikipedia. — Weber's concept from The Protestant Ethic, the entrapment of individuals in a rationalized, bureaucratic order, the German stahlhartes Gehäuse and Parsons's iron cage translation, rationalization and disenchantment, and the specialists-without-spirit warning.

The 'Iron Cage' and the 'Shell as Hard as Steel', Peter Baehr, History and Theory (2001). — the translation of stahlhartes Gehäuse and the argument that a shell as hard as steel better captures Weber's meaning than iron cage.

laws.name: The Division of Labor
aliases: The Division of Labour in Society
laws.statement: Durkheim argued that specialization does more than boost output; it binds a modern society together through interdependence.

sources.text: Durkheim, É. (1893). “De la division du travail social: étude sur l’organisation des sociétés supérieures.” Paris: Alcan. — Durkheim’s thesis; Adam Smith had described the pin factory in 1776, but this is the sociological treatment the entry describes.

The Division of Labour in Society, Wikipedia. — Durkheim's 1893 dissertation, the division of labor as a source of social solidarity, mechanical versus organic solidarity, the collective consciousness, repressive versus restitutive law, and the abnormal anomic and forced forms.

Mechanical and organic solidarity, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — Durkheim's distinction between mechanical solidarity from likeness and organic solidarity from the interdependence of the division of labor.

laws.name: Moral Panic
laws.statement: Society sometimes erupts in fear of a scapegoat far out of proportion to the actual threat it poses.

sources.text: Cohen, S. "Folk Devils and Moral Panics: The Creation of the Mods and Rockers" (1972) — the study that named it.

Moral panic, Wikipedia. — the concept of disproportionate collective fear of a threat to societal values, Cohen's Folk Devils and Moral Panics, folk devils and media amplification, Goode and Ben-Yehuda's five attributes, applications, and the criticisms of disproportionality and misapplication.
Folk Devils and Moral Panics, Wikipedia. — Stanley Cohen's 1972 study of the Mods and Rockers, the creation of folk devils, and the amplifying role of the media.

laws.name: The Presentation of Self
laws.statement: In everyday life we are like actors on a stage, managing the impressions we give to our audience.

sources.text: The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life, Wikipedia. — Goffman's 1956 and 1959 book, the dramaturgical analysis of interaction as theatrical performance, front stage and back stage, impression management, and its influence on microsociology.
Dramaturgy (sociology), Wikipedia. — the dramaturgical perspective, performers and audiences, front and back regions, and impression management as a normal feature of social interaction.

laws.name: Collective Effervescence
laws.statement: When a crowd gathers in shared ritual, a surge of collective energy lifts people beyond themselves.

sources.text: Collective effervescence, Wikipedia. — Durkheim's concept from The Elementary Forms of Religious Life, the shared energy of ritual gatherings, the argument that the sacred force is really society, the study of Aboriginal totemism, the sacred and profane, and applications to crowds and gatherings.
The Elementary Forms of the Religious Life (1912), University of Chicago Durkheim project. — Durkheim's theory of religion, collective effervescence, and the totemic basis of the sacred.

laws.name: Social Facts
laws.statement: Ways of acting and thinking that exist outside us and constrain us are the true subject matter of sociology.

sources.text: Social fact, Wikipedia. — Durkheim's definition of social facts as external, coercive, and general ways of acting, thinking, and feeling, the rule to treat social facts as things, and their explanation by other social facts, establishing sociology's subject matter.

Durkheim, Emile, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Durkheim's Rules of Sociological Method, social facts as external and coercive, treating them as things, society as sui generis, and the anti-reductionist explanation of social facts by social facts.

laws.name: Verstehen
laws.statement: To explain social action, we must grasp the meaning it holds for the people who perform it.

sources.text: Verstehen, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — Verstehen as the interpretive understanding of social action in Weber's sociology, its roots in Dilthey, and its contrast with positivist approaches.

Weber: Antipositivism and Verstehen, EBSCO Research Starters. — Weber's interpretive understanding of social action, the definition of sociology, observational versus explanatory understanding, and the contrast with positivism.

laws.name: The Mind-Body Problem
aliases: The problem of mind and body
laws.statement: How does the mind, with its thoughts and feelings, relate to the physical brain and body?

sources.text: Dualism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the mind-body problem, Descartes's substance dualism of res cogitans and res extensa, the interaction problem and causal closure, the positions of dualism, physicalism, and idealism, and the sub-issues of mental causation and consciousness.

Descartes: Mind-Body Distinction, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Descartes's real distinction between mind and body, the two substances, and the interaction problem pressed by Elisabeth of Bohemia.

laws.name: Dualism
laws.statement: The mind and the physical are, in some fundamental way, two distinct and irreducible kinds of thing.

sources.text: Dualism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — dualism as the view that mind and body are distinct kinds, substance versus property dualism, Descartes, the arguments from the knowledge argument, zombies, and the explanatory gap, and the interaction problem and causal closure objections.
Dualism and Mind, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — substance and property dualism, the case for dualism, and the problem of mental causation.

laws.name: The Hard Problem of Consciousness
laws.statement: Why is any of the brain's physical activity accompanied by subjective experience at all?

sources.text: Hard Problem of Consciousness, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Chalmers's 1995 coining of the hard problem, the distinction from the easy problems of cognitive function, the problem of why processing is accompanied by experience, the links to Nagel and the explanatory gap, and the Dennett and illusionist denials.
Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness, David Chalmers (1995). — the original paper distinguishing the easy problems of consciousness from the hard problem of experience.

laws.name: Qualia
laws.statement: The redness of red, the sting of pain, the taste of coffee: the raw felt qualities of experience.

sources.text: Qualia, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — qualia as the subjective qualitative properties of experience, the etymology and introduction by C. I. Lewis, the ineffable, intrinsic, private, and directly apprehensible features, the anti-physicalist arguments, and Dennett's denial.

Qualia, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the felt qualities of experience, the arguments involving qualia such as the knowledge argument and inverted spectrum, and the debates over their nature and existence.

laws.name: Physicalism
laws.statement: Everything that exists is physical, including the mind, which is grounded wholly in the brain.

sources.text: Physicalism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — physicalism as the thesis that everything is physical or supervenes on the physical, the relation to materialism, supervenience, the varieties in philosophy of mind, and the arguments and challenges including the knowledge argument and the hard problem.
Knowledge Argument Against Physicalism, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the challenge to physicalism from qualia and Mary's room, and the physicalist responses.

laws.name: Functionalism
laws.statement: A mental state is defined by what it does, its causal role, not by what it is made of.

sources.text: Functionalism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — mental states defined by their functional role rather than internal constitution, Putnam's machine-state functionalism, multiple realizability, the relation to the computational theory of mind, and the absent and inverted qualia objections.
Functionalism, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — mental states identified by what they do rather than what they are made of, the developers of the view, and the objections to it.

laws.name: Intentionality
laws.statement: Mental states are about things: a belief is about the world, a fear is of something, a thought points beyond itself.

sources.text: Intentionality, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — intentionality as the aboutness or directedness of mental states, the distinction from intention, Brentano's 1874 reintroduction and the mark of the mental thesis, intentional objects that need not exist, and the project of naturalizing intentionality.
Husserl: Intentionality and Intentional Content, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the development of intentionality in phenomenology and its role in the analysis of consciousness.

laws.name: The Explanatory Gap
laws.statement: Even a full account of the brain seems to leave unexplained why any of it feels like anything.

sources.text: Materialism and Qualia: The Explanatory Gap, Joseph Levine, Pacific Philosophical Quarterly (1983). — the original paper coining the explanatory gap, the pain-versus-water contrast, and the framing of the gap as primarily epistemic.

Explanatory gap, Wikipedia. — the difficulty of explaining how physical processes give rise to phenomenal experience, its relation to the hard problem and qualia, and the epistemic-versus-ontological debate.

laws.name: Panpsychism
laws.statement: Consciousness, in some basic form, may be a fundamental and pervasive feature of all matter.

sources.text: Panpsychism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the view that mentality is fundamental and ubiquitous, the motivation from the hard problem, the historical roots and contemporary defenders, constitutive panpsychism and Russellian monism, the combination problem, and the nuance that only basic experience is attributed to fundamental entities.
Panpsychism, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the view that all things possess some mind-like quality, its history and varieties, and the combination problem.

laws.name: Eliminative Materialism
laws.statement: Our everyday talk of beliefs and desires may be a false theory that neuroscience will discard, not confirm.

sources.text: Eliminative Materialism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — folk psychology as a theory that may be false, the claim that beliefs and desires do not exist, the phlogiston analogy, the Churchlands and earlier figures, the arguments for elimination, and the self-refutation objection and reply.
Paul Churchland, Eliminative Materialism and the Propositional Attitudes (1981). — the foundational modern statement of eliminative materialism and its case against folk psychology.

laws.name: The Turing Test
laws.statement: If a machine's typed conversation is indistinguishable from a human's, Turing proposed, it counts as thinking.

sources.text: Turing, A. M. (1950). "Computing Machinery and Intelligence." Mind LIX(236), 433-460 — the paper proposing the imitation game.

The Turing Test, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Turing's 1950 imitation game, the text-only interrogation of a hidden human and machine, the behavioral criterion replacing can machines think, and the criticisms including the Chinese Room, anthropocentrism, and the ELIZA effect.
Computing Machinery and Intelligence, Wikipedia. — Turing's 1950 paper, the imitation game, the ~30 percent by 2000 prediction, and the significance and objections to the test.

laws.name: The Knowledge Argument
laws.statement: A scientist who knew every physical fact about color still learns something new when she first sees red.

sources.text: Jackson, F. (1982). "Epiphenomenal Qualia." The Philosophical Quarterly 32(127), p. 127 — where Mary's room is introduced.

Qualia: The Knowledge Argument, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Jackson's 1982 knowledge argument and the Mary's Room thought experiment, its logical structure against physicalism, the ability hypothesis and phenomenal concepts replies, and Jackson's later rejection of the argument.
The Knowledge Argument Against Physicalism, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the Mary's Room argument, its structure and conclusion, the main responses, and Jackson's recantation.

laws.name: Emergence
aliases: The whole is more than the sum of its parts
laws.statement: A whole can have properties its parts lack, arising from how they interact: the whole exceeds the sum of its parts.

sources.text: Emergent Properties, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — emergence as dependence plus autonomy, weak versus strong emergence, downward causation, the history in Mill and British Emergentism, and the criticisms of strong emergence including its coherence and lack of evidence.
Emergence, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the concept of emergent properties, the weak and strong distinction, examples, and the debates over reducibility and consciousness.

laws.name: Consequentialism
laws.statement: An action is right or wrong solely according to its consequences; the best outcome makes the right act.

sources.text: Consequentialism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — consequentialism as the view that normative properties depend only on consequences, its teleological character, utilitarianism as the paradigm form, act versus rule consequentialism, theories of the good, and the objections including rights, demandingness, and Williams's integrity objection.
Consequentialism, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the doctrine that actions are judged right or wrong by their consequences, and utilitarianism as its simplest form.

laws.name: Deontology
laws.statement: Some acts are right or wrong in themselves, by rule or duty, whatever consequences they produce.

sources.text: Deontological Ethics, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — deontology as duty-based ethics grounded in rules rather than consequences, the priority of the right over the good, constraints and options, Kant's categorical imperative, Ross's prima facie duties, and the objections including absolutism, conflicting duties, and the paradox of deontology.
Deontological ethics, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the definition of duty-based ethics, its contrast with consequentialism, and its main forms.

laws.name: Virtue Ethics
laws.statement: Ethics begins not with rules or outcomes but with character: what kind of person should I be?

sources.text: Anscombe, G. (1958). “Modern Moral Philosophy.” Philosophy, vol. 33. — the paper that revived virtue ethics as a modern position.

Virtue Ethics, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — virtue ethics as one of three major approaches, its focus on character and the virtues, the Aristotelian concepts of aretē, eudaimonia, the mean, and phronesis, the twentieth-century revival with Anscombe, Foot, MacIntyre, and Hursthouse, and the objections of application, relativity, and situationism.
Virtue Ethics, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the emphasis on character and virtue over duty or consequences, Aristotle's account, and the modern revival and criticisms.

laws.name: Utilitarianism
laws.statement: The right action is the one that produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number.

sources.text: The History of Utilitarianism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — utilitarianism as the consequentialist maximization of happiness, Bentham's principle of utility and hedonic calculus, Mill's higher and lower pleasures, act versus rule utilitarianism, and the objections including rights and the separateness of persons.
Utilitarianism, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the greatest happiness principle, Bentham and Mill, the varieties of utilitarianism, and its significance and criticisms.

laws.name: The Doctrine of Double Effect
laws.statement: It can be permissible to cause a harm as a foreseen side effect that would be wrong to cause as a means.

sources.text: Doctrine of Double Effect, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the doctrine permitting harm as a foreseen side effect but not as an intended means, Aquinas's origin, the four conditions, the intend-versus-foresee and means-versus-side-effect distinctions, the applications in medicine and war, and the closeness problem and debate over intention.
Doctrine of Double Effect, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (archived edition). — the four conditions of the doctrine and its classic applications and criticisms.

laws.name: Moral Realism
laws.statement: There are objective moral facts: some moral claims are simply true, independent of what anyone thinks.

sources.text: Moral Realism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — moral realism as cognitivism plus the objective truth of some moral claims, the naturalist and non-naturalist versions, the contrast with non-cognitivism, error theory, and relativism, and the arguments for and against.
Moral Anti-Realism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Mackie's error theory and his arguments from queerness and relativity against objective moral facts.

laws.name: The Is-Ought Problem
laws.statement: You cannot logically derive what ought to be from what merely is; facts alone do not entail values.

sources.text: Hume's Moral Philosophy, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Hume's is-ought passage in the Treatise, the gap between descriptive and normative statements, its foundational role in metaethics and the fact-value distinction, and the debates over its scope.
Is-ought problem, Wikipedia. — Hume's Law and Guillotine, the famous Treatise passage, the distinction from Moore's naturalistic fallacy, and Searle's 1964 attempt to derive ought from is.
Hume, D. (1739–40). A Treatise of Human Nature, Book III, Part I, Section I. — the is/ought paragraph.

laws.name: The Naturalistic Fallacy
laws.statement: You cannot define good as any natural property; that goodness just is pleasure or the like is a fallacy.

sources.text: Moore's Moral Philosophy, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Moore's naturalistic fallacy from Principia Ethica, the claim that good is simple and non-natural, the open question argument, the distinction from Hume, and the criticisms including the concept-property distinction.
Naturalistic fallacy, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the fallacy of treating good as the name of a natural property, Moore's argument, and its place in metaethics.

laws.name: Moral Relativism
laws.statement: Right and wrong are not absolute but relative to a culture, society, or individual's standpoint.

sources.text: Moral Relativism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — moral relativism as the relativization of moral truth to a standpoint, the descriptive versus metaethical distinction, the tolerance version, the contrast with objectivism, and the objections including the move from disagreement to relativism.
Moral Relativism, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the forms of moral relativism, the reformer's dilemma, and the criticisms of relativism.

laws.name: Moral Luck
laws.statement: We praise and blame people for things partly beyond their control, which seems to violate a basic principle.

sources.text: Moral Luck, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the problem of moral luck from Williams and Nagel's 1976 exchange, the control principle and the paradox, Nagel's four types of resultant, circumstantial, constitutive, and causal luck, and the range of responses.
Moral Luck, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the tension between control and moral assessment, the drunk-driver example, and the significance of moral luck for responsibility.

laws.name: The Golden Rule
laws.statement: Treat others as you would want them to treat you: the near-universal principle of reciprocity.

sources.text: Golden Rule, Wikipedia. — the ethic of reciprocity, the positive and negative forms, the cross-cultural appearances in Christianity, Confucianism, Judaism, and other traditions, the relation to Kant, and the differing-tastes criticism with Shaw's quip.
Golden Rule, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the principle of treating others as one would be treated, its main forms, and its wide occurrence across religious and ethical traditions.

laws.name: Contractualism
aliases: What We Owe to Each Other
laws.statement: An act is wrong if it violates a principle no one could reasonably reject as a basis for shared agreement.

sources.text: Contractualism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Scanlon's contractualism and the reasonable-rejection formula from What We Owe to Each Other, the grounding of morality in justifiability to others, the distinction from Hobbesian contractarianism, the individual standpoints blocking aggregation, and the objections of circularity, scope, and aggregation.
What We Owe to Each Other, Harvard University Press. — T. M. Scanlon's 1998 statement of contractualism and the account of wrongness in terms of principles no one could reasonably reject.

laws.name: Ethical Egoism
laws.statement: One morally ought always to act in one's own self-interest; the right act maximizes one's own good.

sources.text: Egoism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — ethical egoism as the normative claim that one ought to maximize one's self-interest, the distinction from psychological and rational egoism, the arguments for it, and the objections including inconsistency, universalizability, and Rachels's arbitrariness objection.
Egoism, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — ethical versus psychological egoism, Ayn Rand's defense of rational self-interest, and the criticisms of ethical egoism.

laws.name: Justified True Belief
laws.statement: To know something is to have a belief that is both true and justified: the classical analysis of knowledge.

sources.text: The Analysis of Knowledge, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the justified-true-belief analysis as holding that knowledge is justified true belief, the three conditions of truth, belief, and justification as individually necessary and jointly sufficient, the roots in Plato's Theaetetus, and the Gettier problem showing the conditions insufficient.

The Gettier Problem, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the traditional JTB account of knowledge, the requirement that a justified belief be well supported rather than a lucky guess, and Gettier's 1963 counterexamples refuting the sufficiency of JTB.

laws.name: Foundationalism
laws.statement: Beliefs rest on a bedrock of basic beliefs that need no support from other beliefs.

sources.text: Foundationalist Theories of Epistemic Justification, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — foundationalism as the view that some beliefs are foundational, justified without depending on other beliefs, and that all other justified beliefs depend on them, the regress problem, the classical demand for infallible basic beliefs, and modest versions with fallible foundations.

Foundationalism, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — properly basic beliefs supporting the rest of one's beliefs, the regress argument, the arbitrariness objection, and Sellars's myth of the given.

laws.name: Coherentism
laws.statement: A belief is justified by cohering with a web of other beliefs, not by resting on foundations.

sources.text: Coherentist Theories of Epistemic Justification, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — coherentism as the view that justification is holistic and a matter of coherence within a system of beliefs rather than foundations, BonJour's 1985 account of coherence and the role of observational beliefs, and the isolation and alternative-systems objections.

Coherentism in Epistemology, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — coherence as mutual support in a web of beliefs, the contrast with foundationalism and the regress trilemma, the requirement that coherence exceed mere consistency, and the idealist and logical-empiricist figures associated with the view.

laws.name: Philosophical Skepticism
laws.statement: We cannot know what we ordinarily claim to know: doubt raised to a philosophical principle.

sources.text: Skepticism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — philosophical skepticism as the view that we do not know propositions we ordinarily think we know, the distinction of global from local and Cartesian from Humean skepticism, skeptical hypotheses and the closure argument, and responses such as contextualism and relevant alternatives.

Sextus Empiricus, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Pyrrhonian skepticism, the opposition of arguments of equal force, suspension of judgment and tranquility, and the contrast with Academic skepticism's assertion that things cannot be apprehended.

laws.name: Rationalism
laws.statement: Reason, not sense experience, is the chief source and test of knowledge.

sources.text: Rationalism vs. Empiricism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — rationalism as holding that our concepts and knowledge are gained in significant ways independently of experience, the intuition/deduction, innate knowledge, and innate concept theses relativized to a subject area, and the contrast with empiricism.

Rationalism, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — reason as the primary source and test of knowledge, the inherently logical structure of reality, and the Continental rationalists Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz.

laws.name: Empiricism
laws.statement: Knowledge comes from experience: the mind begins as a blank slate written on by the senses.

sources.text: Rationalism vs. Empiricism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — empiricism as holding that we have no source of knowledge or of our concepts other than experience, the rejection of innate ideas, the contrast with rationalism, and the British empiricists Locke, Berkeley, and Hume.

British Empiricism, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Locke's tabula rasa and derivation of ideas from experience, the empiricist rejection of innate ideas, the roots in Aristotle's peripatetic axiom, and Berkeley's and Hume's development of the view.

laws.name: The Analytic-Synthetic Distinction
laws.statement: Some truths hold by meaning alone; others depend on how the world is.

sources.text: The Analytic/Synthetic Distinction, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — analytic sentences as true by virtue of the meanings of their words alone, Kant's containment formulation and the synthetic a priori, the relation to the a priori and the necessary, and Quine's attack on the distinction in Two Dogmas of Empiricism.

A Priori Justification and Knowledge, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the relation of the analytic/synthetic distinction to the a priori/a posteriori and necessary/contingent distinctions, and the prying apart of these distinctions by Kripke and Putnam.

laws.name: Reliabilism
laws.statement: A belief is justified when it is produced by a reliable, truth-conducive process.

sources.text: Reliabilist Epistemology, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — reliabilism as emphasizing the truth-conduciveness of belief-forming processes, process reliabilism as originally formulated by Goldman in What Is Justified Belief? (1979), its base and recursive clauses, its status as a paradigm externalism, and the generality problem.

Internalism and Externalism in Epistemology, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the internalism/externalism distinction, reliabilism as making justification depend on external reliability the subject may not recognize, and the challenges including the new evil demon and BonJour's clairvoyance case.

laws.name: Fallibilism
laws.statement: We can know things without certainty; any belief we hold could turn out to be mistaken.

sources.text: Fallibilism, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — fallibilism as the view that no belief can be rationally supported in a conclusive way, that knowledge is compatible with the possibility of error, the contrast with infallibilism, and the puzzle of concessive knowledge attributions.

Charles Sanders Peirce, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Peirce's fallibilism and anti-foundationalism, the provisional and incomplete status of knowledge, and the self-correcting method of inquiry converging toward truth in the long run.

laws.name: The A Priori
laws.statement: Some things can be known by reason alone, independently of experience.

sources.text: A Priori Justification and Knowledge, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — a priori justification as independent of experience beyond what is needed to grasp the relevant concepts, the paradigm logical and mathematical cases, Kant's synthetic a priori, and Kripke's contingent a priori and necessary a posteriori examples.

A Priori and A Posteriori, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — a priori knowledge as knowable independently of experience and a posteriori as knowable on its basis, the enabling versus justifying role of experience, the three distinct distinctions, and Quine's challenge to the a priori.

laws.name: The Problem of the Criterion
laws.statement: To know what we know we need a method, but to trust the method we must already know things.

sources.text: Problem of the Criterion, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the problem as the circular dependence between which propositions are true and how we can tell, the ancient wheel or diallelus from Sextus Empiricus, and Chisholm's three responses of methodism, particularism, and skepticism.

Roderick M. Chisholm: Epistemology, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Chisholm's framing of the problem of the criterion, his taking of Locke and Hume as methodists, and his own particularism drawing on the common-sense tradition of Reid and Moore, conceding that it begs the question.

laws.name: Virtue Epistemology
laws.statement: Knowledge is true belief that manifests intellectual virtue, so evaluate the knower, not just the belief.

sources.text: Virtue Epistemology, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — virtue epistemology as taking intellectual agents and their virtues as the primary focus of epistemic evaluation, the reliabilist strand of Sosa and Greco and the responsibilist strand of Zagzebski and Code, Sosa's accuracy-adroitness-aptness framework and apt belief, and objections including the fake-barn case and the value problem.

Virtue Epistemology, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — virtue epistemology as giving intellectual-virtue concepts a fundamental role, virtues as reliable truth-conducive faculties or as cultivated character traits, and Sosa's 1980 paper The Raft and the Pyramid resolving the foundationalism-coherentism conflict.

laws.name: The Problem of Other Minds
laws.statement: I know my own mind directly, but can only observe others' behavior: how do I know they have minds at all?

sources.text: Other Minds, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the epistemological problem of justifying belief in other minds and the conceptual problem, attributed to Nagel, of forming the concept of others' mental states, the argument from analogy and its criticisms including the single-case objection, and approaches via inference to the best explanation, criteria, theory-theory, and simulation.

Solipsism and the Problem of Other Minds, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the problem of other minds and its link to solipsism, the argument from analogy associated with Mill, Russell, and Ayer, the one-case objection, and Wittgenstein's private language considerations.

laws.name: Falsifiability
laws.statement: A theory is scientific only if it forbids something: if some possible observation could prove it wrong.

sources.text: Karl Popper, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Popper's criterion of falsifiability as the demarcation of science from non-science, the rejection of induction and verification, conjecture and refutation, corroboration, the logical asymmetry between verification and falsification, and his treatment of Marxism, psychoanalysis, and Adlerian psychology.

Karl Popper: Philosophy of Science, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — falsifiability as the mark of the scientific, the Einstein light-bending example, the degeneration of Marxism into an unfalsifiable theory through ad hoc rescues, and the criticisms including the Duhem-Quine problem and theory-ladenness.
Science and Pseudo-Science, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the demarcation criterion, its criticisms, and the unresolved status of the problem.

laws.name: The Demarcation Problem
laws.statement: Where is the line between genuine science and pseudoscience, and what criterion marks it?

sources.text: Science and Pseudo-Science, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the demarcation problem of distinguishing science from pseudoscience and from metaphysics, Popper's falsifiability and the positivists' verifiability criteria, Kuhn, Lakatos, and Thagard's proposals, Laudan's rejection of the project, and the use of falsifiability in the 1981-1982 creationism case.

Pseudoscience and the Demarcation Problem, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the problem of demarcating science from pseudoscience, the criteria proposed by Popper and others, Laudan's demise argument, and the revived defense of demarcation.

laws.name: Paradigm Shift
laws.statement: Science advances not by steady accumulation but by revolutions that overturn one worldview for another.

sources.text: Kuhn, T. (1996). “The Structure of Scientific Revolutions.” — the book that introduced paradigms and their shifts; this is the third edition.

Thomas Kuhn, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Kuhn's account of paradigms, normal science as puzzle-solving, anomaly and crisis leading to scientific revolutions and paradigm shifts, the disciplinary matrix and exemplar, incommensurability and the non-algorithmic character of theory choice, the Copernican, Newton-to-Einstein, and chemical revolutions, and Kuhn's rejection of the relativist charge.

Margaret Masterman, The Nature of a Paradigm, in Criticism and the Growth of Knowledge (1970). — the identification of at least twenty-one different senses of paradigm in Kuhn's book, prompting his later refinements.

laws.name: The Duhem-Quine Thesis
laws.statement: No hypothesis is tested alone: an experiment tries a whole web of assumptions at once.

sources.text: Underdetermination of Scientific Theory, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the Duhem-Quine thesis that hypotheses are tested only with auxiliary assumptions, so a failed prediction does not reveal which element is at fault, Duhem on the impossibility of a crucial experiment, Quine's radical global holism, and the differing scope of the two versions.

Pierre Duhem, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Duhem's biography, The Aim and Structure of Physical Theory (1906), his claim that an experiment condemns only a whole theoretical group, his restriction of the thesis to physics, and Quine's extension of it to all knowledge.

laws.name: Underdetermination
laws.statement: The evidence never quite forces one theory on us: rival theories can fit the same facts.

sources.text: Underdetermination of Scientific Theory, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — underdetermination as the insufficiency of evidence to fix theory choice, the distinction between holist and contrastive underdetermination, empirical equivalence, Newton's absolute-rest example, the connection to the Duhem-Quine thesis and the realism debate, and the realist responses.

Scientific Realism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — underdetermination and empirical equivalence as arguments against scientific realism, their role in van Fraassen's constructive empiricism, and the realist replies appealing to theoretical virtues.

laws.name: Incommensurability
laws.statement: Rival paradigms may share no common measure, so no neutral standard can rank them.

sources.text: The Incommensurability of Scientific Theories, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — incommensurability as the lack of a common measure between paradigms, its Greek mathematical origin, its introduction by Kuhn and Feyerabend in 1962, the methodological, semantic, and perceptual strands, local incommensurability and untranslatability, and Kuhn's denial that it means incomparability or irrationality.

Thomas Kuhn, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Kuhn's incommensurability across paradigm change, the Newtonian versus Einsteinian mass and phlogiston versus oxygen examples, the absence of a neutral algorithm for theory choice, and Kuhn's rejection of the charge of relativism.

laws.name: Research Programmes
laws.statement: Judge science not by single theories but by whether a whole programme keeps predicting new facts.

sources.text: Lakatos, I. (1978). "The Methodology of Scientific Research Programmes" (Philosophical Papers Volume 1, Cambridge University Press) — the account itself.

Imre Lakatos, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the methodology of scientific research programmes as a revision of Popper mediating with Kuhn, the hard core held irrefutable by methodological fiat, the negative heuristic, the protective belt of auxiliaries, the positive heuristic, and the appraisal of programmes as theoretically and empirically progressive or degenerating.

Imre Lakatos, Wikipedia. — Lakatos's methodology of scientific research programmes, The Methodology of Scientific Research Programmes: Philosophical Papers Volume 1 (eds. Worrall and Currie, 1978), the hard core and protective belt, and progressive versus degenerating programmes.

laws.name: The Pessimistic Induction
laws.statement: The history of science is a graveyard of successful theories later found false, so today's may be too.

sources.text: Realism and Theory Change in Science, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the pessimistic meta-induction against scientific realism, Laudan's 1981 list of successful but now-rejected non-referring theories, Putnam's meta-induction framing, and the selective and deployment-realist responses of Worrall, Psillos, and Kitcher.

Structural Realism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Worrall's 1989 structural realism as a response to the pessimistic induction, the retention of mathematical structure across theory change, and the survival of Fresnel's equations through the shift from the ether to Maxwell's field.

laws.name: Scientific Realism
laws.statement: Our best theories are approximately true, and the unobservable things they posit really exist.

sources.text: Scientific Realism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — scientific realism analyzed along metaphysical, semantic, and epistemic dimensions, the no-miracles argument as an inference to the best explanation, the anti-realist rivals of instrumentalism and constructive empiricism, the underdetermination and pessimistic-induction objections, and entity and structural realism.

Scientific Realism and Antirealism, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the realist commitment to the approximate truth of theories and the reality of unobservables, the no-miracles argument and Boyd's version, and the anti-realist positions and objections.

laws.name: Instrumentalism
laws.statement: Theories are tools for prediction, not portraits of a hidden reality: judge them useful, not true.

sources.text: Scientific Realism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — instrumentalism as the anti-realist view that theories are merely instruments for predicting phenomena or systematizing observation reports, the semantic claim that theoretical terms lack literal truth values, the contrast with realism and the no-miracles argument, and the distinction from van Fraassen's constructive empiricism.

Instrumentalism, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — instrumentalism as the view that scientific theories are tools for prediction and problem-solving whose value lies in usefulness rather than literal truth, and its association with the pragmatism of John Dewey.

laws.name: Inference to the Best Explanation
laws.statement: Accept the hypothesis that, if true, would best explain the evidence before you.

sources.text: Harman, G. H. (1965). "The Inference to the Best Explanation." The Philosophical Review 74(1), p. 88 — the paper that named it.

Abduction, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — inference to the best explanation as ampliative reasoning in which explanatory considerations justify a hypothesis, its relation to and difference from Peirce's abduction, the explanatory virtues, and van Fraassen's bad-lot argument and the objection from probabilistic coherence.

Scientific Realism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — inference to the best explanation applied at the meta-level in the no-miracles argument for realism, and the bad-lot objection to inferring truth from best explanation.

laws.name: The No-Miracles Argument
laws.statement: Science works so well it would be a miracle if its theories were not roughly true.

sources.text: Scientific Realism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the no-miracles or miracle argument that the success of science would be miraculous unless theories were approximately true, its form as an inference to the best explanation, Putnam's formulation and Boyd's version, and objections including the base-rate fallacy and van Fraassen's Darwinian explanation of success.

Scientific Realism and Antirealism, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the no-miracles argument as realism's inference to the best explanation at a meta-level, Boyd's grounding of methodological reliability in true background theories, and the pessimistic-induction challenge.

laws.name: The Theory-Ladenness of Observation
laws.statement: There is no pure seeing: what scientists observe is shaped by the theories they already hold.

sources.text: Theory and Observation in Science, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the dependence of observation on theoretical assumptions, Hanson's theory-laden seeing and the Tycho-Kepler and Gestalt examples, the challenge to a neutral observational basis, the connection to incommensurability, and the point that rival theorists can still give similar lower-level reports.

Theory-ladenness, Wikipedia. — the thesis that observation is laden with theory, its introduction by Hanson and role in Kuhn, Feyerabend, and Popper, the distinction between perceptual and semantic theory-ladenness, and the debate over how far theory penetrates observation.

laws.name: Sense and Reference
laws.statement: A term has both a referent it stands for and a sense, the way that referent is presented.

sources.text: Gottlob Frege, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Frege's distinction between sense and reference from On Sense and Reference (1892), the informativeness puzzle of identity statements, the objective sense versus private idea, the sense of a sentence as a thought and its reference as a truth value, and the later Kripkean challenge to descriptivism.

Frege, Gottlob, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the sense/reference distinction, the morning-star and evening-star example and the informativeness of identity, the objective third-realm status of senses, and the reference of a sentence as its truth value and its sense as a thought.

laws.name: The Theory of Descriptions
laws.statement: The phrase the so-and-so is not a name but a disguised claim that exactly one thing fits.

sources.text: Descriptions, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Russell's theory of descriptions, the analysis of the F is G into existence, uniqueness, and predication with its formal logical form, definite descriptions as incomplete symbols, the King-of-France and excluded-middle puzzles, the avoidance of Meinong's objects, and Strawson's presupposition critique.

Bertrand Russell, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Russell's theory of definite descriptions from On Denoting (1905), incomplete symbols, the George IV and Scott example of substitution and scope, and the contrast of grammatical with logical form.

laws.name: Speech Act Theory
aliases: Austin and Searle on speech acts
laws.statement: In saying something we do something: language performs actions, not just descriptions.

sources.text: Speech Acts, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the theory of speech acts from Austin and Searle, the constative-performative distinction and its breakdown, the locutionary, illocutionary, and perlocutionary acts and illocutionary force, felicity conditions, misfires and abuses, Searle's five-way taxonomy, and indirect speech acts.

John Langshaw Austin, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Austin's How to Do Things with Words and the William James Lectures, performatives versus constatives, felicity conditions, misfires and abuses, and the three-fold theory of speech acts.

laws.name: Conversational Implicature
laws.statement: We mean more than we say: hearers infer the rest from the assumption that we are cooperating.

sources.text: Implicature, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Grice's distinction between what is said and what is implicated, the Cooperative Principle, the maxims of Quantity, Quality, Relation, and Manner named after Kant, implicature by flouting, the conversational versus conventional distinction, and the properties of cancelability, non-detachability, and calculability.

Paul Grice, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Grice's 1967 William James Lectures, Logic and Conversation, Studies in the Way of Words (1989), and the theory of conversational implicature and speaker meaning.

laws.name: The Causal Theory of Reference
laws.statement: A name refers to its bearer through a chain of use tracing back to a first naming, not a description.

sources.text: Reference, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the causal-historical model on which words refer via chains of use leading back to an initial baptism, the contrast with descriptivism, reference fixing by dubbing and transmission through communication, the Feynman case, and the challenge of multiple bearers.

Names, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Kripke's causal picture of names, reference determined by the chain from whom one learned the name, the Feynman and Godel examples against descriptivism, and the connection to rigid designation.

laws.name: The Private Language Argument
laws.statement: A language only you could understand is impossible: meaning needs a public standard of correctness.

sources.text: Private Language, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Wittgenstein's private language argument in Philosophical Investigations 243-315, the target of private ostensive definition, the section 258 diarist and the lack of a criterion of correctness, the section 293 beetle-in-a-box, and the interpretive controversy over its structure and conclusion.

Wittgenstein, Ludwig, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the private language argument, the beetle-in-a-box passage, meaning as requiring public criteria and shared practice, and Wittgenstein's denial that he was a behaviorist.

laws.name: Rigid Designation
laws.statement: A name picks out the same thing in every possible world; a description need not.

sources.text: Rigid Designators, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the definition of a rigid designator as designating the same object in all possible worlds in which it exists, the contrast with non-rigid descriptions, the modal argument against descriptivism, the necessary a posteriori, and the treatment of natural kind terms as rigid.

Names, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Kripke's argument that names are rigid designators while descriptions are not, the modal argument against descriptivism, and the connection to the causal theory of reference.

laws.name: The Use Theory of Meaning
laws.statement: Don't ask what a word stands for; ask how it is used in the life of the language.

sources.text: Ludwig Wittgenstein, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the later Wittgenstein's view that meaning is use, the meaning-is-use remark at Investigations 43, language-games and the builders example, forms of life, family resemblance and the example of games, and the critique of the referential Augustinian picture.
Wittgenstein, Ludwig, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Wittgenstein's later philosophy, meaning as use, language-games, forms of life, and the influence on ordinary language philosophy.

laws.name: The Picture Theory of Language
laws.statement: A meaningful sentence is a picture of a possible fact, sharing its logical structure.

sources.text: Ludwig Wittgenstein, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the Tractatus picture theory that a proposition is a picture of reality sharing its logical form, names going proxy for objects, the showing-saying distinction, the limits of sense and the closing proposition, the ladder metaphor, and the later rejection of the theory.

Wittgenstein, Ludwig, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the early Wittgenstein's picture theory of meaning, logical form and representation, the world as the totality of facts, and the move to the later use-based philosophy.

laws.name: Semantic Externalism
laws.statement: What your words and thoughts mean depends partly on your environment, not just what is in your head.

sources.text: Externalism About the Mind, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — content externalism as the thesis that mental content depends on the nature of the environment beyond the individual, Putnam's Twin Earth and the H2O versus XYZ case set around 1750, Burge's arthritis thought experiment and social externalism, and the challenge to privileged self-knowledge.

Internalism and Externalism in the Philosophy of Mind and Language, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the internalism-externalism contrast, narrow versus world-involving content, the causal individuation of content, and the self-knowledge worry.

laws.name: Verificationism
laws.statement: A statement is meaningful only if it can be verified by experience, or is true by definition.

sources.text: Vienna Circle, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the Vienna Circle and logical positivism, the verifiability criterion that synthetic statements are cognitively meaningful only if empirically testable, the anti-metaphysical program, the 1929 manifesto, and the influence of Wittgenstein and Ayer.

Logical Empiricism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the verifiability theory of meaning, strong versus weak verifiability, Hempel's critique of the empiricist criterion of meaning, the self-refutation objection, and the decline of logical positivism under Quine's and Popper's criticisms.

laws.name: Performative Utterances
laws.statement: Some sentences don't describe an act; uttering them is the act, like I promise or I do.

sources.text: Speech Acts, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Austin's performative utterances versus constatives, performative sentences and their felicity conditions, misfires and abuses, explicit versus implicit performatives, and the breakdown of the distinction into the general theory of speech acts.

John Langshaw Austin, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Austin's introduction of performatives in How to Do Things with Words, the examples of naming, betting, and bequeathing, felicity conditions, and infelicities as misfires and abuses.

laws.name: Compositionality
laws.statement: The meaning of a whole is built from the meanings of its parts and how they are combined.

sources.text: Compositionality, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the principle that the meaning of a complex expression is determined by its structure and the meanings of its constituents, the contested attribution to Frege, the arguments from productivity and systematicity, Montague's homomorphism, and challenges from idioms, context-sensitivity, and opaque contexts.

Compositionality in Language, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the principle of compositionality, its label as Frege's Principle and the debate over the attribution, the link to learnability, and counterexamples such as idioms and belief contexts.

laws.name: Personal Identity
laws.statement: What makes you the same person over time: your body, your memories, or something else?

sources.text: Personal Identity, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the persistence question of what it takes for a person to persist over time as a matter of numerical identity, its distinction from the characterization question, the psychological-continuity, brute-physical, and animalist views, the transitivity objection to memory criteria, and Parfit's fission cases and the claim that identity is not what matters.

Personal Identity, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — personal identity as the conditions for the survival of persons, numerical versus qualitative identity, psychological continuity, the bodily and somatic criteria, the simple view, teletransportation, and the claim that identity is not what matters in survival.

laws.name: Free Will
laws.statement: The control over our actions that makes us morally responsible, and whether we really have it.

sources.text: Free Will, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — free will as a significant kind of control over action required for moral responsibility, the leeway and sourcehood conceptions, the compatibilism-incompatibilism divide, libertarianism and free-will skepticism, and arguments including the consequence argument, Frankfurt cases, and Strawson's basic argument.

Free Will, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — free will as the capacity to control one's actions, its link to moral responsibility, the conflict with determinism, and the compatibilist, libertarian, and skeptical positions.

laws.name: Determinism
laws.statement: Given the state of the world and the laws of nature, only one future is possible.

sources.text: Causal Determinism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the standard formulation of determinism as the state at a time fixing the way things go thereafter as a matter of natural law, Laplace's demon, the distinction from predictability, fatalism, and mere causation, and the bearing of classical and quantum physics on whether the world is deterministic.

Foreknowledge and Free Will, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — theological and logical determinism, divine foreknowledge and predestination, and the relation of determinism to freedom, with the Aristotelian problem of future contingents.

laws.name: Compatibilism
laws.statement: Free will and determinism can both be true: you can act freely even if your choice was caused.

sources.text: Compatibilism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — compatibilism as the thesis that free will is compatible with determinism, classical compatibilism and the conditional analysis, Frankfurt's hierarchical mesh theory, Fischer and Ravizza's reasons-responsive guidance control and semicompatibilism, and the objections from sourcehood and manipulation.

Free Will, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the compatibilist position that agents can have free will even if determinism is true, the analysis of freedom as unconstrained action, and the contrast with incompatibilism.

laws.name: The Consequence Argument
laws.statement: If our acts follow from the fixed past and laws, and those aren't up to us, neither are our acts.

sources.text: Arguments for Incompatibilism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the Consequence Argument as the most influential argument for incompatibilism, van Inwagen's informal statement, the fixity of the past and laws, the N operator and Rule Beta, the three formalized versions, and the McKay-Johnson agglomeration objection and Lewis's local-miracle response.

Compatibilism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the transfer of powerlessness principle, the McKay and Johnson (1996) objection to it, and Lewis's local-miracle compatibilism distinguishing strong and weak abilities to render a law false.

laws.name: The Problem of Universals
laws.statement: When many things share a feature, is there one repeatable entity they share, or only the particulars?

sources.text: Nominalism in Metaphysics, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the problem of universals, universals as multiply instantiable and the contrast with particulars, immanent realism, the varieties of nominalism including predicate, resemblance, class, and austere nominalism, and trope theory as a moderate nominalism.

Universals, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — universals as mind-independent entities grounding qualitative identity, the one-over-many problem, Platonic and immanent realism, nominalism and conceptualism, and the Third Man regress.

laws.name: Nominalism
laws.statement: Only particular, concrete things exist; there are no universals or abstract objects.

sources.text: Nominalism in Metaphysics, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the two senses of nominalism as denial of universals and denial of abstract objects, the varieties including predicate, resemblance, class, and austere nominalism, trope theory, and the medieval and modern figures.

Abstract Objects, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — nominalism as the thesis that there are no abstract objects, the contrast with Platonism, the Quine-Putnam indispensability argument, and Field's nominalist reconstrual of science.

laws.name: Possible Worlds
laws.statement: A complete way things could have been; necessity is truth in all of them, possibility in some.

sources.text: Possible Worlds, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — possible worlds as maximal ways things could be, the analysis of necessity, possibility, and contingency, the actual world as one among many, Lewis's concrete modal realism with actuality as indexical and counterpart theory, and ersatzist abstract accounts.

David Lewis's Metaphysics, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Lewis's modal realism from On the Plurality of Worlds (1986), the plurality of concrete isolated worlds, the incredulous stare, and counterpart theory.

laws.name: Causation
laws.statement: The relation by which one thing brings about another, harder to analyze than it looks.

sources.text: The Metaphysics of Causation, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the central question of what the causal relation consists in, token and type causation, and the range of theories including regularity, counterfactual, probabilistic, process, and manipulability accounts, with the problems of preemption and overdetermination.

Counterfactual Theories of Causation, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Lewis's 1973 analysis of causation as counterfactual dependence via possible-world similarity, the treatment of preemption and overdetermination through chains of dependence, and Hume's counterfactual-flavored second definition.

laws.name: Presentism
laws.statement: Only the present exists; the past is gone and the future not yet real.

sources.text: Presentism, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — presentism as the view that only present things exist, stated as the conjunction that only present things exist and that what is present changes, the contrast with eternalism and the growing block, and the truthmaker and cross-temporal-relations problems.

Time, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — presentism, eternalism, and the growing block, the A-theory and B-theory, McTaggart's A-series and B-series, the truthmaker objection, and the challenge to presentism from the relativity of simultaneity.

laws.name: Eternalism
laws.statement: Past, present, and future all equally exist; the flow of time is a perspective, not a fact.

sources.text: Eternalism, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — eternalism as the equal existence of past, present, and future, the changeless four-dimensional world, now as indexical, the association with the B-theory, the Rietdijk-Putnam argument from relativity, and objections from the experience of passage and from fatalism.

Being and Becoming in Modern Physics, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — special relativity as a theory of Minkowski spacetime, the relativity of simultaneity, and the Rietdijk (1966, 1976) and Putnam (1967) arguments that relativity supports the equal reality of all events.

laws.name: Mereology
aliases: The theory of parts and wholes
laws.statement: The formal theory of parts and wholes, and of when some things compose a further thing.

sources.text: Mereology, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — mereology as the theory of parthood relations, the primitive part relation and its partial-order axioms, the definitions of proper part, overlap, and fusion, extensional mereology and extensionality, and the puzzles of material constitution.

Material Composition, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — van Inwagen's special composition question, mereological nihilism and simples arranged objectwise, universalism and scattered objects like the trout-turkey, and moderate answers such as composition constituting a life.

laws.name: Substance
laws.statement: The fundamental things that exist in their own right and bear properties, rather than being had by anything.

sources.text: Substance, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — substance as the fundamental beings that possess properties without being had by other things and persist through change, the independence criterion, Locke's substratum and the Humean bundle theory, and the accounts of Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz.

Aristotle's Metaphysics, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Aristotle on substance or ousia, primary substance as the individual, the candidates of matter, form, and compound, and the argument that form or essence is the primary substance.

laws.name: The Definition of Art
laws.statement: What makes something a work of art, and whether art can be defined at all.

sources.text: The Definition of Art, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the problem of defining art in terms of necessary and sufficient conditions, the classical mimetic, expression, and formalist definitions, Weitz's open-concept argument drawing on family resemblance, Duchamp's Fountain, and the institutional, historical, functional, and cluster definitions.

The Definition of Art, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the representation, expression, and form theories of art, the de-definition period and Weitz's anti-essentialism, and the institutional and other definitions responding to the challenge of the avant-garde.

laws.name: The Institutional Theory of Art
laws.statement: Something is art not because of how it looks but because the artworld confers that status on it.

sources.text: The Definition of Art, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the institutional theory as a relational definition of art, Danto's artworld and the atmosphere of art theory, Warhol's Brillo Box, Dickie's conferral of the status of candidate for appreciation, the Art Circle's interrelated definitions, and the circularity objection.

The Definition of Art, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Dickie's institutional theory and its 1974 and 1984 formulations, the conferral of art status by the artworld, and the criticisms of circularity and arthood by fiat.

laws.name: The Intentional Fallacy
laws.statement: Judging a work by what the author intended is a mistake: the meaning is in the text, not the mind.

sources.text: Intentional fallacy, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — the intentional fallacy as the problem of judging a work of art by assuming the intent of the artist, its origin with Wimsatt and Beardsley in The Verbal Icon, and the thesis that intention is neither available nor desirable as a standard.

Art and Interpretation, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — anti-intentionalism and Beardsley's principle that a work's meaning is tested against the work itself, the internal versus external evidence distinction, Wimsatt and Beardsley's dilemma, and later actual and hypothetical intentionalism and the death of the author.

laws.name: Aesthetic Experience
laws.statement: The distinctive, valued experience we have in appreciating art or the beauty of nature.

sources.text: The Concept of the Aesthetic, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — aesthetic experience and the aesthetic, the internalist versus externalist approaches, the eighteenth-century concept of disinterestedness, Kant's disinterested pleasure, Beardsley's features of aesthetic experience, and Dickie's myth-of-the-aesthetic-attitude challenge.

Aesthetic Judgment, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the affect-oriented and epistemic conceptions of aesthetic experience, Kant's account of the judgment of taste and the free play of imagination and understanding, and the role of aesthetic experience in defining the aesthetic.

laws.name: The Sublime
laws.statement: The overwhelming greatness that stirs awe and even terror, exceeding the merely beautiful.
