sources.text: Kant's Aesthetics and Teleology, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Kant's account of the sublime in the Critique of the Power of Judgment (1790), the mathematical and dynamical sublime, and the location of sublimity in the mind rather than in nature, revealing the power of reason.

On the Sublime and Beautiful, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — Edmund Burke's 1757 Enquiry distinguishing the sublime, rooted in pain, vastness, and power and evoking awe and terror, from the beautiful, connected with pleasure, smallness, and delicacy.

laws.name: Mimesis
laws.statement: Art as the imitation or representation of nature, life, and human action.

sources.text: Plato's Aesthetics, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Plato's account of mimesis in the Republic, the three beds and the imitator at a third remove from the truth, the appeal of mimetic art to the lower soul, and the restriction of mimetic poetry from the city.

Aristotle's Aesthetics, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Aristotle's account of mimesis in the Poetics as natural to humans and pleasurable, poetry as more philosophical than history in depicting the universal, and tragic mimesis arousing pity and fear and effecting catharsis.

laws.name: Formalism in Art
laws.statement: What makes something art and gives it value is its form, not its subject matter or context.

sources.text: Aesthetic Formalism, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — aesthetic formalism as the view that a work's art-making and value-determining properties are formal and accessible by direct sensation, Bell's significant form and aesthetic emotion, the circularity charge, Hanslick's musical formalism, Kant as precursor, and Walton's anti-formalist Categories of Art.

The Concept of the Aesthetic, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — formalism about aesthetic properties and the aesthetic, the emphasis on form over content and context, and Walton's argument that aesthetic properties depend on the art-historical category of perception.

laws.name: The Expression Theory of Art
laws.statement: Art is the expression of emotion: the artist's feeling made manifest and communicated.

sources.text: Collingwood's Aesthetics, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Collingwood's expression theory in The Principles of Art (1938), expression as the clarification of an inchoate emotion, the distinctions from craft, arousal, betrayal, magic, and amusement, the artwork as an imaginative object, and the pairing with Croce.

The Definition of Art, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the expression theory of art as a reaction against mimesis emphasizing the communication of emotion, Tolstoy's account, and the objections that expressiveness is neither necessary nor sufficient for art.

laws.name: The Paradox of Fiction
aliases: The paradox of emotional response to fiction
laws.statement: How can we feel real emotions for characters we know do not exist?

sources.text: The Paradox of Fiction, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the paradox as an inconsistent triad, Radford's 1975 paper and his conclusion that the responses are irrational, and the illusion, thought, and pretend or make-believe solutions of the illusion theorists, Lamarque and Carroll, and Walton.

Imagination, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the role of imagination in emotional engagement with fiction, Walton's make-believe theory and quasi-emotions, and the relation of imagining to belief and feeling.

laws.name: The Paradox of Tragedy
aliases: The paradox of negative emotion in art
laws.statement: Why do we seek out and enjoy art that makes us feel sorrow, fear, and distress?

sources.text: Paradox of Tragedy, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the paradox as the puzzle of pursuing and enjoying art that elicits disagreeable feelings, framed as jointly inconsistent propositions, Hume's Of Tragedy and conversion theory, compensation and control theories, Feagin's direct and meta-response distinction, and the links to the paradoxes of fiction and horror.

Hume's Aesthetics, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Hume's essay Of Tragedy (1757), the unaccountable pleasure spectators take in sorrow and terror, and the conversion of the painful passions into pleasure by the eloquence of the representation.

laws.name: The Aesthetic Attitude
laws.statement: A special disinterested way of attending to things, contemplating them for their own sake.

sources.text: The Concept of the Aesthetic, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the aesthetic-attitude tradition, disinterestedness from Shaftesbury and Hutcheson through Kant, Schopenhauer's will-less contemplation, and Dickie's myth-of-the-aesthetic-attitude argument that there is only attention differently directed.

Aesthetic Attitude, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the aesthetic attitude as a disinterested frame of mind, Bullough's psychical distance with under- and over-distancing, Stolnitz's disinterested and sympathetic attention for its own sake alone, and Dickie's critique.

laws.name: The Standard of Taste
laws.statement: Is there any objective standard for judgments of beauty, or is taste merely subjective?

sources.text: Hume's Aesthetics, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Hume's Of the Standard of Taste (1757), the tension between sentiment-based judgment and the possibility of a standard, the joint verdict of true judges, the five qualities of a good critic, the wine-tasting delicacy story, and the two sources of blameless variation.

Kant's Aesthetics and Teleology, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Kant's account of the judgment of taste as subjective yet claiming universal validity, disinterested pleasure, the free play of imagination and understanding, the antinomy of taste, and the sensus communis.

laws.name: Catharsis
aliases: The catharsis of pity and fear
laws.statement: Tragedy's cleansing of the emotions: the purgation, purification, or clarification of pity and fear.

sources.text: Aristotle's Aesthetics, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — catharsis as the most enigmatic term of the Poetics, effected by tragedy through pity and fear, Aristotle's failure to define it explicitly, and the contested purgation, purification, and clarification interpretations.

Catharsis, Encyclopaedia Britannica. — catharsis in Aristotle's Poetics as the purgation or purification of the emotions of pity and fear aroused by tragedy, and its later use in criticism and psychology.

laws.name: Goldbach's Conjecture
laws.statement: Every even number greater than 2 is the sum of two primes.

sources.text: Goldbach's conjecture, Wikipedia. — the strong conjecture that every even integer greater than 2 is a sum of two primes, the 1742 Goldbach-Euler correspondence, the weak ternary conjecture and Helfgott's 2013 proof, Vinogradov's 1937 theorem, Chen's 1973 theorem, and computational verification beyond four times ten to the eighteenth.
Christian Goldbach, MacTutor History of Mathematics. — Goldbach's correspondence with Euler and the origin of the conjecture that every even number is a sum of two primes.

laws.name: The Twin Prime Conjecture
laws.statement: There are infinitely many pairs of primes that differ by 2.

sources.text: Twin prime, Wikipedia. — the twin prime conjecture that there are infinitely many primes p with p plus 2 prime, its relation to Polignac's 1849 conjecture, Brun's 1919 theorem and Brun's constant, the first Hardy-Littlewood conjecture, and the bounded-gaps breakthroughs of Zhang, Maynard, and Polymath8 down to a gap of 246.

Unheralded Mathematician Bridges the Prime Gap, Quanta Magazine. — Yitang Zhang's 2013 proof that infinitely many prime pairs differ by at most seventy million, the first finite bound, and the subsequent improvements toward the twin prime conjecture.

laws.name: The Poincaré Conjecture
laws.statement: Any closed 3D space with no holes is topologically a sphere; proved by Perelman.

sources.text: Poincaré Conjecture, Clay Mathematics Institute. — the conjecture characterizing the three-sphere as the unique simply connected closed three-manifold, its status as a Millennium Prize Problem, and its solution by Grigori Perelman.

Poincaré conjecture, Wikipedia. — the statement that every simply connected closed three-manifold is homeomorphic to the three-sphere, Poincaré's 1904 formulation, Smale's and Freedman's higher-dimensional proofs, Perelman's 2002-2003 proof via Hamilton's Ricci flow with surgery and geometrization, and his declining the Fields Medal and Clay prize.

laws.name: Hilbert's Problems
laws.statement: A list of 23 problems posed in 1900 that set the agenda for 20th-century mathematics.

sources.text: Hilbert's problems, Wikipedia. — the 23 problems published by Hilbert with 10 presented at the 1900 Paris ICM, their range and influence, the continuum hypothesis and its independence, the second problem and Godel's incompleteness, the eighth including the Riemann hypothesis, and the tenth shown unsolvable by the MRDP theorem.

Hilbert's Problems, MacTutor History of Mathematics. — Hilbert's 1900 address Mathematical Problems, the problems presented and their significance, and his optimism about the vitality of open problems.

laws.name: Navier-Stokes Existence and Smoothness
laws.statement: Do the equations of fluid flow always have smooth solutions, or can they blow up?

sources.text: Navier-Stokes Equation, Clay Mathematics Institute. — the Navier-Stokes equations governing fluid flow, the unsolved Millennium Prize Problem of proving existence and smoothness of solutions in three dimensions, and its connection to turbulence.

Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness, Wikipedia. — the problem of global existence and smoothness of solutions to the three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, the two-dimensional result, Leray's 1934 weak solutions, the blow-up alternative, and Tao's averaged-equation result.

laws.name: The Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture
laws.statement: The number of rational points on an elliptic curve is encoded in its L-function at s = 1.

sources.text: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture, Clay Mathematics Institute. — the conjecture relating the number of rational points on an elliptic curve to the behavior of its zeta function at s equals 1, its status as a Millennium Prize Problem, and the weak form linking vanishing to infinitely many rational points.

Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, Wikipedia. — the conjecture that the rank of the group of rational points equals the order of the zero of the Hasse-Weil L-function at s equals 1, the Mordell-Weil group and rank, the origin in EDSAC computations, and the proofs of Coates-Wiles, Gross-Zagier, and Kolyvagin for analytic rank at most 1.

laws.name: The Hodge Conjecture
laws.statement: On nice complex geometric spaces, certain topological classes all come from algebraic subvarieties.

sources.text: Hodge Conjecture, Clay Mathematics Institute. — the conjecture that on projective algebraic varieties the Hodge cycles are rational combinations of algebraic cycles, its status as an unsolved Millennium Prize Problem, and its place in algebraic geometry.

Hodge conjecture, Wikipedia. — the conjecture that on a non-singular complex projective variety every Hodge class, a rational class of type p, p, is a rational combination of classes of algebraic cycles, Hodge theory and the 1950 ICM address, and the Lefschetz theorem on 1, 1 classes as a proved case.

laws.name: The abc Conjecture
laws.statement: If a + b = c with a, b, c coprime, then c is rarely much bigger than the primes dividing abc.

sources.text: abc conjecture, Wikipedia. — the conjecture on coprime triples with a plus b equals c, the radical of abc, the epsilon-bounded finiteness statement, the Oesterle-Masser origin around 1985, the many consequences including Fermat's Last Theorem and Faltings's theorem, Goldfeld's assessment, and the Mochizuki proof claim with the Scholze-Stix objection.

Titans of Mathematics Clash Over Epic Proof of ABC Conjecture, Quanta Magazine. — Mochizuki's claimed proof via inter-universal Teichmuller theory, the 2018 Scholze-Stix report of a serious gap near Corollary 3.12, Mochizuki's dispute, and the lack of community consensus.

laws.name: The Classification of Finite Simple Groups
laws.statement: A complete list of the building blocks of all finite groups, proved across tens of thousands of pages.

sources.text: Classification of finite simple groups, Wikipedia. — the theorem listing every finite simple group as cyclic of prime order, alternating, of Lie type in sixteen families, or one of the 26 sporadic groups, the Monster and its order, simple groups as building blocks via Jordan-Holder, the tens of thousands of pages and roughly hundred authors, and the quasithin gap filled by Aschbacher and Smith in 2004.

Michael Aschbacher, The Status of the Classification of the Finite Simple Groups, Notices of the American Mathematical Society, August 2004. — an authoritative account of the classification, its structure, the sporadic groups, and the completion of the proof including the quasithin case.

laws.name: The Millennium Prize Problems
laws.statement: Seven great open problems, each worth a million dollars, chosen for the year 2000.

sources.text: The Millennium Prize Problems, Clay Mathematics Institute. — the seven problems selected by the Clay Mathematics Institute, each carrying a one-million-dollar prize, and the list comprising P versus NP, the Hodge, Poincare, Riemann, Yang-Mills, Navier-Stokes, and Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer problems.

Millennium Prize Problems, Wikipedia. — the seven problems announced in Paris on 24 May 2000, the one-million-dollar prizes, the Poincare conjecture as the only one solved by Perelman who declined the award, the homage to Hilbert's 1900 problems, and the Riemann hypothesis on both lists.

laws.name: The Yang-Mills Mass Gap
laws.statement: Prove the quantum theory behind the strong force exists and that its lightest particle is massive.

sources.text: Yang-Mills and the Mass Gap, Clay Mathematics Institute. — the problem of proving the existence of a quantum Yang-Mills theory with a mass gap, its relation to the Standard Model and the short range of the strong force, and its status as an unsolved Millennium Prize Problem.

Yang-Mills existence and mass gap, Wikipedia. — the two-part problem of constructing a rigorous quantum Yang-Mills theory for a compact simple gauge group on four-dimensional space and proving a positive mass gap, Yang and Mills 1954, quantum chromodynamics with gauge group SU(3), and the Jaffe-Witten formulation.

laws.name: The Langlands Program
aliases: A grand unified theory of mathematics
laws.statement: A vast web of conjectures linking number theory, geometry, and representation theory.

sources.text: Langlands program, Wikipedia. — the Langlands program as a web of conjectures connecting number theory, algebraic geometry, and representation theory, the correspondence between Galois representations and automorphic forms, the generalization of reciprocity and class field theory, functoriality, and the modularity theorem, the fundamental lemma, and the Fields Medals and Abel Prize connected to it.

Monumental Proof Settles Geometric Langlands Conjecture, Quanta Magazine. — the Langlands program as a grand unified theory of mathematics and the 2024 claimed proof of the geometric Langlands conjecture by a team led by Dennis Gaitsgory and Sam Raskin.

laws.name: Byzantine Fault Tolerance
laws.statement: Reach agreement in a system even when some components lie and send conflicting information.

sources.text: Byzantine fault, Wikipedia. — the Byzantine fault as a component presenting different symptoms to different observers, the Byzantine Generals Problem allegory, Byzantine fault tolerance, the Lamport-Shostak-Pease 1982 result with the three-times-plus-one bound and the effect of signed messages, Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance by Castro and Liskov, and blockchain relevance including Bitcoin.

Leslie Lamport, Robert Shostak, and Marshall Pease, The Byzantine Generals Problem, ACM Transactions on Programming Languages and Systems, 1982. — the foundational paper introducing the problem and the bound on tolerable Byzantine faults.

laws.name: The Gini Coefficient
laws.statement: The Gini coefficient measures income or wealth inequality within a population on a scale from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality).

sources.text: Gini coefficient, Wikipedia. — the definition, range, geometry, origin, and comparative country values.
Ceriani & Verme, "The origins of the Gini index," Journal of Economic Inequality (2012). — the 1912 origin and Gini’s original formulations.

laws.name: The Kuznets Curve
laws.statement: The Kuznets curve hypothesises that income inequality first rises then falls as a country’s economy develops, tracing an inverted U-shape.

sources.text: Kuznets curve, Wikipedia. — the definition, mechanism, origin, extensions, and criticisms.
Kuznets, "Economic Growth and Income Inequality," American Economic Review 45(1), pp. 1-28 (1955). — the original hypothesis and its stated caveats.

laws.name: The Beveridge Curve
laws.statement: The Beveridge curve shows an inverse relationship between the unemployment rate and the job vacancy rate across the business cycle.

sources.text: Beveridge curve, Wikipedia. — the definition, origin, mechanism, and Great Recession and COVID shifts.
Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, "Finding a Soft Landing along the Beveridge Curve" (2022). — the 2022 US unemployment/vacancy data and policy use of the curve.

laws.name: The Herfindahl–Hirschman Index
laws.statement: The Herfindahl-Hirschman Index measures market concentration as the sum of the squared market shares of all firms in an industry.
laws.namedAfter: Orris C. Herfindahl and Albert O. Hirschman

sources.text: Herfindahl-Hirschman index, Wikipedia. — the formula, range, mechanism, and dual origin.
US Department of Justice, "Herfindahl-Hirschman Index." — the DOJ/FTC concentration thresholds and worked example.

laws.name: The Solow–Swan Model
laws.statement: Long-run growth in output per worker comes only from technological progress, since capital accumulation alone runs into diminishing returns.

sources.text: Solow-Swan model, Wikipedia. — the development history, mechanism, steady-state and convergence predictions, and limitations.
The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences 1987, NobelPrize.org. — Solow’s 1987 award for his contributions to the theory of economic growth.

laws.name: The Harrod–Domar Model
laws.statement: An economy’s growth rate is set by its savings rate divided by its capital-output ratio, with no automatic tendency toward balanced growth.

sources.text: Harrod-Domar model, Wikipedia. — the mechanism, the warranted/actual/natural distinction, origins, and criticisms.
Harrod, "An Essay in Dynamic Theory," The Economic Journal 49(193), pp. 14-33 (1939). — the original growth-dynamics framework.

laws.name: The Malthusian Trap
laws.statement: Population grows exponentially while food supply grows only linearly, so any gain in resources is eventually erased by population growth back to subsistence.

sources.text: Malthusianism, Wikipedia. — the mechanism of preventive and positive checks, origin, criticisms, and the industrial-revolution escape.
Malthus, "An Essay on the Principle of Population" (1798), Project Gutenberg. — the original argument that population grows geometrically against arithmetic growth in food.

laws.name: The Greater Fool Theory
laws.statement: An overpriced asset can still be profitably bought if a "greater fool" is later willing to pay an even higher price for it.

sources.text: Greater fool theory, Wikipedia. — the definition, psychological mechanism, and examples including tulip mania and cryptocurrency.
"Greater Fool Theory," Corporate Finance Institute. — the definition and mechanism of profiting by reselling overvalued assets to a less-informed buyer.

laws.name: Prospect Theory
laws.statement: People evaluate outcomes as gains and losses relative to a reference point, weighting losses roughly 1.5–2.5 times more heavily than equivalent gains.

sources.text: Kahneman, D. & Tversky, A. (1979). "Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk." Econometrica 47(2), p. 263 — the original statement.
Prospect theory, Wikipedia. — the value function, reference dependence, loss aversion, probability weighting, and origin.
The Prize in Economic Sciences 2002, NobelPrize.org. — Kahneman’s award and Tversky’s ineligibility due to his 1996 death.

laws.name: The Black–Scholes Model
laws.statement: A European option’s price can be derived from the underlying asset’s price, strike, volatility, time to expiry, and the risk-free rate.

sources.text: Black-Scholes model, Wikipedia. — the 1973 publication, assumptions, Nobel Prize, Merton’s role, and critiques.
Long-Term Capital Management, Wikipedia. — Scholes’s and Merton’s board roles, the leverage, and the 1998 collapse and bailout.

laws.name: The Kelly Criterion

Wolfram MathWorld's entry on the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, stating that an n×n matrix is annihilated by its monic degree-n characteristic polynomial — supports the statement.

laws.name: The Hall-Petch Relationship
laws.statement: A polycrystalline metal's yield strength rises as its grain size shrinks, in proportion to the inverse square root of the average grain diameter.
laws.namedAfter: E. O. Hall and N. J. Petch

sources.text: Hall, E. O. (1951). "The Deformation and Ageing of Mild Steel: II. Characteristics of the Lüders Deformation." Proceedings of the Physical Society. Section B 64(9), p. 742.

Wikipedia's article on grain-boundary strengthening, giving the σy = σ0 + ky/√d form, the dislocation-pile-up mechanism, the validity range, and the inverse Hall-Petch reversal near 10 nm — supports the statement, mechanism, and limits.
Wikipedia's article on strengthening mechanisms of materials, corroborating that smaller grain diameter raises yield strength via boundary impedance of dislocations — supports the mechanism.

laws.name: Paris' Law
laws.statement: In the stable regime, a fatigue crack's growth rate per cycle scales as a power of the stress-intensity range: da/dN = C(ΔK)^m.

sources.text: Wikipedia's article on Paris' law, giving da/dN = C(ΔK)^m, the 1961 Paris / 1963 Paris-Erdogan history, the Region II applicability with threshold and toughness bounds, and typical m of 2–4 — supports the statement, mechanism, and limits.

Wikipedia's article on fatigue in materials, confirming the Paris-Erdogan equation is used to predict component life during the crack-growth phase and that growth stops below a threshold — supports the application and limits.

laws.name: Griffith's Criterion
laws.statement: A crack in a brittle solid propagates catastrophically once its length exceeds a critical value set by the balance of released strain energy and new surface energy.

sources.text: Wikipedia's article on fracture mechanics, giving Griffith's 1921 paper, the energy-balance criterion, the glass strength paradox, and the Irwin-Orowan plastic-term modification — supports the statement, mechanism, and limits.

Wikipedia's article on fracture, confirming fracture strength was first theoretically estimated by Alan Arnold Griffith in 1921, relating it to Young's modulus, surface energy, and micro-crack length — supports the attribution.

laws.name: Archard's Wear Equation
laws.statement: The volume of material worn away in sliding contact is proportional to the normal load and sliding distance, and inversely proportional to hardness.

sources.text: Archard, J. F. (1953). "Contact and Rubbing of Flat Surfaces." Journal of Applied Physics 24(8), p. 981.

Wikipedia's article on the Archard equation, giving Q = KWL/H, the 1953 publication, the asperity-contact basis, and K values from about 10⁻⁸ to 10⁻² — supports the statement, mechanism, and examples.
Wikipedia's article on wear, corroborating the adhesive-wear form with worn volume proportional to load times sliding distance over hardness, and the abrasive-wear analogue — supports the statement.

laws.name: Fourier's Law of Heat Conduction
laws.statement: Heat flux through a material is proportional to the negative of the local temperature gradient, with thermal conductivity as the constant: q = -k∇T.

sources.text: Fourier, J. (1822). "Théorie analytique de la chaleur" — the treatise stating the conduction law. Cambridge Library Collection reissue.
Wikipedia's article on thermal conduction, giving Fourier's law q = -κ∇T, the one-dimensional form, and the conduction mechanism — supports the statement and mechanism.

Encyclopaedia Britannica's entry on Fourier's law of heat conduction, confirming q = -k∇T with heat-transfer rate proportional to the negative temperature gradient — supports the statement and attribution.

laws.name: Fick's Laws of Diffusion
laws.statement: Diffusive flux flows down the concentration gradient, with a magnitude proportional to that gradient's steepness: J = -D dφ/dx.

sources.text: Fick, A. (1855). "Ueber Diffusion." Annalen der Physik 170(1), p. 59.
Wikipedia's article on Fick's laws of diffusion, giving the first law J = -D dφ/dx, the second law, the 1855 origin, and the non-Fickian limits — supports the statement, mechanism, and limits.
Encyclopaedia Britannica's entry on diffusion, confirming flow is proportional to the concentration gradient with flux directed from high to low concentration — supports the statement.

laws.name: The Chandrasekhar Limit
laws.statement: A white dwarf supported by electron degeneracy pressure cannot exceed about 1.44 solar masses before it collapses.

sources.text: Wikipedia's article on the Chandrasekhar limit, giving the ~1.44 solar-mass value and the electron-degeneracy-pressure mechanism — supports the numerical limit and the physical cause of collapse.

Encyclopaedia Britannica's entry on the Chandrasekhar limit, attributing the 1.44 solar-mass limit to Chandrasekhar and noting remnants above it become neutron stars or black holes — supports the discoverer and outcome.

laws.name: The Roche Limit
laws.statement: A moon held together only by its own gravity disintegrates if it orbits inside its planet's Roche limit.

sources.text: Wikipedia's article on the Roche limit, giving the definition, the fluid-body coefficient of about 2.44, and examples like Saturn's rings and Shoemaker-Levy 9 — supports the formula and illustrative cases.
Encyclopaedia Britannica's entry on the Roche limit, attributing the 1848 calculation to Édouard Roche and citing Saturn's rings — supports the attribution, date, and example.

laws.name: The Tully-Fisher Relation
laws.statement: A spiral galaxy's luminosity scales with roughly the fourth power of its rotation velocity.
laws.namedAfter: R. Brent Tully and J. Richard Fisher

sources.text: Wikipedia's article on the Tully-Fisher relation, describing the luminosity-rotation-velocity correlation, its 1977 origin, and its use as a distance indicator — supports the definition, attribution, and application.

The NASA/IPAC Extragalactic Database Level 5 review (Jacoby et al.), calling the luminosity-line-width (Tully-Fisher) relation one of the most widely used extragalactic distance indicators — supports its role as a distance indicator.

laws.name: The Faber-Jackson Relation
laws.statement: An elliptical galaxy's luminosity scales with roughly the fourth power of its central stellar velocity dispersion.

sources.text: Faber, S. M. & Jackson, R. E. (1976). "Velocity dispersions and mass-to-light ratios for elliptical galaxies." The Astrophysical Journal 204, p. 668.

Wikipedia's article on the Faber-Jackson relation, giving luminosity proportional to dispersion to roughly the fourth power, the 1976 attribution, and its status as a fundamental-plane projection — supports the power law and origin.

The NASA/IPAC Level 5 review (Kormendy), stating the fundamental correlation between velocity dispersion and total blue luminosity from Faber and Jackson (1976) with an exponent of about 4 — supports the relation, exponent, and attribution.

laws.name: The Jeans Instability
laws.statement: A gas cloud collapses under its own gravity once its mass exceeds the Jeans mass, overwhelming thermal pressure.

sources.text: Jeans, J. H. (1902). "The Stability of a Spherical Nebula." Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A 199, p. 1.

Wikipedia's article on the Jeans instability, defining the gravity-versus-thermal-pressure balance, the Jeans mass/length threshold, and the Jeans swindle — supports the mechanism, threshold, and caveat.

The peer-reviewed analysis "Jeans instability criterion" (arXiv:1407.6431), considering the Jeans instability for self-gravitating fluid and stellar systems — supports that the Jeans mass is the collapse threshold for self-gravitating gas.

laws.name: Thorndike's Law of Effect
laws.statement: Responses followed by a satisfying outcome grow more likely to recur, while those followed by discomfort grow less likely.

sources.text: Thorndike, E. L. (1911). “Animal Intelligence: Experimental Studies.” New York: Macmillan. — the book stating the law of effect.
Wikipedia's "Law of effect" article — supports Thorndike's authorship, the definition that satisfying or discomforting effects strengthen or weaken responses, and the puzzle-box method.
Encyclopaedia Britannica's entry on Thorndike's law of effect — supports the attribution to Edward L. Thorndike and the principle that response probability depends on its consequences.

laws.name: The Premack Principle
laws.statement: A more-probable, preferred behavior can reinforce a less-probable one, so access to the favored activity is made contingent on the lesser.

sources.text: Premack, D. (1959). "Toward empirical behavior laws: I. Positive reinforcement." Psychological Review 66(4), p. 219.
Wikipedia's "Premack's principle" article — supports the attribution to David Premack, the definition that more-probable behaviors reinforce less-probable ones, and the response-deprivation critique.
Simply Psychology's "The Premack Principle" — supports the definition that a more desirable activity can reinforce a less desirable one and its use in applied settings.

laws.name: Flashbulb Memory
laws.statement: A shocking, consequential event can imprint a vivid, confidently held memory of the moment one learned of it, though not necessarily an accurate one.

sources.text: Brown, R. & Kulik, J. (1977). "Flashbulb memories." Cognition 5(1), p. 73.

Wikipedia's "Flashbulb memory" article — supports the 1977 Brown & Kulik coinage, the characteristic features, and the finding that these memories are special in perceived rather than actual accuracy.
Simply Psychology's "Flashbulb Memory" — supports the definition as exceptionally clear memories of emotionally significant events and the 1977 coinage.

laws.name: The Misinformation Effect
laws.statement: Misleading information encountered after an event can distort a person's memory of what they originally witnessed.

sources.text: Wikipedia's "Misinformation effect" article — supports the definition that post-event information reduces recall accuracy, the blending/overwriting and source-misattribution mechanisms, and Loftus's central role.
Simply Psychology's "Loftus and Palmer (1974)" — supports the smashed/hit speed-estimate findings and the false recall of broken glass demonstrating reconstructive memory.

laws.name: The Semmelweis Reflex
laws.statement: New evidence is reflexively rejected when it contradicts established beliefs, norms, or paradigms.

sources.text: Wikipedia's "Semmelweis reflex" article — supports the definition of reflexive rejection of evidence contradicting norms, the named-after attribution, Wilson's popularization, and the associated biases.
Wikipedia's "Ignaz Semmelweis" article — supports the 1847 chlorinated-lime handwashing discovery, the sharp mortality drop, and the medical community's rejection of his ideas.

laws.name: Naïve Realism
laws.statement: People assume they see reality objectively and conclude that those who disagree must be uninformed, irrational, or biased.

sources.text: Robinson, R. J., Keltner, D., Ward, A. & Ross, L. (1995). "Actual versus assumed differences in construal: 'Naive realism' in intergroup perception and conflict." Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 68(3), p. 404.
Wikipedia's "Naïve realism (psychology)" article — supports the definition, the three tenets from Ross and Ward, the 1990s development, and links to the hostile media and bias blind spot findings.
Wikipedia's "Hostile media effect" article — supports the Vallone, Ross, and Lepper (1985) study in which opposing partisans each saw identical coverage as biased against them.

laws.name: The Actor-Observer Bias
laws.statement: People tend to attribute their own actions to the situation but others' identical actions to enduring disposition.

sources.text: Wikipedia's "Actor-observer asymmetry" article — supports the 1971 Jones & Nisbett origin, the situational-versus-dispositional definition, and Malle's 2006 meta-analytic challenge.
Bertram F. Malle (2006), "The Actor-Observer Asymmetry in Attribution: A (Surprising) Meta-Analysis" — supports the finding that the asymmetry is far weaker and more conditional than long assumed.

laws.name: The Rashomon Effect
laws.statement: Different witnesses to a single event produce contradictory yet sincerely held accounts shaped by their own subjective perspective.

sources.text: Wikipedia's "Rashomon effect" article — supports the definition of contradictory subjective accounts of one event, the origin in Kurosawa's 1950 film, and legal usage.
Encyclopaedia Britannica's entry on Kurosawa's film Rashomon — supports the 1950 film presenting a single event from multiple conflicting perspectives.

laws.name: The Environmental Kuznets Curve
laws.statement: As a nation's income grows, pollution first rises then falls, tracing an inverted-U curve, but the pattern is contested and fails for greenhouse gases.

sources.text: Grossman and Krueger's NBER working paper "Environmental Impacts of a North American Free Trade Agreement," reporting that sulfur dioxide and smoke rise then fall with per capita GDP — supports the original inverted-U finding.

Wikipedia's "Kuznets curve" article, defining the environmental Kuznets curve, its inverted-U form, and the major criticisms including the carbon-dioxide failure and pollution offshoring — supports the definition and contested status.

laws.name: The Heckscher-Ohlin Model
laws.statement: Countries export goods that intensively use their locally abundant factor of production and import goods intensive in their scarce factors.

sources.text: Wikipedia's "Heckscher-Ohlin model" article, defining the factor-endowment trade theory, its 1919/1933 origins, and the Leontief paradox — supports the theorem statement and empirical challenges.

Wikipedia's "Bertil Ohlin" article, confirming he developed the model with Eli Heckscher, published Interregional and International Trade in 1933, and won the 1977 Nobel — supports authorship and dates.

laws.name: The Lorentz Transformation
laws.statement: Space and time coordinates transform between inertial frames by the Lorentz transformation, mixing them so light's speed stays constant for all observers.

sources.text: Wikipedia's "Lorentz transformation" article, giving the equations, the Lorentz factor, the historical development by Lorentz, Poincaré, and Einstein, and the physical consequences — supports the definition and mechanism.

Encyclopaedia Britannica's "Lorentz transformations" entry, describing them as equations relating space and time coordinates of frames in relative motion, created by Lorentz in 1904 — supports the definition and origin.

laws.name: The Weibull Distribution
laws.statement: The Weibull distribution flexibly models time-to-failure, its shape parameter capturing decreasing, constant, or increasing failure rates over time.

sources.text: Wikipedia's "Weibull distribution" article, giving the definition, the shape-parameter hazard interpretation, reliability uses, and the Weibull/Fréchet/Rosin-Rammler history — supports the definition, mechanism, and origin.

The NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, stating the Weibull distribution is used extensively in reliability applications to model failure times — supports the reliability use and parameters.

laws.name: The No-Cloning Theorem
laws.statement: An arbitrary unknown quantum state cannot be copied exactly, because the linearity of quantum mechanics forbids any universal cloning device.

sources.text: The bibliographic record for Wootters and Zurek's "A single quantum cannot be cloned," Nature vol. 299 (1982), stating the linearity of quantum mechanics forbids amplifying an arbitrary polarization — supports the original theorem and its proof basis.

Wikipedia's "No-cloning theorem" article, stating an arbitrary unknown quantum state cannot be copied, crediting Wootters, Zurek, and Dieks (1982), and explaining the linearity-based proof — supports the statement, authorship, and mechanism.

laws.name: The CNN Effect
laws.statement: Real-time global news coverage of crises can pressure policymakers to act, especially on humanitarian intervention, though its power is disputed.

sources.text: Wikipedia's "CNN effect" article, defining the theory, dating its emergence to the 1990–91 Gulf War, and citing Baker's "real-time mode" and Robinson's two conditions — supports the definition, origin, and contested status.

The Internet Archive record for Piers Robinson's book The CNN Effect: The Myth of News, Foreign Policy and Intervention (Routledge, 2002), which frames the effect critically — supports the contested, qualified interpretation.

laws.name: The Freundlich Adsorption Isotherm
laws.statement: On a heterogeneous surface, the amount adsorbed grows as an empirical power law of gas pressure or solute concentration, without a saturation limit.

sources.text: Wikipedia's "Freundlich equation" article, giving the 1909 attribution, the power-law form, and its empirical heterogeneous-surface rationale and high-pressure failure — supports the statement and limits.
Wikipedia's "Herbert Freundlich" article, confirming his dates, nationality, and authorship of the adsorption work — supports the attribution.

laws.name: The Nernst Heat Theorem
laws.statement: For reactions among condensed phases, the entropy change approaches zero as the temperature approaches absolute zero.

sources.text: Wikipedia's "Nernst heat theorem" article, stating that the entropy change tends to zero as temperature tends to zero and its role in the third law — supports the statement and mechanism.
Wikipedia's "Walther Nernst" article, confirming his authorship of the heat theorem and third law and his 1920 Nobel Prize — supports the attribution.

laws.name: YAGNI
laws.statement: Build a capability when you actually need it, never when you merely foresee needing it.

sources.text: Fowler, M. (26 May 2015). "Yagni." martinfowler.com — the cost-of-build, cost-of-delay, cost-of-carry, cost-of-repair analysis, and the distinction between presumptive features and modifiability.
"You aren't gonna need it." Wikipedia — the Jeffries formulation and the dependency on refactoring, unit testing and continuous integration.

laws.name: The DRY Principle
laws.statement: Every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system.

sources.text: Hunt, A. & Thomas, D. (1999). The Pragmatic Programmer: From Journeyman to Master. Addison-Wesley. — the principle, in the wording quoted, and the repeated-'comment' example.
"Don't repeat yourself." Wikipedia — the canonical wording, the WET backronym, and the AHA / 'prefer duplication over the wrong abstraction' counterweights.

laws.name: The KISS Principle
laws.statement: Most systems work best if they are kept simple rather than made complicated, so simplicity should be a design goal and needless complexity avoided.

sources.text: "KISS principle." Wikipedia — the Kelly Johnson attribution and the field-repair anecdote, the 1960 U.S. Navy 'Project KISS' record, Johnson's comma-free wording, and the 1938 'keep it short and simple' antecedent.

laws.name: The Liskov Substitution Principle
laws.statement: An object of a superclass must be replaceable by an object of any subclass without breaking the program.

sources.text: Liskov, B. & Wing, J. (1994). "A Behavioral Notion of Subtyping." ACM Transactions on Programming Languages and Systems 16(6). — the formal statement of the substitution property.
Martin, R. C. (1996). "The Liskov Substitution Principle." Engineering Notebook, C++ Report. — the naming and the practitioner formulation.
"Liskov substitution principle." Wikipedia — the 1987 keynote, the Liskov–Wing formalisation, and the behavioural conditions on subtypes.

laws.name: The Law of Demeter
aliases: Only talk to your immediate friends
laws.statement: Each unit should talk only to its immediate friends, and never to strangers.

sources.text: "Law of Demeter." Wikipedia — Ian Holland's authorship at Northeastern in 1987, the Demeter Project naming, the formal statement of which methods may be called, and the documented criticisms.
Lieberherr, K. & Holland, I. (1989). "Assuring Good Style for Object-Oriented Programs." IEEE Software 6(5). — the law as published by the Demeter group.

laws.name: Knuth's Optimization Principle
aliases: Premature optimization is the root of all evil
laws.statement: We should forget about small efficiencies, say about 97% of the time: premature optimization is the root of all evil, yet we should not pass up our opportunities in that critical 3%.

sources.text: Knuth, D. E. (1974). "Structured Programming with go to Statements." ACM Computing Surveys 6(4), 261–301. — the passage, in full, at section 1.

Wikiquote: Donald Knuth — the full quotation with its surrounding sentences, the 1974 citation, and Knuth's later reference to it as Hoare's Dictum in "The Errors of TeX" (1989), noted there as a doubtful attribution.

laws.name: SOLID
aliases: The first five principles of object-oriented design
laws.statement: Five design principles (single responsibility, open–closed, Liskov substitution, interface segregation and dependency inversion) meant together to keep object-oriented code understandable and changeable.

sources.text: Martin, R. C. (2000). "Design Principles and Design Patterns." — the paper collecting the five principles.
"SOLID." Wikipedia — the five statements as usually quoted, Martin's 2000 paper, and Michael Feathers's coining of the acronym around 2004.

laws.name: The Single Responsibility Principle
laws.statement: There should never be more than one reason for a class to change.

sources.text: Martin, R. C. (2000). "Design Principles and Design Patterns." — the principle as first collected, with the payroll example.
"SOLID." Wikipedia — the canonical wording, 'there should never be more than one reason for a class to change', and its place in the set.

laws.name: Separation of Concerns
laws.statement: Study one aspect of a subject at a time, in isolation, even though the aspects are not truly independent. It is the only available technique for ordering one's thoughts effectively.

sources.text: Dijkstra, E. W. (1974). "On the Role of Scientific Thought." EWD447. — the coinage and the quoted qualification.
"Separation of concerns." Wikipedia — Dijkstra's 1974 coinage, and the protocol-stack, HTML/CSS/JS and aspect-oriented examples.

laws.name: The Principle of Least Astonishment
laws.statement: A component should behave the way most of its users already expect, so that using it produces no surprise.

sources.text: "Principle of least astonishment." Wikipedia — the statement, the 1967 PL/I Bulletin reference, the 1972 print formulation, the parseInt and keyboard-shortcut examples, and the audience-dependence qualification.

laws.name: The Bus Factor
laws.statement: The number of people who would have to vanish before a project stalls for want of anyone who knows how it works.

sources.text: "Bus factor." Wikipedia — the definition, the 1994 McLay instance, the 1995 and 2004 published appearances, the alternative names, and the GitHub study finding 65% of 133 projects at a bus factor of two or less.
Avelino, G., Passos, L., Hora, A. & Valente, M. T. (2016). "A Novel Approach for Estimating Truck Factors." IEEE ICPC. — the measurement of 133 GitHub projects.

laws.name: The Horn Effect
laws.statement: One bad trait colours the whole judgement: a person seen as failing in one respect is assumed to be failing in others.

sources.text: "Horn effect." Wikipedia — the definition, the devil's-horns etymology, the relation to the halo effect, and the cited attractiveness-and-sentencing findings.
Thorndike, E. L. (1920). "A Constant Error in Psychological Ratings." Journal of Applied Psychology 4(1), 25–29. — the original demonstration that ratings of separate traits move together.

laws.name: The Overconfidence Effect
laws.statement: People's confidence in their own judgements is reliably greater than the accuracy of those judgements.

sources.text: "Overconfidence effect." Wikipedia — the three-way distinction between overestimation, overplacement and overprecision, and the Adams & Adams (1960), Oskamp (1965), Svenson (1981), Kruger (1999), Taylor & Brown (1988) and Gigerenzer (1993) findings cited here.
Oskamp, S. (1965). "Overconfidence in case-study judgments." Journal of Consulting Psychology 29(3), 261–265. — confidence rising with information while accuracy does not.

laws.name: The Impostor Phenomenon
laws.statement: People who are demonstrably competent can persistently believe their success is a fraud they have not yet been found out for.

sources.text: Clance, P. R. & Imes, S. A. (1978). "The Impostor Phenomenon in High Achieving Women: Dynamics and Therapeutic Intervention." Psychotherapy: Theory, Research & Practice 15(3), 241–247. — the naming paper.

"Impostor syndrome." Wikipedia — the 1978 coinage and population, the phenomenon-not-syndrome distinction, the absence from DSM-5 and ICD-11, and the 2019 systematic review finding none of 62 studies assessed treatment efficacy.

laws.name: The Friedman Doctrine
aliases: The social responsibility of business is to increase its profits
laws.statement: A company's one social responsibility is to increase its profits for its owners, so long as it stays within the rules of the game: open and free competition, without deception or fraud.

sources.text: Friedman, M. (13 September 1970). "A Friedman Doctrine — The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits." The New York Times Magazine. — the essay, with the 'rules of the game' qualification.
"Friedman doctrine." Wikipedia — the 1970 essay and the earlier statement in Capitalism and Freedom (1962), the agency argument, and the stakeholder-theory and Duska criticisms cited here.
